### 15. The twelve signs of the Elect

**(1) The Great King.** "If a *dēnāvar* holds within the tree of the first,
the Great King, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he does not
like to stay long in one place, just as a king is free and does not always
stay in one place: at times he goes out on progress with his troops, fully
armed and equipped, and makes all evil beasts and enemies go into hiding.
Second, he is not grasping: wherever he goes, if he receives offerings he
does not keep them secretly for his own use, but hands them all to the
community. Third, he is chaste and guards against faults. He can keep
himself pure, and he also urges others who study and practise to keep
themselves pure. Fourth, he always keeps close to his own honoured teacher
and to those who have wisdom. From the foolish, who love idle talk and
quarrels, he keeps well away. Fifth, he always loves to live together with
the pure community. Wherever he goes, he does not leave the others to sleep
alone in a room of his own. Anyone who does this is called a sick man. Just
as a sick man in the world, troubled by his illness, always likes to be
alone and does not want to be near his family and friends, so is one who
does not love the community.

**(2) Wisdom.** "If a *dēnāvar* who keeps the precepts holds within the
nature of wisdom, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he always
loves to praise pure and wise people, and loves to meet with the pure and
wise community; his heart is glad, and he never tires of them. Second, if his
own root of wisdom and understanding is narrow and weak, he feels no envy
when he hears the wise words of the wise. Third, in all the work he has to
do, he always studies diligently and his heart is never slack. Fourth, he
himself always studies diligently at wisdom, skilful means and all good
conduct, and urges others to practise them with him. Fifth, he keeps the
prohibitions and precepts with care and does not break them, and if he
breaks one by mistake, he at once confesses it openly before the community
and repents.

**(3) Constant Victory.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of
victory, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he does not like
slander, flattery or spite, and keeps away from people like that. Second,
he does not like quarrels and commotion. If there is a quarrel he quickly
withdraws, and if someone comes and forces a quarrel on him, he can bear
it patiently. Third, if someone gives way in debate, he does not press his
advantage or gloat over it. Fourth, he does not speak rashly, or speak
without being asked. If someone comes with a question, he thinks it over
before answering, so that in the end the questioner is not shamed by what

**(4) Joy.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of joy, know that
this teacher has five signs. First, in all the prohibitions, precepts and
rules of conduct of the holy teaching he rejoices, one by one, and keeps
them with all his strength until the end of his life, never letting his
heart give them up. Second, he gladly and reverently keeps what the holy
ones laid down, one change of clothes a year and one meal a day, and does
not find it hard. Nor does he falsely claim that the holy ones made this
rule only as a temporary measure, misquoting scriptures and treatises to
say that one may eat twice, or that those who seek liberation need not keep
this precept. Third, he studies only the pure Law of his own school, and
does not go looking for other, corrupt teachings. Fourth, his heart is
always humble towards his fellow students, and he does not resent those above
him.
Fifth, if he holds a lower rank, he does not overstep it; if he holds the
highest place as head, he regards the community as himself and loves them
all without favouring anyone.

**(5) Diligence.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of
diligence, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he does not like
sleep that gets in the way of the work of the Way. Second, he always loves
reading and recitation, and spurs his heart on without slackening. When
fellow students teach him, he is especially glad and grateful, and does not
resent being taught. He is always diligent himself, and urges others to be
so too. Third, he always loves to expound the pure, true Law. Fourth, in
hymns, prayers and recitation, in chanting, copying, remembering and
reflecting, he lets no time go by wasted. Fifth, he keeps the prohibitions
and precepts firmly, without a lapse.

**(6) Truthfulness.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of
truthfulness, know that this teacher has five signs. First, all the
scriptures and teachings he speaks are true. He keeps wholly to the holy
teaching and does not proclaim it falsely: where something is, he says it
is; where it is not, he says it is not. Second, his heart and intention are
always at one with the truth, and he does not wait for outside events to
set his rule by. Third, the precepts and practices he keeps are always
true, whether he is alone or with others; his heart is not divided. Fourth,
he is always settled in his heart towards his own teacher, serves him with
all his strength, and has no doubts, until the end of his life, with no
other intention. Fifth, he urges his fellow students to practise, and
guides everyone with truthful conduct.

**(7) The Believing Heart.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of
a believing heart, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he
believes the meaning of the Two Principles; his heart is pure and without
doubt; he leaves the darkness and follows the light, as the holy ones have
said. Second, his heart is settled in all the precepts and rules. Third, he
does not dare to add or take away a single sentence or a single word of the
holy scriptures. Fourth, he is glad of everything that benefits the true
Law and helps it with his heart. If he sees it harmed or troubled by the
demons, he feels compassion and shares in the grief. Fifth, he does not
falsely spread the faults of others, nor slander, carry tales or speak with
a forked tongue. His nature is always gentle, honest and undivided.

know that this teacher has five signs. First, his heart is always kind and
good, and no rage arises in it. Second, he is always glad and no anger
rises in him. Third, he bears no grudge anywhere. Fourth, his heart is not
hard and his mouth speaks no coarse or evil words. He always speaks gently,
in a way that pleases everyone. Fifth, whether inside (the community) or
outside it, if evils and troubles come to meet him and insult him, he can
bear them all, gladly and without resentment.

**(9) Straightforwardness.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of
straightforwardness, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he is not
bound by the passions; he is glad of himself, pure and straightforward.
Second, in the Law, whatever is asked of him, great or small, he receives
it with respect, and answers gladly and well. Third, with his fellow
students he does not argue back, or defend his own shortcomings and grow
angry. Fourth, his words and deeds match; his heart is always honest; he
does not go looking for others' faults and so start quarrels. Fifth, if
brothers within the Law have hearts that differ from the holy teaching, he
at once keeps away from them, does not live with them or keep close to
them, and does not join forces with them to trouble the good community.

**(10) Merit.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature of merit, know
that this teacher has five signs. First, nothing he says harms anyone. He
always uses a kind heart and skilful means, and can make everyone glad.
Second, his heart is always pure; he holds nothing against others, nor does
he do wrong so as to make others angry. His speech is always gentle and
free of the four faults (of speech). Third, he is not jealous of those above
him or those below. Fourth, he does not take scriptures, treatises or
disciples away from the community. Wherever he goes, he is glad to stay in
whatever pure dwelling there is, and does not choose one that is fine and
pleasant. Fifth, he always loves to teach and admonish all people, with
skill and wisdom, so that they practise the true Way.

**(11) Concord of One Heart.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the nature
of a heart in concord, know that this teacher has five signs. First, in the
wisdom, skilful means and conduct taught by the masters of the Law, the
teachers and bishops, he follows every point and does not dare to change
it, and does not insist on his own views. Second, he always loves concord
and living together with the community, and does not want to live apart,
each pursuing different plans. Third, his heart is in concord with the
others, and because of this concord the offerings received together become
merit for all. Fourth, he always has the respect, offerings, love and praise
of the hearers. Fifth, he always loves to keep far from frivolity,
joking and laughter, and from quarrels, and guards well what is within and
without, keeping the two natures in concord.

**(12) Light Within and Without.** "If a pure *dēnāvar* holds within the
nature of light in both, know that this teacher has five signs. First, he
pulls up the filthy heart and does not let it be greedy or lustful, so
that his light-nature is always free. Faced with women, he can see them as
unreal, and is not held back by any form, like a bird flying high that does
not fall into the net. Second, he does not form special, close friendships
with the hearers, nor cling to the hearers' houses as though they were his
own. If he sees losses or troubles in a lay household outside the Law, his
heart is not grieved; if they gain some profit or happy event, his heart is
unchanged too. Third, walking or standing, sitting or lying down, he does not
pamper the body of flesh by seeking fine soft clothes, bedding, food,
medicines, birds, horses or carriages to make it splendid. Fourth, he always
remembers the day of the end of life, with its dangers, pains and distress.
He always keeps impermanence and the King of Equal Justice before his eyes,
and never for a moment lets them go. Fifth, he himself is gentle and
yielding. He does not trouble his brothers or friends, or make them angry,
nor does he hope to prove anything against them and give others a bad name.
He can always keep his heart steady and abide in the pure Law.

### 16. The Envoy's charge

### 16. The Envoy's charge

"Such as these are called the jewelled trees of the twelve kings of light.
For your sake I have brought them here from the world of light, where joy
is constant. I wish to plant these trees in your pure community. You men and
women of excellent form and good wisdom must each plant these trees in your
pure hearts and make them grow, like good ground free of sand and salt,
where one seed sown yields ten thousand, and so on, to a number without
measure. Now, if you want to win the pure fruit of the supreme great light,
you must all adorn yourselves with these jewelled trees and make them
complete. Why? Because, good sons, by the fruit of these trees you will
escape the four hardships and every kind of bodily existence, leave birth
and death behind, be victorious for ever, and come to the place of peace and
joy."

### 17. The hymn of the teachers

When the teachers (慕闍) in the assembly heard this scripture, they leapt for
joy and marvelled at what they had never heard before. The gods and good
spirits, bounded and unbounded, the kings, the
ministers, the men and women, and the four orders of the community,
countless beyond number, heard this scripture and were all filled with joy,
and every one of them was able to set his heart on the supreme Way, like
plants meeting the spring sun: all of them grew, flowered, bore fruit and
ripened, except for rotten roots, which could not grow.

Then the teachers bowed their heads to the Envoy of Light, knelt upright
with their hands joined, and said:

"You alone are the Great Holy One, alone honoured in the three worlds, the
compassionate father and mother of all beings, the great guide of the three
worlds, the great healing lord of all who have life. You are the wondrous
space that can hold all forms; the high heaven that embraces everything;
the true ground that bears true fruit; the great sea of ambrosia for all
beings; the vast fragrant mountain of all treasures; the diamond pillar that
bears up the multitude; the skilful, wise helmsman on the great sea; the
compassionate hand that rescues from the fiery pit; the giver of constant
life in the midst of death; the nature within the light-nature of beings;
the bright gate of release from all the strong prisons of the three
worlds."

The teachers spoke again to the Envoy of Light and said: "Only the One
Great Light can praise the holy virtue. With our tongues of flesh and our
poor wisdom we cannot know even a small part in ten million of the merit and
wisdom of the Tathāgata. Now we stir up our small virtue and small wisdom
and offer a little of our meaning in praise of the Holy One's great mercy.
We pray only that the Great Holy One will look on us with compassion, and
take away and destroy the heavy sins of ignorance that we have committed

that we overcome our enemies. By these wondrous robes and crowns of every
form, adorn us, so that we are complete. By this pattern of light of the

sweet food of a hundred flavours, satisfy us, so that we are free of hunger
and thirst. By this countless wondrous music, delight us, so that we are
free of sorrow and trouble. By these many rare treasures, provide for us,
so that we become rich. By this net of light, draw us out of the great sea
and set us in the jewelled ship.

special marks and beauty of the Great Holy One, and have heard the wondrous

our hearts have been opened and awakened, we have received the
wish-granting pearl, and in its majestic light we have been able to walk

reached the world of light, and receive joy without measure. We pray only

whether it sees or hears it, may, like the holy ones of old and like us
today, hear the Law with joy, have its heart opened and awakened, receive it
with reverence on bowed head, and have no doubts."

content.content: 安住淨法。如是等者。名為十二明王寶樹。我從常樂光明世界。為汝等故。持至於此。欲以此樹栽於汝等清淨眾中。汝等上相善慧男女。當須各自於清淨心栽植此樹。令使增長。猶如上好無砂鹵地。種一收萬。如是展轉。至無量數。汝等今者。若欲成就無上大明清淨果者。皆當莊嚴如是寶樹。令得具足。何以故。汝等善子。依此樹菓得離四難及諸有身。出離生死。究竟常勝。至安樂處。爾時會中諸慕闍等。聞說是經。歡喜踴躍。歎未曾有。諸天善神。有礙無礙。及諸國王。群臣士女。四部之眾。無量無數。聞是經已。皆大歡喜。悉能發起無上道心。猶如卉木值遇陽春。無不滋茂敷花結菓得成熟。唯除敗根不能滋長。時慕闍等。頂禮明使。長跪叉手。作如是言。唯有大聖。三界獨尊。普是眾生慈悲父母。亦是三界大引道師。亦是含靈大醫療主。亦是妙空能容眾相。亦是上天包羅一切。亦是實地能生實果。亦是眾生甘露大海。亦是廣大眾寶香山。亦是任眾金剛寶柱。亦是巨海巧智船師。亦是火坑慈悲救手。亦是死中與常命者。亦是眾生明性中性。亦是三界諸牢固獄解脫明門諸慕闍等。又啟明使。作如是言。唯大明一尊能歎聖德。非是我等肉舌劣智稱讚如來功德智惠。千萬分中能知少分。我今勵己小德小智。舉少微意歎聖弘慈。唯願大聖。垂怜愍心。除捨我等曠劫已來無明重罪。令得銷滅。我等今者不敢輕慢。皆當奉持無上寶樹。使令具足緣此法。水洗濯我等諸塵重垢。令我明性常得清淨。緣此法藥及大神呪。呪療我等多劫重病。悉得除愈。緣此智惠堅牢鎧伏。被串我等。對彼怨敵。皆得強勝。緣此微妙眾相衣冠。莊嚴我等。皆得具足。緣此本性光明模樣。印𮃞我等。不令散失。緣此甘膳百味飲食。飽足我等。離諸飢渴。緣此無數微妙音樂。娛樂我等。離諸憂煩。緣此種種奇異珍寶。給施我等。令得富饒。緣此明網。於大海中撈渡我等。安置寶船。我等今者上相福厚。得覩大聖殊特相好。又聞如上微妙法門。蠲除我等煩惱諸穢。心得開悟。納如意珠。威光得履缶道過去諸聖不可稱數。皆依此門得離四難及諸有身。至光明界。受無量樂。唯願未來一切明性得遇如是光明門者。若見若聞。亦如往聖及我今日。聞法歡喜。心得開悟。尊重頂受。不生疑慮。時諸大眾。聞是經已。如法信受。歡喜奉行。校注祆祅電雷電雷電

pure hearts and make them grow, like good ground free of sand and salt,
where one seed sown yields ten thousand, and so on, to a number without

and death behind, be victorious for ever, and come to the place of peace and
joy."

Bei Beurteilung der Umschreibung in lateinische Buchstaben bitte 
ich zu berücksichtigen, daß die hier gewählte Transkriptionsart eine Rück- 
schreibung in die Originalschrift leicht und jederzeit ermöglichen sollte. 
Der Umschreibung in hebräische (wie von Salemann angeraten), arabische 
und syrische Lettern stehen Bedenken anderer Art entgegen, auf die für 
dieses Mal einzugehen zu weit führen würde. Das Richtige und Einfachste 
wäre die Wiedergabe in der Originalschrift — wenn derartige Lettern vor- 
handen wären.

stücke M. 470, 473 ließ sieh noch nieht ermitteln. Wahrscheinlich wird 
sich auch noch ein oder das andere Fragment später finden.

input.content:
---
title: "The Šābuhragān: the Turfan fragments on the end of the world"
text: true
group: scripture
order: 90
summary: Mani's own Middle Persian book for Shapur I, in the fragments found at Turfan, describing the Last Judgement, the great fire and the gods' final gathering of the light.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 475, M 477, M 482, M 472, M 470, M 473 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 10–25. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his Middle Persian in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

The *Šābuhragān* ("the book for Shapur") is the one book Mani wrote in
Middle Persian, the language of the Persian court, and dedicated to the
Sasanian king Shapur I (reigned 240–270). Al-Bīrūnī quotes it on Mani's
place among the prophets ([see that page](al-biruni-quotations.html)).
At Turfan, in Chinese Turkestan, the German expeditions found leaves of a
Manichaean book whose red running heads read *Šābuhragān*. They come from
its part on the end of the world.

The fragments open with the Last Judgement in a form close to Matthew 25,
with additions not found in the Gospel. A god called *Xradešahr* (the
"Lord of the world of wisdom", Jesus as judge) sets the righteous on his
right and the evildoers on his left. Then the world is broken up, the gods
who hold it together let it go, the great fire burns for 1,468 years, and
the last of the light is drawn up to the sun and moon and into the New
Paradise, while the damned are shut away for ever. An Arabic summary of the
same passage survives in al-Nadīm's *Fihrist*, which Müller printed beside
the Turfan text.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's
first edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition. Müller called his
German "a first attempt", and modern readings differ in many places. Gaps
in the leaves are marked [ … ]. Words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?) here. The running heads in red or black are given in small capitals
as headings. Square-bracketed words inside the text are Müller's
restorations.

## The translation

### M 475, front. Head: "[The coming] of the Son of Man"

… he, the righteous; they will say: "Our Lord, if you [ … ] before you we
would say it." To them *Xradešahr* the god will give answer: "Look at me,
and be glad. The evil that has been done to you, I will judge it for you,
and I will hold an assembly (?) [ … ]. All that you wish to [ … ] to me, I
know it."

Then he will bless them, and set their hearts at rest; he will set them on
his right side, and the gods (angels) will guard them in joy.

And he will part the evildoers from the righteous, and set them on his left
side. He will curse them, and he will say: " [ … ] may it be [ … ] the sin
that you have done [ … ] violent (?) [ … ]" (the rest cannot be read).

### M 475, back. Head: "On the Judgement"

[He will say] to the righteous who stand on the right: " [ … ] For I was
hungry and thirsty, and you gave me food and drink. I was naked, and you
clothed me. I was sick (?), and you made me well. I was bound, and you set
me free. I was a prisoner, and you redeemed me. And I was a stranger and a
wanderer (?), and you took me into your house."

[Then] they, the righteous, the helpers, will do him reverence, and then
they will say: "Lord, you are a god and immortal, whom desire and craving
(?) do not overcome; you do not hunger or thirst, and grief does not come
upon you. When was it that we [did] you this service?"

Then the Lord will say to them: "What you have done [ … ] you have done it
to me [ … ] to you

### M 477, front. Head: "And the decision"

[ … ] I will give you the reward of Paradise." He will give them great joy.

Then he will say to them, the evildoers, who stand on the left side: "You
evildoers, (full of) sensuality (?) and lust, desire, evil doing and
worldliness: you have been [ … ] by you I am [ … ]. For I was hungry and
thirsty, and you gave me no food or drink. And I was naked, and you did not
clothe me. And I was sick (?), and you did not make me well. I was a
prisoner and a stranger, and you did not take me into your house."

They, the evildoers, will say to him: "Our god and lord, when was it that
you were so unhappy, and were not set free by us?" The Lord will say to
them: "What you [did not do] to the righteous, you [did not do] to me
[ … ]

### M 477, back. Head: "The two great principles"

"And you are sinners, for you have been violent enemies of the righteous;
by you they have not been forgiven [ … ] sinfulness [ … ]." He will charge
the angels over them, the sinners. They will take them and [throw them]
into hell.

And when the Lord, the god, guards the world, then they will measure (?)
day, month and year; and lust and craving will come near, and grief and
[ … ] and need [ … ] wind, water and fire in the world [ … ]

### M 482, front. Head: "Šābuhragān"

(Only scattered words survive: "they will pass", "their own seed", "they
will say", "the evil dead", "we keep in …".)

*In red: "Ended is the Coming of the Life-giver."*

*After a space of four lines, a new red title: "This raising up (?) …"*

[ … ] *Xradešahr* the god [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 482, back. Head: "The two principles of …"

[ … ] this earth and heaven [ … ] the whole world [ … ] the righteous to
[ … ] and trees [ … ] and the creatures with [ … ] the earth from the
world [ … ] wind, water and fire from the lowest earth, (on) which the
*Mānbed* (the house-guardian) and the god who raises the wind stand, will
be destroyed; and that new world, and the dwelling (?) of the demons
[ … ] *Šahrāpur* the god will show (?) [ … ] Paradise [ … ] god [ … ]

### M 472, front. Head: "Šābuhragān"

[ … ] that light [ … ] raises up (?), and the ship (?) [ … ] and they will
make the heaven, and the highest heaven, which on that lowest, wholly
[ … ] he will seize, and from [ … ] he will be washed (?).

Then the sun-god, from the vehicle (?) of the sun, [will … ] the whole
earth, and a call (?) will be called. And the gods who in every heaven and
every earth are guardians of the house, the village, the clan, the
district and the watch, and who keep the world in order, will not call
*Āz* and Ahriman and the demons and the *parīg*s; all [ … ] will become
[ … ] the *mazan*s and [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 472, back. Head (in black): "On the gathering together"

Then that god the *Mānbed*, who stands on that lowest earth and keeps the
earths in order, and that god who raises the wind, with whom he raises
wind, water and fire, and that god the *Wisbed*, who stands on this earth
and holds the *mazan* Aždahāg (?) bound in [ … ], will go (?) together
from the helpers to Paradise. Then over the whole earth those four
deposits (?) of the dwelling of the demons, one above the other, purified,
they will lay (?) together [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 470, front. Head: "[ … ] the great fire"

[ … a thousand] four hundred and sixty-eight years [ … ] they will turn
[ … ] and that might and [ … ] of this light, and of the gods who are on
the earth and in the heaven of the whole world. And *Āz* and the demons
(will be) struck down and done away with. That which is in it, (in) the
hell (?), from it brightness will come forth (?). He will become pure, and
will be raised up (?) to the sun and the moon, and will become of the
substance of the god Ohrmizd; and from the sun and the moon they will be
raised up (?) together to Paradise. And the god Ohrmizd from the upper
(northern) region, and the god of the realm of light from the east, and the
god of the new world from the south, and the sun-god from the western
region, [ … ] the places [ … ] together over that [ … ] the new Paradise
[ … ] the hell (?) [ … ] will look (?), and they [the righteous] who [ … ]
in Paradise [ … ] will settle (?).

### M 470, back

[ … ] the gods will come, and they will stand [around] the hell (?); [the
sinners] in the hell [ … ] and will turn about and [ … ] suffer. And they,
the righteous, [ … ] now also this fire, sun and moon [ … ].

And those sinners, when in [ … ] they turn about, they will look (?) up,
and will know the righteous, and will make requests (?) to them, and will
say: "May your goodness [ … ] be over us [ … ] this burning [ … ] comes
upon us [ … ] our greed [ … ] you are, and you [ … ] I have become …"

### M 473, front

[ … ] of the moon and the [planets] and the stars, a great sign will
appear.

Then the Lord, the god, the first, he, the man, the creature, the first,
mind and knowledge [ … ] the second (?), mind and knowledge [ … ] the
original (?) [ … ] will send that [ … ] the last, near to [ … ] *Xradešahr*
[ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 473, back

[ … ] they will receive (them), and the greedy man, [ … ] the sinners and
[ … ] will repent. And then the Lord, the god, will send the angels to the
east and to the west, and they will go, and the man with the helpers, and
those sinners [ … ] in the midst [ … ] before the Lord (the rest is lost).

### M 473b, back

[ … ] and a great call will sound (?), and the whole world (will receive)
the news [ … ]. The gods who in the heavens and earths of the whole world
are guardians of the house, the village, the clan, the district and the
watch, and callers (?) of the demons, will praise that Lord, *Xradešahr*;
and men in the world will become rulers [ … ] the demons will come before
him [ … ] (do) reverence [ … ] command (the rest is lost).

### M 473b, front

[ … ] and they say: "Our [ … ] of the gods I am [ … ] with this counsel
which we [ … ] sent (?) to man; all [ … ]." They will walk in sinfulness
and craving; and the righteous man who will not believe in the religion
will also join them. And at the time when there is such wealth in the
world [ … ] earth and heaven and [ … ] (the rest is lost).

## Al-Nadīm's summary of the same passage

Müller printed beside M 470 the German of an Arabic summary of this part of
the book, from al-Nadīm's *Fihrist* (10th century), as translated by
Kessler. In English:

"[Mani teaches:] Then the First Man comes from the world of the Pole Star
(the north), and the Envoy from the east, and the Great Builder from the
south, and the Living Spirit from the world of the west, and they look upon
the great new building, which is the new Paradise, going round that hell
and looking down into it. Then the righteous come from Paradise to this
light and settle in it. Then they hasten to the meeting-place of the gods
and stand around this hell. Then they look upon the sinners, how they turn
this way and that in hell, wander about and sink ever deeper. But the hell
can do the righteous no harm. When these sinners catch sight of the
righteous, they beg them and humble themselves before them; but they answer
them only with replies that do them no good, that is, with reproaches, and
the sinners feel only greater remorse, grief and sorrow. In this state they
remain for all eternity."

## Notes to this edition

- **The order of the leaves** is Müller's. He found that M 475, M 477,
  M 482 and M 472 follow one another, because the red headings had printed

---
title: "Mani's Gospel and Epistles: the Turfan fragments"
text: true
group: scripture
order: 15
summary: The opening words of Mani's Living Gospel and quotations from his Epistles, in Middle Persian leaves from Turfan.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 17, M 733 and M 731 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 25–33. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his Middle Persian in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

Mani wrote his *Living Gospel* in twenty-two parts, one for each letter of
the Syriac alphabet, and many letters to his churches, which were later
collected as the *Epistles*. Neither survives. Among the Turfan leaves,
F. W. K. Müller found in 1904 a page that quotes the opening of the
Gospel, with Mani's own words "I, Mani, the apostle of Jesus the Friend",
and two damaged leaves of extracts from the Epistles.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Müller's first edition
of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first attempt".
Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked (?);
square-bracketed words inside the text are his restorations. Headings in
the manuscripts are given as headings here.

## The translation

### M 17: from the Living Gospel

**Front.** *Blue heading: "The ālaf is taught (?)".*

*In red:* The virgin light, the head of all excellences;

*second column:* and [about the speakers] and the hearers of the famous
(holy) word.

*After a large space, in red:* Praised has been, and praised will be, the
holy religion, *in black:* by the power of the Father, by the praise of the
Mother [ … ]

*Second column:* May there be praise and glory (?) to the Father and to the
Son and to the Spirit, the holy one, and [ … ]

**Back.** *Heading: "… of Mani". Second heading: "From the Gospel".*

[ … ] is taught (?), and the food of truth is offered (?).

*Second column:* [ … ] then all that is, and all that was and will be,
stands by his power.

*After a large space:* I, Mani, the apostle of Jesus the Friend, in the
love of the Father, the god [ … ] of the famous (holy) [ … ] from him came
[ … ]

*Second column, in red:* The blessed will receive this offering; the wise
will know; the strong will put on the goodness of those who know [ … ]

### M 733: extracts from the Epistles and the Gospel

*A damaged fragment of a larger leaf; one side is torn away with loss of
text.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] oath, oath [ … ] oath [ … ].

And in the Epistle of the [ … ]-āstagān he says: [ … ] (the words cannot be
made out).

And in the Epistle of Hatā he says: [ … ] night and day [ … ] he asks
[ … ] he stands [ … ] by that [ … ] of the Life-giver [ … ].

And in the Gospel of the Living he says: "On the earth and [ … ]"

**Back (?).** (Müller gave no translation of this side. It contains the
words "brothers" and "helper": "[ … ] and I am the helper of all of you
[ … ] I say that this is my own [ … ]".)

### M 731: extracts from letters

*A fragment of a small octavo leaf. Below: from the Epistle of M[esvan].*

**Front.** [ … ] and to admonish the disciples. Five men of the worldly he
brings with them [ … ]; he says: "[ … ] may it not be." To the hearers he
says: "Let no one make you faint-hearted because you are in the world, for
you are friends of the friends [ … ]"

**Back.** [ … ] head of the brothers and sisters, plain [ … ]

*(One line left empty.)*

From the Epistle of M[esvan] on the two bodies. He says: "For myself and
for you, we long for our own place, and I will lead you on the way. This
goodness which you have received, with one [ … ] in truth, leads you there.
With clothing for one year and food for one day, and in all [ … ]"

## Notes to this edition

- **"The ālaf is taught (?)"** (M 17, Müller: *’arab nicihed*): Müller
  compared a heading in the St Petersburg fragment, "The Gospel of ālaf is
  taught … the Gospel of tau is taught", and the reports that Mani's
  Gospel had twenty-two parts named after the letters of the alphabet. He
  left the reading open.
- **"Jesus the Friend"** (M 17, *’ariyāmān*): Müller connected the word
  with the Avestan *airyaman*, "friend". Augustine says that all Mani's
  letters began "Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ".
- **The Epistle of Hatā** (M 733) is one of the letters in al-Nadīm's list
  (Flügel, *Mani*, pp. 76 and 104).
- **"M[esvan]"** (M 731): the manuscript has only *M…*; Müller suggested
  *Mesvan* (?) as the name of the addressee.
- **"Clothing for one year and food for one day"** (M 731) is the rule of
  the Elect that al-Bīrūnī reports: Mani "forbade them to acquire any
  property except food for one day and dress for one year".

---
title: "The building of the world: a Turfan cosmogony"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 60
summary: A Middle Persian account of how the Living Spirit fixed the planets, built the sun and moon as ships of light, and raised the heavens, earths, walls and pillars of the cosmos.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 98 and M 99 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 37–43. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his Middle Persian in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

This is one of the longest Manichaean accounts of the making of the world
to survive in an Iranian language. It comes from two leaves of a
Middle Persian book found at Turfan. A god, who is not named in what
survives but is the Living Spirit (the demiurge), binds the powers of
darkness in the sky, builds the sun and moon from the light that has been
purified out of the mixture, and sets up the layered heavens and earths,
with their walls, gates, pillars, ditches and prisons, to hold the demons
and to drain the light upwards. The blue running heads, which belong with
the text that follows them, read "To me, the child of Jesus" and "The
writing of the new and the …".

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. Where Müller notes that the
scribe corrected a word, the correction is followed silently.

## The translation

### M 98, first page. Blue heading: "To me, the child of Jesus"

[ … ] he fastened the seven planets, and he bound and fettered the two
dragons, and tied them up above on that lowest heaven; and so that they
should turn (it) at the call, he charged two angels above, a male and a
female.

Then he led them up to the border and the height of the light. And from
wind and light, water and fire, which had been purified out of the
mixture, he made two vehicles (?) of light: that of the sun, of fire and
light, with five walls, of ether, wind, light, water and fire, and twelve
gates, five houses, three thrones and five soul-gathering angels, in the
fiery wall; and that (vehicle) of the moon-god, of wind and water, with
five walls, of ether, wind, light, fire and water, and fourteen gates,
five houses, three thrones and five soul-gathering angels, in the watery
wall. These he made and set in order. He clothed them within.

### M 98, second page. Blue heading: "The writing of the new and the …"

Then he clothed the sun-god, from the same purifying, in three garments,
of wind, water and fire; and what had been purified (out) sank (?) down to
the earth of darkness.

And to praise above the great mystery (?), the new Paradise, he filled (?)
those five [ … ] of death and made them whole (?); and, corresponding (?)
to the heavens, he drew out (?) and laid down (?) above the earth of
darkness four deposits (?), one deadly and dark, one fiery, one watery,
one above the other.

And he raised one wall along (the edge of) the earth of light, to the
east, the south below and the west, and joined it back (?) to the earth
of light. He made another great earth, and laid it down over the deposits;
and over it he made the *Mānbed* (the house-guardian) the commanding god.
And on that same earth, within, (he made) another wall, beyond (?) the
east, south and west, and in those same three regions three pillars and
five crowns (?) (the rest is destroyed).

### M 99, third page. Blue heading: "Which is the least in splendour"

[ … ] the west to the western pillar; and the second from the western
pillar to the southern pillar; and the third from the southern pillar to
the eastern pillar; and the fourth from the eastern pillar to the wall,
the beginning, which is in the east; and the fifth, the great one, from
the east to the western pillar.

And (he made) an earth, great and firm, with twelve gates that correspond
(?) to the gates of the heavens; and on that same earth, round about, he
made four walls and three ditches; and in the innermost ditch he fastened
(?) the demons.

And (he set) the lowest heaven above its head, and so that his hand might
keep the heaven in order round about from there, he set up seven pillars
within; and Mānbed the god laid down that great earth upon the pillars and
the crowns (?) and the two walls; then (?) [ … ] to the east, the south
(the rest is destroyed).

### M 99, fourth page. Blue heading: "And all the …"

[ … ] and to the west, over the furthest wall, and to the north, in the
earth of light, he set (it) in order. And over that great earth (he made)
the *mazaman* earth (?); and below the ditches, two other mixed earths.
The door of all [ … ] he made, to lead up much wind, water [and fire].

And round the earth he set in order one wall with four gates. And in the
four regions he set four angels, who hold up the lowest heaven,
corresponding (?) to and dressed like those above.

And to tear away (?) the darkness of the four regions, he made twelve
hells, three in each region. And below them, round about, (he made) a
rampart (?) because of the sea; and on that same rampart (?) he set up a
prison because of the risings (?) of the *mazan*s.

Then over the face of the earth, mountains [ … ] (the rest is destroyed).

## Notes to this edition

- **The two vehicles** (M 98): Müller compares Augustine, *On Heresies*
  46: the Manichaeans say the moon was made of good water and the sun of
  good fire. Here the sun is of fire and light and the moon of wind and
  water.
- **"Soul-gathering angels"**: Müller compares Bar Hebraeus, who reports
  that the Good One made two great ships in the sky, the sun and the moon,
  in which he gathers the souls of men.
- **The heavens and earths** (M 99): Müller compares al-Nadīm: "He built
  ten heavens and eight earths, and charged one angel to carry the heavens
  and another to hold up the earths." The four angels who hold the lowest
  heaven correspond to these.
- **The two last leaves** of the same quire contain a hymn in praise of
  Mani in couplets, which Müller only sampled: "A messenger came from the
  Paradise of light, of shining name, the chosen one, the god Mār Mānī."
- ***Mānbed*** is the Persian title, "master of the house", of one of the
  Living Spirit's five sons.
- ***mazan*** (M 99): giant demons; the word is related to Mazandaran,
  the land of demons in Iranian legend.

input.content:
---
title: "Hymns and prayers from a Turfan hymnbook (M 4)"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 62
summary: Two double leaves of a Parthian and Middle Persian hymnbook, with hymns on the last days, body and soul and the soul's going out, Mani's hymn "I have come forth from the land of Babel", and prayers to the angels.
original_language: Parthian and Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan manuscript M 4 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 49–59. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

M 4 is two double leaves (eight pages) of a Manichaean hymnbook from
Turfan. Red rubrics tell the cantor which hymn to have sung next ("Let him
have sung the hymn of …") and mark where each cycle ends. Most hymns are
in Parthian; the prayers to the angels at the end invoke Jacob, Raphael,
Michael, Gabriel and Sarael, and ask blessing on "the whole church of the
province of Khorasan".

The best-known piece is a hymn spoken in Mani's own voice: "I have come
forth from the land of Babel … to call a call in the world." Müller set
beside it al-Bīrūnī's report of Mani's words about himself, and a Mandaean
hymn of the Envoy of Light: "A call have I raised in the world."

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. Rubrics are given in
italics.

## The translation

### Page 1

*Red heading of the page: "Let him have sung (the hymns) of the last
days."*

*In red: "Let him have sung the hymn of Body and Soul."*

[ … ] rest, good deed of the garden (?): may you become for me rest and a
good deed. Come again; may you dwell in me; may I become one who praises
(?) your good deed.

*In red: "Ended are the hymns of Body and Soul."*

*(Three lines left empty.)*

*"Let him have sung the hymn of the Last Days (*frašegird*)."*

Heaven's command and earth's answer (?) [ … ] your kingdom [ … ] the word
to the Lord. Let us call (?) on the gods who will save us from this time of
sin, from the oppression of the world and the unbelievers. O angels and
guides (?), save us from every shame and hardship (?). This time has come
[ … ]

### Page 2

*Red heading of the page: "Ended is the …"*

[ … ] as the Saviour (Mani) has written.

*In red: "Ended is the hymn of the Last Days."*

*(One line left empty.)*

*In red: "Let him have sung the hymn of the … (*mōqarānīg*)."*

I am a hearer (?), a favoured one (?),
for I have come forth from the land of Babel.
I have come forth from the land of Babel,
and I have been set at the gate (?) of truth.

I am a singer (?), a hearer (?),
who have gone out from the land of Babel.
I have gone out from the land of Babel,
to call a call in the world.

You gods, I will beseech you all:
forgive me my sin, in mercy.

*In red: "Ended is the hymn."*

*(One line left empty.)*

*In red: "Let him have sung: 'United (?) is the friend of the shining
ones'."*

United (?) is the friend of the shining ones with peace (?); I give
strength and [ … ]

*(There may be a gap between pages 2 and 3.)*

### Page 3

*Red heading of the page: "Let him have sung (the hymn) of the going
out."*

World of rest, you are worthy of the teaching (?). O you, soul of light, I
will give you much counsel, so that you may find salvation.

Come, souls, to this ship of light! My soul, most glorious, [ … ], where
have you gone? Turn back again!

Awake, soul of splendour, from the slumber of drunkenness in which you
have fallen asleep [ … ]. I will have you adorned. Follow (me) to the place
of the earth praised in prayer (?), where you were from the beginning.

From lust and greed, and from the burning fire [ … ] soul [ … ].

A messenger has come from Paradise, a herald (?) of the glories.

*In red: "Ended is the middle of the soul-hymns."*

*In red: "Let him have sung the hymns of the going out."*

I have been set up [ … ]

### Page 4

*Red heading: "Ended is (the hymn) of Body and Soul."*

[ … ] in this noble, divine (form) I saw the Saviour, when, smiling, he
spoke to me. There came to me (the message?) that I have been chosen. Free
from oppression, (light) will shine on me. He has made order [ … ] my
heart (?) [ … ] of my life. Free me from hardship and oppression on this
day of the going out.

May you come, my Saviour, in praise, life-giving (?) god, Mār Mānī, among
the three sons of God. Remember, kind god, this son of insight, the
hearer, the troubled soul who has given you answer.

God who does good, remember me: my thought was on the day of the going
out. Come, god, look on me: (be) my help in this time [ … ]

*In red: "Ended are the hymns of the going out."*

*(Probably a gap here.)*

### Page 5

*Red heading: "Bar Simus."*

[ … ] assembly, the god Mihr, the deliverer and merciful one, with good
Frēdōn and all the angels, may they protect and guard the holy religion,
the blessed leader (the head of the church), the lord of excellent name.

Shining sun, unwounded (?) god, with the Mother of the Living, deity,
together with the five angels and the twelve: may they all be praised by
the holy church.

New blessing and new victory come from the god Zurwān upon the glories and
angels, the spirits of this world, so that it may receive the holy
religion and become its watcher within and without, helper and protector.

I call on the angels, the strong and mighty, Raphael, Michael, Gabriel and
Sarael, that they may protect us from every adversity and free us from the
wicked Ahriman. I revere [ … ]

### Page 6

*Black heading: "Prayer."*

[ … ] the god Jacob the angel, with the glories, the powers and the good
spirits, who may protect us themselves with strong power. May they help
(?) us themselves within and without.

I confess (?) in joy the strong power of Jacob the angel, the leader of
the angels. Receive, strong one, from the whole holy church every new
blessing and praise.

Joy and new welfare come from the god Zurwān; blessing and new gladness
from the rays and the angels. May he strengthen (?) the glories and spirits
over you; may he lead us ourselves on this way of welfare.

New strength come from Jacob the angel, new [ … ] from all the angels. May
he strengthen (?) the support of this kingdom; may they lead us ourselves
with every new joy.

Come (?), glories, spirits and powers! Take the right hands [ … ]

*(A gap between pages 6 and 7.)*

### Page 7

*Red heading: "[Invocation] of the angels."*

[ … ] come, live yourself with the strong angels; hide (?) and protect the
holy religion and [ … ]

Raphael, Michael, Gabriel, Sarael, with all the strong angels: may they
themselves increase joy and trust for the whole church of the province of
Khorasan.

Blessing to the angels, the stronger ones, [ … ] the powers, so that they
themselves may protect the sons of the right hand from the [ … ] and the
powers.

I bless the god Mani, the Lord; I revere your great and shining majesty; I
confess (?) the holy Spirit with the glories and the strong angels.

Praise to the angels, the stronger ones; may they protect and [ … ]

### Page 8

*Black heading: "Invocation of the [angels]."*

[ … ] may they strike (?) the oppressors (?) of truth. The angel
Rāymast (?), the loving god, with the strong gaze, the god of pure name,
Frēdōn the king, and Jacob Narimān: may they themselves protect the
religion and us, the sons.

May blessing and praise from all of us be received before the [ … ], so
that they themselves may send us strength and power on this day and in
this time of gladness.

Blessing come from the radiant ones of the Highest, and new [ … ] from the
mighty power over the kingdom and the ruler, so that they may be in the
holy faith.

I revere Bar Simus; I praise [ … ] Bar [ … ] that they themselves may
increase every new joy [ … ] (end of the fragment).

## Notes to this edition

- **"Let him have sung"** (Müller: *nisārād*, "er lasse rezitieren")
  introduces each hymn; "ended is" (*hanzaft*) closes it. The hymns are
  grouped in cycles: the Last Days (*frašegird*), Body and Soul, and the
  Going Out (of the soul at death).
- **Mani's hymn of Babel** (page 2): Müller compares Ephrem's "Mani from
  Babel", Mani's own statement reported by al-Bīrūnī (Sachau's edition of
  the *Chronology*, p. 208), and a Mandaean hymn: "A call have I raised in
  the world; in the world have I raised a call."

---
title: "Stories of Mani: the king's audience and Mihršāh's garden"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 64
summary: Two Middle Persian accounts from Turfan of Mani before Persian royalty, one of his hostile audience with the king and one of the conversion of Mihršāh, the brother of Shapur I.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 3 and M 47 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 80–84. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

The Manichaean church kept accounts of its founder's life, and two leaves
from Turfan preserve pieces of them in Middle Persian.

**M 3** tells of an audience at the Persian court. Mani arrives while the
king is at a meal after hunting; he is kept waiting at the door, and the
king, still angry, tells him he has sworn not to let him into the country,
and asks what use he is, since he neither fights nor hunts. Mani answers
that he has done the king's house nothing but good, driving out demons and
raising many from sickness. Müller took the king to be Shapur I. Later
scholars have read the scene as Mani's last audience, before Bahram I,
which ended in his imprisonment and death.

**M 47** (first leaf) tells how Mani converted Mihršāh, a brother of Shapur
I and an enemy of the faith, by showing him the Paradise of light while he
feasted in his own famous garden.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### M 3: Mani at the court

*A large leaf, mostly preserved.*

**Front.** [ … ] came [ … ] I, the first-born (?), the interpreter (?) and
[ … ] the Persian [ … ] I have become. And the king was at the banquet,
eating, and had not yet washed his hands. And the attendants saw (him) and
said: "Mani has come, and he is standing at the door." And the king sent
the Lord a message: "Wait a while, until I come to you myself." And the
Lord sat down again to one side of the [ … ], until the king had washed
his hands; for he had himself gone hunting, and he rose from his meal. He
threw one (arm) over the [ … ] of the queen (?), and one over the [ … ] of
the nobles, [ … ] forward [ … ] with his head [ … ] said [ … ]

**Back.** *(The writing is washed out and for the most part cannot be
read.)*

[ … ] "Why has my cause been ruined? (Have I done some wrong?)"

And the king said: "I have sworn an oath that I will not let you come
into this land." In anger he said this to the Lord: "Ah! What need is
there of you, when you neither go to war nor hunt? But (?) [ … ] for this
art of medicine (?) and for bringing healing, there is need of you. And you
do not even do that."

The Lord gave him this answer: "I have done no wrong to you. I have always
done good to you and to your family. And many and [ … ] of your house, from
whom by me demons and demonesses [were driven out] [ … ] and many there
have been whom I have raised up from sickness [ … ]" (end of the
fragment).

### M 47, first leaf: Mihršāh and the garden

*A fragment of a double leaf, written by two different scribes. First
leaf: from a Manichaean legend.*

[ … ] to the light he went [ … ] my brother [ … ]

*In red: "Mesvan the lord. Mihršāh."*

Now the king of kings Shapur had two brothers, Mesvan the lord and
Mihršāh by name. And he (Mihršāh) was a great enemy of the religion of the
wonderful [Apostle of Light]. He had laid out a garden, beautiful, splendid
(?) and wonderfully wide, so that there was none to equal it.

Then the Apostle, when the hour of salvation had come near, rose and went
before Mihršāh, who was at a banquet in the garden, in great joy. Then the
Apostle [ … ] he commanded [ … ]

**Back.** Then [the king said to the] Apostle: "In the Paradise that you
praise (?), can there be a garden like this garden of mine?"

Then the Apostle punished (?) this unbelieving word. At once, by his
power, he showed him the Paradise of light, with all the gods and deities,
and the immortal wind of life, and the garden all [ … ] and other things
[ … ]. Though he lay senseless for three hours, he kept in his heart the
memory of what he saw. Then the Apostle laid his hand on his head, and he
came to himself. When he had risen, he fell at the Apostle's feet and
took his right hand. And the Apostle [said this … ]

## Notes to this edition

- **"The Lord"** (*xwadāwan*) in M 3 is Mani.
- **The king in M 3**: Müller gave the leaf the heading "the meeting with
  King Shapur I". The scene of the hunt, the oath and the king's anger
  agrees better with the Manichaean accounts of Mani's last audience
  before Bahram I, and later scholars read it that way.
- **"The immortal wind of life"** (M 47): Müller compares al-Nadīm: "the
  gentle breeze … is the life of the world".
- **The second leaf of M 47**, in a later hand, contains part of a parable
  about a king, a man who prepared a meal and lamps that were not lit. It
  is too broken to translate as a whole and is left out here.

parable='''
### M 47, second leaf: the parable of the lamps

*In a later hand. From a parable.*

[ … ] garment [ … ] they received many gifts. They went in; the food was
eaten, the gift was accepted, they were glad; and the man was content, but
he had not lit the lamps in time, and the king was in doubt. One of those
near him said: "This man has made the food well, and was given a gift, but
the lamp was not lit: perhaps he means to commit a crime." The man took it
to be true (?); he was afraid, and fainted. Then this man's servants set a
thousand lamps before the king. Then the king saw that the man was
blameless, and had acted so from forgetfulness, not meaning harm. The king
rebuked the man a little, and then gave him a gift in friendship, and did
not (punish him?).

*The explanation (the moral):* the [ … ] man is the hearers.

**Back.** [ … ] the king [ … ] the messenger of the gods [ … ] the house
[ … ] the shady (place) is the reading (preaching?); the hearers make it
for the religion, they show a dwelling. Those standing around the king are
the pure ones (the Elect). The adorned garment he made is picture and
writing. The lamp is goodness. The one that was not lit in time is that of
the hearers, who at all times grow slack and forgetful in their deeds. It
may be asked: will they afterwards gain the victory, the salvation of the
soul? The servants who lit the lamps and became the man's helpers are the
good deeds, which become helpers to the hearers. So it is with the
[ … ] of the hearers: if they can revere the religion from the heart with
love (?), they become friends of the gods, and from the glory of the
religion they gain the victory [ … ] (end of the fragment).

t=t.replace("while he\nfeasted in his own famous garden.","while he\nfeasted in his own famous garden. Its second leaf, in a later hand,\nhas a parable for the hearers about lamps lit too late.")

p='docs/texts/index.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a='[a hymnbook (M 4)](turfan-hymnbook-m4.html) (new translation, draft);'; assert a in s

## Introduction

The Manichaeans read the Christian Gospels and retold them in their own
books. Two leaves from Turfan quote the end of the Gospel story in Middle
Persian: Pilate's hand-washing and the soldiers' orders (M 18), the trial
before Pilate and Herod and the mocking (M 132), and the women at the tomb
(M 18). The text weaves the four Gospels together. Müller noticed that it
follows the Syriac Gospels rather than the Greek: it calls Salome
*Šalōm* and the governor *hegmōn*, as the Syriac does. One leaf of M 132 is
in Turkish; only the Middle Persian leaf is translated here.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. Gospel parallels are given
in the notes.

## The translation

### M 132: the trial and the mocking

*A fragment of a double leaf; one leaf Turkish, one Middle Persian. Only
the Middle Persian is given.*

**Front.** [ … ] Jesus [ … ] when he came in [ … ] the governor and Pilate
[ … ] asked him about the matter [ … ]: "[I am not … ] in the house of
Jacob and in the seed of Israel." [ … ] gave answer to Pilate: "My kingdom
is not of this world." Yet, through the pressure of the Jews, bound [ … ]
(he was sent) to King Herod [ … ] (the rest is lost).

**Back.** [ … ] a robe [ … ] (a crown of thorns) they set upon his head
[ … ] with a reed they strike him on the jaw; in his eye they spit (?);
and they cry: "Our [ … ] ruler, Messiah!" Then three times [ … ] came, and
three times they fell down [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 18: Pilate and the women at the tomb

*Half a leaf. Heading: "Hymns".*

**Front.** "[ … ] the truth is the Son of God." And Pilate answered thus:
"I am without part in the blood of this Son of God." The centurions and
soldiers received an order from Pilate there: "Keep this secret command,
and (let) the Jews give a pledge (?)."

But (the Gospel) shows that on the Sunday, at the first cock-crow, Mary,
Šalōm and Mary, among many other women, came; they brought sweet-smelling
herbs and nard. They had come near to the tomb; they [ … ] the angel
[ … ] (the rest is destroyed).

**Back.** *Heading: "The section on the crucifixion".*

See the greatness of what Mary, Šalōm and Arsenia (?) did, when the two
angels said to them: "Do not seek the living among the dead. Remember
Jesus' word, how in Galilee he taught you: 'They will hand me over and
crucify me; on the third day I will rise from the dead.' He goes ahead to
Galilee [ … ]; and give word to Simon and the others [ … ]" (the rest is
destroyed).

## Notes to this edition

- **Gospel parallels.** Pilate's words and the guard: Matthew 27:24 and
  27:62–66. The women and the spices: Mark 16:1 and Luke 24:1. "Do not seek
  the living among the dead … remember how he told you in Galilee": Luke
  24:5–7. "He goes ahead of you to Galilee … tell his disciples and Peter":
  Mark 16:7. "My kingdom is not of this world": John 18:36. Herod: Luke
  23:7. The mocking: Matthew 27:28–30 and Mark 15:17–19.
- **"Šalōm" and "hegmōn"**: Müller points out that the Syriac Peshitta has
  *Šalōm* at Mark 16:1, and *hegmōn* for "governor" at Matthew 27:2. So the
  Manichaean text was made from the Syriac Gospels.
- **"Arsenia (?)"** (M 18): a third woman named alongside Mary and Šalōm,
  not in the canonical Gospels. Müller suggested Arsenia or Arsinoe.
- **"At the first cock-crow"**: the Gospels say "very early" or "at
  dawn"; the cock-crow is the Manichaean text's own wording.

input.content:
---
title: "Smaller hymns and prayers from Turfan"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 63
summary: Short Middle Persian and Parthian pieces from Turfan, among them Mani's own song "I am the first stranger", the Manichaean Sanctus, Mār Ammō's meeting with the spirit of the frontier, and a prayer for an Uyghur khan.
original_language: Middle Persian and Parthian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 383, "M. liturg.", M 442, M 2, M 75, M 331 and M 43 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 28–30, 70–71 and 78–79. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition). More fragments from the same edition are still to be added."
---

## Introduction

Besides the longer leaves, Müller's 1904 edition prints many small pieces
of hymns, prayers and stories. This page gathers some of the most
important: a hymn to Mani with a meditation on death (M 383); Mani's own
song, from a little liturgical book, "I am the first stranger, the son of
the god Zurwān" ("M. liturg."); a line of a hymn of the soul (M 442); a
scene from the mission of Mār Ammō, who took the faith to Khorasan (M 2);
the Manichaean *Sanctus*, with the Hebrew *qādōš*, "holy" (M 75, M 331);
and a prayer for an Uyghur khan (M 43).

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### M 383: a hymn to Mani, and a meditation

*The remains of a small leaf.*

[ … ] and before [ … ] let us praise, [ … ] let us praise, [ … ] together
(?). Mani, lord of fair name; Mani, lord of fair name, fair, lovely
[ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] the [ … ].

*In red, a heading, partly lost.*

I know where I was born,
and I do not know where I shall die;
for I have enjoyed in the body [ … ],
for I have given in the soul [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### "M. liturg.": Mani's own song

*A small book, a kind of liturgy, damaged at the top and bottom edges. It
contains this passage.*

*In red: "This in his own song".*

I am the first stranger,
the son of the god Zurwān,
the child of the ruler.

*(The same text then follows again, drawn out syllable by syllable for
chanting.)*

### M 442: a line of a hymn

*A fragment with two and a half double lines each side. It begins:*

For I am the soul of the faith [ … ]

### M 2: from the story of Mār Ammō

*A large double leaf, almost complete. Page 3, column 2.*

That spirit said: "I do not receive you. Turn back to where you have come
from." [ … ] And she hid herself (vanished), in the form of a maiden [ … ].

She asked me: "What are you doing? Where have you come from?" I said: "I
am a believer, a disciple of Mani the Apostle."

[ … ] Ammō, for two days in praises [ … ] I stayed before the sun. Then
the angel appeared and said: "Do not be faint-hearted [ … ]"

### M 75: the Sanctus

*About half a page. Heading: "Bless[ing]".*

[Holy!] to your Greatness, all-shining (?), most high, [and to your]
radiant beauty, which is imperishable. Holy! Holy! Holy! Holy! Holy! Holy!
to your praised Kingdom. Holy! Holy! Holy! to you, Father! Holy! to your
chosen Name! Holy! Holy! Holy! to you, Father! Holy! Holy! Holy! [ … ]

**Back.** *Heading: "[ … ]-udagān".*

To your great Thought, from which every thought and good deed (came).
Holy! Holy! Holy! (to your Word), from which every word and good deed, and
the Strongest, came. Holy! Holy! Holy! to you, Father! Holy! To your great
and praised Air, which is above every air, for in the kingdoms [ … ] (the
rest is destroyed).

### M 331: the Sanctus (another copy)

*A badly preserved piece of a larger leaf.*

[Holy!] [ … to your] Kingdom [ … ] Holy! Holy! Holy! to your [ … ] Holy! to
your chosen Name! Holy! Holy! [to you,] Father! Holy! Holy! Holy! [to your]
Light [and your] Power, Father, who shine above all. Holy! Holy! [Holy!] to
you, Father! Holy! to you [ … ] from which all splendour [came]. Holy!
Holy! [Holy!] to you, Father! Holy! to you [ … ] (the rest is destroyed).

**Back.** *(Müller gave no German for this side. It contains the words
"all praise", "all life", "of the shining ones", "the rulers", "king",
"praise", "for ever and ever", and the refrain "you are, you are, you
are".)*

### M 43: a prayer for an Uyghur khan

*A small oblong leaf; the writing is rubbed away in places.*

[ … the religion … of] Khorasan, the holder of the throne, *Tängrimiz
Xan* (Turkish: "our divine khan"). May they keep it always, for ever, with
the seed (the line) of the shining ones. Live well and glad! Dwell in joy
and welfare! Live for ever!

The stronger, the warlike, the mighty god, praised in prayer, first (?)
commander of the heroes, seeker of battle, excellent, Jacob the great
angel; [and] the mighty ones, the glories, the spirits:

**Back.** May they bless you, ruler, famous holder of the throne, wearer

input.content:
---
title: "Further fragments from Turfan: aeons, angels and hymns"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 65
summary: Small Middle Persian and Parthian pieces from Turfan, with the twelve aeons of light and of darkness, lists of angels, and hymns to the Father, Jesus, Mani and the god Naresaf.
original_language: Middle Persian and Parthian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 14, M 34, M 20, M 33, M 309, M 8, M 40, M 730, M 176 and M 32 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 44–49 and 60–64. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

These are small leaves and pieces from Müller's 1904 edition: two lists of
the twelve "glories" (aeons) of light and of darkness; lists of angels;
a number of the angels of the heavens; and hymns of praise to the Father of
Greatness, to Jesus at the new moon and the full moon, to Mani, and to the
god Naresaf (Narisah, the Third Envoy).

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. Where Müller gave no
meaning for a word, it is given in italics.

## The translation

### M 14: the twelve glories of light

*Among other things, the names of the aeons.* The twelve Glories (the
aeons of light):

1. Lordship
2. Wisdom
3. Salvation
4. Contentment
5. Youth (?)
6. Righteousness
7. *hamdānēft*
8. Long-suffering (?)
9. *razwarēft*
10. Good action
11. *huabsagāft*
12. Light

### M 34: the twelve glories of darkness

*Among other things, the names of the aeons of darkness.* The twelve dark
Glories:

the first, evil knowledge; the second, greed; the third, *gahrādanēft*;
the fourth, confusion; the fifth, [ … ]; the sixth, fettering; the seventh,
*wigānišn*; the eighth, destruction (?); the ninth, death; the tenth, evil
[ … ]; the eleventh, oppression; and the twelfth, darkness.

### M 20: names of angels

*A fragment, the lower part of a small double leaf.*

[ … ] the demon. Jacob the angel; the lord Bar Simus; Qaftinus the mighty;
Raphael, Gabriel, Michael, Sarael; Narsus, Nastikus.

**Back.** [ … ] of the Father, forgiven, and [ … ]. *Invocation:* [ … ] our
voice [ … ]; for I am of the righteous, and not of the [ … ]

**Second leaf.** [ … ] may it be [ … ] see, and [ … ] make in this religion
[ … ] the holy one, the bride of the king; to receive the holy gift of the
Saviour (?) [ … ].

*(The back has only scattered words: "the Father", "and the way of the
religion", "the voice of our songs", "hear you", "guardian", "see the
power".)*

### M 33: the angels of the heavens

*A fragment, lower piece, front.*

[ … ] three hundred and eleven myriads and four hundred angels. Through
the course (?) of night and day, from each one [ … ] become [ … ] twenty
and four [ … ] the ten heavens become [ … ]

*Second column.* [ … ] the heavens [ … ] I lament (?) to your glory;
reverence to the lord Mani, by whom this mystery has been rightly taught
(?).

### M 309: the reward of the righteous

*A leaf fragment.*

[ … ] ruler [ … ] a new, shining throne from the Mother of the Living, a
new diadem, a golden crown, from [ … ] a new dwelling and [ … ] (the rest
is lost).

### M 8: a hymn with names of angels

*The upper half of a leaf. Red heading: "The angels".*

Blessing and praise to Narsus, Nastikus, and to Bar Zaqāh, to the blessed
angel (apostle?) [ … ] great weapon [ … ] (the second column and the back
are hard to read).

### M 40: a hymn to the Father

*The upper half of a small leaf. The front cannot be read. Back, red
heading: "The great ones".*

All-shining (?), first: praised and blessed are you, Father, living,
[ … ], who are the first and the highest; King of Light, [ … ] strongest
and mighty. You are the Father of all this work, of the "lords", the
"powers", the "lights" and the "hosts", as has been said: from you born,
from you sprung, from you come forth, from you revealed [ … ], through you
they become mighty [ … ] (the rest is lost).

### M 730: the twelve great ones

*The upper right corner of a larger leaf in two columns. Heading in
ornamental letters, incomplete.*

He holds twelve diadems of light. They stand before the twelve great ones,
the sons of insight (?), like the twelve shining faces of the Father of
light. Many *yazads*, *bags* and *radans* (princes?) of the Lord of
Paradise, blessed, called, answered, and [ … ] from them, from the twelve
great first-born, the kings and rulers [ … ]

**Back.** *(Badly preserved; the first three lines in red. Second
column:)* Mighty one of the gods, highest god [ … ], lord of the gods, most
divine! Praise to the god of the shining ones, the glory, the high rampart
of light, the blessed kingdom in which you dwell, pure and shining [ … ]
all full of joy, [ … ] trust, life [ … ] (end).

### M 176: hymns of the new moon and the full moon

*A leaf fragment, much worn and hard to read. Blue heading: "King …".*

[ … ] living [ … ] to us [ … ] new moon [ … ] Paradise and new joy came
to the whole religion [ … ]

Jesus, first of the gods! New moon, you are god, and you are [ … ], full
moon!

Jesus, O Lord, of growing fame! Full moon, O Jesus, Lord! [ … ] to all
hearts, worship.

Jesus, god (?), and Wahman! Splendour of god! Let us praise the god
Naresaf; let us bless Mār Mānī.

New full moon and spring, [ … ] Lord, let us bless [ … ] the angels, the
gods [ … ]

*(Another piece:)* [ … ] new sun [ … ] Mihr [ … ]

**Back.** *(Much worn, with a blue heading almost destroyed. A prayer.)*

May a new full moon shine on the religion! Welfare over you, O Lord! Come
with welfare, Lord, [ … ] peaceful (?) Mār Mānī, O god, save me! O god, save
me!

A new day has come, and new joy; a new day has come. Come, new [ … ] of the
living, full of joy. Holy Jesus, forgive my sins! God, Mār Mānī, save my
soul! Holy god!

O Light! Look on me! O Power! O Wisdom! O god, save me! [ … ] heard the
offering of this ruler and the voice of those who praise (?) [ … ] O
awakener (?), to you [ … ] chosen Son, chosen Son [ … ] (the rest is
destroyed).

### M 32: a hymn, and a hymn to the god Naresaf

*The upper half of a leaf, fairly well preserved. Heading: "Hymn".*

[ … ] who proclaim the Glory (the majesty). O crowned (?) Father, worthy
of the blessing of every mouth! O Son of the gods, who gives life to many!
O great Caller, who awakens (?) this soul of mine from slumber! O shining
lamp (?), who made my heart and eye bright! O perfect seal of my hand, my
mouth and my thought! O spear [ … ]; O good sword (?) [ … ] my wisdom and
sign [ … ] my eyes [ … ]

**Back.** *Heading: "The god Naresaf".*

Praise the great Light! Bring [ … ]; with one word let us give praise to
this Glory; let us become singers of praise, let us praise this Ruler, the
Father who does good, the guide (?) of souls, power and youth, so that you
may give to us. Let us give praise and make worship to his Greatness.
Blessed Father, beauty of light, in which there is no flaw [ … ] ruler of
all the kingdoms (aeons) [ … ] (end of the fragment).

## Notes to this edition

- **The twelve glories** (M 14, M 34) are the "twelve aeons" of the
  Father of Greatness and their dark counterparts. Several of the names
  are abstract nouns in *-ēft*, whose meaning Müller could not give.
- **The angels** (M 20, M 8, M 4): Müller notes that another passage, not
  yet found again in 1904, names Jacob, Seth, Bar Simus, Nukhael and
  Qaftinus.
- **"The seal of my hand, my mouth and my thought"** (M 32): the three
  "seals" of the Elect, which Augustine calls the *signacula oris et
  manuum et sinus*.
- **"O Light! O Power! O Wisdom!"** (M 176): Müller compares al-Nadīm's
  "God, his Light, his Power and his Wisdom", and the Greek abjuration
  formula that curses "the four-faced Father of Greatness".
- **Naresaf** (M 176, M 32): the god Narisah, the Third Envoy.
- **Wahman** (M 176): the Great Nous (the Light-Nous).

## Introduction

These are small leaves and pieces from Müller's 1904 edition: two lists of
the twelve "glories" (aeons) of light and of darkness; lists of angels;
a number of the angels of the heavens; and hymns of praise to the Father of
Greatness, to Jesus at the new moon and the full moon, to Mani, and to the
god Naresaf (Narisah, the Third Envoy).

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. Where Müller gave no
meaning for a word, it is given in italics.

### M 14: the twelve glories of light

*Among other things, the names of the aeons.* The twelve Glories (the
aeons of light):

1. Lordship
2. Wisdom
3. Salvation
4. Contentment
5. Youth (?)
6. Righteousness
7. *hamdānēft*
8. Long-suffering (?)
9. *razwarēft*
10. Good action
11. *huabsagāft*
12. Light

### M 34: the twelve glories of darkness

*Among other things, the names of the aeons of darkness.* The twelve dark
Glories:

the first, evil knowledge; the second, greed; the third, *gahrādanēft*;
the fourth, confusion; the fifth, [ … ]; the sixth, fettering; the seventh,
*wigānišn*; the eighth, destruction (?); the ninth, death; the tenth, evil
[ … ]; the eleventh, oppression; and the twelfth, darkness.

*A fragment, the lower part of a small double leaf.*

[ … ] the demon. Jacob the angel; the lord Bar Simus; Qaftinus the mighty;
Raphael, Gabriel, Michael, Sarael; Narsus, Nastikus.

**Back.** [ … ] of the Father, forgiven, and [ … ]. *Invocation:* [ … ] our
voice [ … ]; for I am of the righteous, and not of the [ … ]

**Second leaf.** [ … ] may it be [ … ] see, and [ … ] make in this religion
[ … ] the holy one, the bride of the king; to receive the holy gift of the
Saviour (?) [ … ].

religion", "the voice of our songs", "hear you", "guardian", "see the
power".)*

[ … ] three hundred and eleven myriads and four hundred angels. Through
the course (?) of night and day, from each one [ … ] become [ … ] twenty
and four [ … ] the ten heavens become [ … ]

input.content:
---
title: "Further fragments from Turfan: prayers to Mani and Jesus"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 67
summary: Short Middle Persian and Parthian hymns and prayers from Turfan, among them "what eye has not seen", a further Sanctus, prayers to Mani as life-giver, an alphabetic hymn and prayers for rulers and church leaders.
original_language: Middle Persian and Parthian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 102, M 311, M 551, M 789, M 554, M 544, M 555, M 324, M 74, M 38, M 173 and M 543 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 64–80. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

More small hymns and prayers from Müller's 1904 edition. Several call on
Mani as the life-giver who "brings the dead to life and gives light to
those in darkness", and ask to be saved "from this being-born-and-dying".
Two (M 551 and M 789) promise "what you have not seen with the eye, nor
heard with the ear, nor grasped with the hand", a saying also known from
Paul (1 Corinthians 2:9) and the Gospel of Thomas (17). M 173 is an
alphabetic hymn that begins "Ālaf, the first, are you, Lord, and Tau, the
last". M 74 and M 543 are prayers for a lay patron and for a ruler or
church leader of Khorasan.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's first
edition of 1904, the only public-domain edition, which he called "a first
attempt". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### M 102: a hymn to "our lords of praised name"

*A leaf fragment, large octavo. Blue heading: "Our lords of praised
name".*

[ … ] of the religion, because he is a great ruler [ … ] into, and he is
full of splendour. He is the one over whom an enemy [has no power],
because he is a friend [ … ]. He is the one over whom no foul smell [ … ]
has come, because he is all fragrance. He is the one whom death does not
[touch], because he is all life. He is the one over whom darkness [has no
power], because he is strong light [ … ] full. He is the one who [ … ],
because he is all living and light [ … ] darkness not [ … ] welfare and
joy [ … ]

**Back.** *Blue heading: "Mār Zindag Yišō' (?), the servant".* (Müller gave
no German for this side. It is a hymn of praise with the words "great,
living ruler", "pure, shining", "praised", "the blessed kingdoms" and "the
angels".)

### M 311: a prayer to Mani

*A fragment of a small leaf. Line 5, a red heading in the Parthian
"dialect", untranslated.*

Mani, son of the gods, lord, life-giver (?) of the faith, great chosen one:
I bring you worship. May you be of shining face, Mani, life-giving lord!
He brings the dead to life and gives light to those in darkness. Lead (?)
me, Mani, lord; and Maiden of Light, answer me with splendour [ … ]

**Back, lower half, line 10.** O shining Mani, lord of growing fame,
life-giver! Protect me in the body. Jesus, Lord, save my soul from this
being-born-and-dying! Save my soul from this being-born-and-dying! Splendid
is your shining throne [ … ]

### M 551: a prayer

*A small leaf fragment.*

[ … ] forgive! I have been washed (?) from the filth and much stench;
forgive me [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] save [ … ] destruction [ … ] you, what you have not seen
with the eye, nor heard with the ear, nor grasped with the hand [ … ]
(the rest is destroyed).

### M 789: the same text

  "what no hand has touched".
- **"Being-born-and-dying"** (M 311, M 38; Müller: *Geboren-Tot(sein)*,
  from *zādmurd*) is the Manichaean term for bodily existence, the round of
  rebirth.
- **"Ālaf … Tau"** (M 173): compare Revelation 22:13, "I am the Alpha and
  the Omega, the first and the last", here with the Syriac letters.
- **"The Mazdayasnian faith"** (M 543): Müller's reading *dēn māzdēs*; it
  is unusual in a Manichaean prayer and may be a title borrowed from
  Zoroastrian usage.
- **Mithras** (M 38): Mihr, the god of the sun, is in these texts a name of
  the Third Envoy or the Living Spirit.
