input.content:
---
title: "Further fragments from Turfan: stories, teaching and polemic"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 68
summary: Middle Persian pieces from Turfan, with the Apostle's flight with Ardāv into the air, Mani as "a physician from the land of Babel", the conversion of a household, the hearer Khebrā, a hymn, a teaching on the fast days, and polemic against Zoroastrians and Christians.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan fragments M 48, M 566, M 45, M 64, M 16, M 28 and M 50, and an unnumbered leaf of a conversion story (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Handschriften-Reste in Estrangelo-Schrift aus Turfan, Chinesisch-Turkistan. II. Teil", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1904 (public domain), pp. 86–96. New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1904 readings and German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

The last group of Middle Persian pieces in Müller's 1904 edition. M 48 and
M 566, in the same hand, tell of the Apostle (Mani) carrying a man called
Ardāv up into the air, and of Mani before a king as "a physician from the
land of Babel"; Müller compared al-Bīrūnī's report that Mani rose into the
air with King Shapur. A leaf of a conversion story lists the evils of
anger, killing and wine, and tells how a righteous man prayed for the soul
of Dārāv's son. M 45 belongs to a story about a hearer called Khebrā. M 64
is a hymn written out a second time, syllable by syllable, for chanting.
M 16 is from a teaching on the fast days; M 28 is polemic against the
fire-worshippers and the Christians; M 50 is a calendar table.

that one is Lord of the All, his son, who made [ … ] They, the wicked,
come rightly to hell, for by themselves sinfulness was made, and the
destruction (?) of the sinners is like what they have done. He, the god of
Marcion, [ … ] took his own [ … ] and killed [ … ]

**From page 4.** Then at the end (the Last Day) all who worship idols will
come, on that last day, and go to destruction (?).

### M 50: a calendar table

*A badly damaged larger leaf, worm-eaten, in black and red, in a late,
very cursive hand. A table belonging to a chronological or calendrical
work.*

One column gives the names of the Persian days of the month: Srōš,
Mahraspand, Rašn, Dēn, Anērān, Frawardīn, Ard, Wahrām, Āštād, Rām, Asmān,
Wād, Zāmyād. Beside Zāmyād is written in red: "[ … ] of Mercury and Mars"
(in Arabic). A column on the back gives, in Arabic but in Manichaean
script, the signs of the zodiac: Lion, Virgin (the "ear of corn"), Balance,
Scorpion, Bow(man), Goat, Water-carrier, Fishes. The other columns are
filled with letters and notes in a very cursive hand.

## Notes to this edition

- **Ardāv and the Apostle** (M 48): the word *frēstag* means both "angel"
  and "apostle". Müller suggests that the Apostle of Light, Mani, is meant,
  and compares al-Bīrūnī: "the king Shapur came to believe in him when he
  had ascended with him towards heaven, and they had been standing in the
  air between heaven and earth".
- **"A physician from the land of Babel"** (M 566): compare Mani's hymn of
  Babel in [the hymnbook M 4](turfan-hymnbook-m4.html), and the king's
  remark about "this art of medicine" in [M 3](turfan-mani-legends.html).
- **"When I weep over the bodily son, I kill the spiritual one"** (M 45):
  Müller compares the Zoroastrian ban on mourning the dead with tears.
- **Ohrmizd and Ahriman as brothers** (M 28): the Zurvanite teaching, which
  Müller compares with Eznik of Kołb, *Against the Sects*.
- **The god of Marcion** (M 28): Marcion of Sinope taught that the god of
  the Old Testament was a different, lesser god from the Father of Jesus.
- **The Parthian "dialect" texts**: Müller's edition goes on to print
  samples in what he called a "Pehlevi dialect" (Parthian), with Turkish
  and trilingual leaves (M 172). Those are on the queue to be done next.

input.command:
python -I - <<'EOF'
p='docs/texts/turfan-gospel-epistles.md'; t=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
sec='''### M 172: the opening of the Gospel, in two languages

*A double leaf. The first leaf gives the same doxology as M 17, each
sentence first in Middle Persian and then in Parthian (Müller's "Pehlevi
dialect"). The second leaf is in Turkish in Manichaean script; Müller
printed it without a translation.*

Praised has been, and praised will be, the Virgin of Light, the head of all
excellences.

Praised has been, and praised will be, the holy religion, by the power of
the Father (Parthian: "the power of the Father, the god Zurwān"), by the
blessing of the Mother, and by the goodness of the Son (Parthian: "the Son
Jesus").

Welfare and blessing upon the sons of welfare, and upon the speakers and
hearers of the famous word (Parthian: "of the command of the Holy
Spirit")!

May there be praise and glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the
holy Spirit (Parthian: "the chosen breath, the Holy Spirit"), and to the
holy elements (Parthian: "the begetting (?) elements")!

The discourse of the Living Gospel of the eye and the ear is taught (?),
and the fruit of truth [is offered].

'''
a='### M 733: extracts from the Epistles and the Gospel'; assert a in t
t=t.replace(a,sec+a,1)
t=t.replace("source: 'Turfan fragments M 17, M 733 and M 731 (Berlin)","source: 'Turfan fragments M 17, M 172, M 733 and M 731 (Berlin)")
t=t.replace("pp. 25–33. New English translation.'","pp. 25–33 and 100–103. New English translation.'")
a="and two damaged leaves of extracts from the Epistles."; assert a in t
t=t.replace(a,"a second copy of that opening in Middle Persian and Parthian side by side\n(M 172), and two damaged leaves of extracts from the Epistles.")
note='''- **M 172** is the leaf Müller used to show that the "Pehlevi dialect" (now
  known to be Parthian) was a separate language: he set the Middle Persian
  and Parthian of each sentence under one another. He compares the Greek
  abjuration formula, which names Mani's "Living Gospel".
'''
a='- **The Epistle of Hatā**'; assert a in t; t=t.replace(a,note+a)
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(t)

p='docs/texts/turfan-hymns-prayers.md'; t=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
add='''
*Müller adds in his corrections three related verses from other leaves.
From the same small book, page 1:*

I am a man, a seed (?) of light, living and shining.

*From its back:*

I am a ruler's son [ … and] I have become a stranger, (far) from the
Greatness.

*From M 7:*

From the light and from the gods am I,
and I have become a stranger to them.
The enemies have fallen (?) upon me,
and by them I have been led down (?) to the dead.
'''
a='*(The same text then follows again, drawn out syllable by syllable for\nchanting.)*\n'; assert a in t
t=t.replace(a,a+add,1)
note='''- **"From the light and from the gods am I"** (M 7): Müller compares the
  apocryphal Gospel of Philip quoted by Epiphanius: "I am from those
  above".
'''
a='- **Mār Ammō**'; assert a in t; t=t.replace(a,note+a)
t=t.replace("source: 'Turfan fragments M 383,","source: 'Turfan fragments M 383, M 7,")
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(t)

p='research/SCOPE.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
a="Still to do: the Parthian (\"Pehlevi-Dialekt\") samples and M 172 (Müller pp. 96–end)."; assert a in s
s=s.replace(a,"M 172 (Parthian/Middle Persian Gospel doxology) is in `turfan-gospel-epistles`. Müller 1904 is now fully translated except the untranslated Turkish leaves (M 172 pp. 3–4, M 443), the Syriac and Turkish Nestorian scraps (M 151, 152, 515) and the New Persian M 106, which Müller only described."); open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
p='queue.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
i=s.index('1. **[Translation] Müller 1904, remaining small fragments**'); s=s[:i].rstrip('\n')+'\n'
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
p='devlog.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read().rstrip('\n')
s+="\n- 2026-10-21 Müller 1904 finished: added M 172 (the Gospel doxology in Middle Persian and Parthian) to `turfan-gospel-epistles`, and Müller's addenda verses (\"I am a man, a seed of light\", \"I am a ruler's son … a stranger\", M 7 \"From the light and from the gods am I\") to `turfan-hymns-prayers`. Only pieces Müller printed without any translation are left.\n"
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
EOF

A.  VON  LE  COQ. 
PML-kist.  Klasse.    Wll.    Anhang.   Abh.  VI. 
Vorgelegt  von  Hrn.  Müller  in  der  Sitzung  der  phil.-hist.  Klasse  am  19.  Oktober  1911. 
Zum  Druck  verordnet  am  gleichen  Tage,  ausgegeben  am  25.  April  1912. 
Uie  vorliegenden  türkischen  Texte  manichäisch-religiösen  Inhalts  gehören 
zum  Teil  zur  Ausbeute  der  ersten,  zum  Teil  zu  der  der  zweiten  Turfan- 
expedition.  Erstere  hat  Hr.  Prof.  Grünwedel  mir  zur  Verfügung  gestellt, 
wofür  ich  ihm  hier  meinen  Dank  ausspreche;  es  sind  die  Manuskriptbruch- 
stücke T.  M.  1 59,  282  und  T.  Iä,  die  sämtlich  aus  der  buddhistischen  Tempel- 
ruine ot*)  in  Chotscho  (Idiqut-Schähri)  bei  Turfan  stammen. 
Die  vier  größeren  Handschriftenreste  T.  II  D.  171,  172,  173  und  176 
wurden  von  meiner  Expedition  in  einem  Gewölbe  des  nordwestlichen  Teiles 
der  manichäischen  Ruinengruppe  K*)  gefunden;  alle  bisher  in  den  Publi- 
kationen der  Berl.  Akad.  d.  Wiss.  behandelten  türkisch-manichäischen  Schrift- 
und  Miniaturfragmente**)  gehören  zu  diesem  größeren  Fund.  Inhaltlich  ge- 
hören alle  diese  Handschriften  der  religiösen  Literatur  der  Manichäer  an; 
es  sind  Reste  von  Gebeten  (T.  II  D.  1 7 1 )  und  von  durch  Gleichnisse  er- 
läuterten Predigten  und  kosmogonischen  Schilderungen  (Buchrest  T.  II 
D.  173a,  b,  d***).  Das  Buchblatt  T.  II  D.  176  endlich  enthält  eine  grauen- 
erregende, legendenhafte  Erzählung. 
Alle  diese  Manuskripte  sind  Übersetzungen,  und  zwar  anscheinend 
Übersetzungen  aus  dem  Mittelpersischen  oder  Soghdischen.    Die  Übersetzer 
*)  Vgl.  den  Plan  der  Ruinenstadt  Chotscho  (Idiqut-Schähri)  in  A.  Grünwedel,  »Be- 
richt über  archäologische  Arbeiten  in  Idiqutschari«,  Abhandlungen  der  Königl.  Bayer.  Akad. 
d.  Wiss.:  I.Klasse,  XXIV.  Band,   I.Abteilung,  München  1905. 
**)  A.  von  Le  Coq,  Ein  manichäisch-uigurisches  Fragment.  Derselbe,  Ein  christliches 
und  ein  manichäisches  Manuskriptfragment  1909  XL VIII.  Derselbe,  Chuastuanift,  Anhang 
zu  den  Abhandlungen  der  Berl.  Akad.  d.  Wiss.  voi^  Jahre  1910.  Berlin  191 1  (T.  II  D.  178, 
Blatt  III— VI). 
***)  Diese  zusammengehörigen  Buchblätter  sind  in  der  Reihenfolge,  in  der  sie  sich  im 
Augenblick  des  Fundes  darboten,  numeriert  worden;  wahrscheinlich  enthält  aber  Blatt  a* 
den  Schlußhymnus  und  das  Kolophon  des  ganzen  Buches  oder  doch  eines  Abschnittes.  Die 
Blätter  b '  und  c  sind  noch  nicht  publikationsfähig. 
4  A.  VON  Le  Coq  : 
haben  unseres  Erachtens  den  Versuch  einer  wörtlichen  Wiedergabe  so  weit 
getrieben,  daß  die  an  sich  durch  unsere  Unkenntnis  der  Realien  schon  un- 
gemein schwierige  Verdeutschung  durch  die  ungewöhnlichen  Konstruktionen 
noch  wesentlich  erschwert  wird.  Wenn  trotz  mancher  Zweifel  diese  Texte 
heute  schon  der  Öffentlichkeit  übergeben  werden,  so  geschieht  es  einerseits, 
um  anderen,  besonders  Hrn.  V.  Thomsen,  die  Teilnahme  an  ihrem  Stu- 
dium zu  ermöglichen,  anderseits,  weil  wir  mit  anderen  Dingen  sehr  stark 
beschäftigt  sind.  Die  hier  gegebenen  Übersetzungen  machen  keinen  An- 
spruch darauf,  mehr  als  ein  Versuch  zu  sein. 
Von  nicht  unbedeutendem  historischen  Interesse  ist  die  Erwähnung 
des  ulwy  mozaJc  aus  Tocharistan,  den  wir  ßir  den  Mudja  der  Inschrift  von 
Kara-Balgassun  halten  möchten*),  sowie  die  des  Schülers  und  Zeitgenossen  des 
Mani,  Mar  Amu,  des  Mozak,  der  zu  den  frühesten  manichäischen  Sendboten 
gehört.  Wichtig  ist  ferner  das  Datum  im  Kolophon  des  Blattes  T.  II  173a', 
das  einen  Schluß  auf  die  Entstehungszeit  des  betreffenden  Textes  und  zu- 
gleich auf  das  genaue  Datum  des  Todes  des  Mani  zuläßt,  und  endlich  die 
Auffährung  der  Titel  des  türkischen  Fürsten  im  polychromen  Buchblatt 
T.  II  D.  171,  welches  unseres  Erachtens  auch  ein  Kolophon,  und  zwar  das 
eines  Gebetbuches,  sein  dürfte.

---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean texts from Qočo"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 70
summary: Uyghur Manichaean leaves from Qočo near Turfan, with a grim legend, parables of rebirth, the rescue of Ohrmizd and the making of heaven and earth, a prayer to the souls' Father dated 522 years after Mani's death, a royal prayer-book colophon, and Mār Ammō's meeting with a sorcerer.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II D 176, T II D 173a–d, T Ia, T II D 171 and others (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. I", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1911, Anhang, Abh. VI (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1911 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

These leaves in Old Turkish come from Qočo (Idiqut-šähri), the Uyghur
capital near Turfan. Albert von Le Coq published them in 1911. They are
translations, he thought from Middle Persian or Sogdian, and they cover
several kinds of text: a grim legend (T II D 176); a book of sermons with
parables, a cosmogony, and a closing prayer dated 522 years after Mani's
death (T II D 173); smaller pieces of cosmogony and mythology; and a richly
coloured leaf (T II D 171) that ends a prayer book with the titles of a
Turkish prince and of a Tocharian "great *možak*". An appendix tells how
Mār Ammō, Mani's disciple, met a sorcerer at a temple.

Le Coq called his German translations "no more than an attempt", and said
the Turkish follows its originals so literally that it is often hard to
construe. Modern editions read many passages differently.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense, many of them his. The "••" that divide
the Turkish sentences are not reproduced.

## The translation

### T II D 176: the man and the corpse (a legend)

*Leaf 1, front. The story begins in the middle.*

[ … ] he saw, and thought: "This is someone of my household." He went in
and lay down beside the corpse. And because of his drunkenness and folly
he embraced the corpse and did shameless things, and was joined with the
corpse. Through his exertions the corpse burst. The blood and pus in its
loathsome body, murky and foul, were pressed out and spilled. And that
righteous man, his whole body and clothes from head to foot drenched in
blood and pus, made senseless by his shameless intent and his
drunkenness, thought in his heart: "I have become one who rejoices in
evil."

Like blood (?) the morning shone, and the sun rose. The righteous man's
drunkenness passed, and he woke from his sleep.

**Back.** Raising his head high, he went into the inside of the stupa.
In his bosom (?) the corpse lies; pus and blood flow out; everything
stinks. He looked at himself. When he saw himself all stained with blood
and drenched in uncleanness, he started up; dreadful fear seized him; he
screamed aloud. Quickly coming out of the [ … ] (the mourning robe?), he
fled as fast as he could run, so full was he of loathing and horror. That
[ … ] he tore it quickly to pieces, and threw it out, and hurried away in
grief. He came upon one of his [ … ]. He threw himself into that [ … ] of
his, and washed and cleansed himself [ … ] (end of the back).

### T II D 173a: from a book of sermons

*Parts of a book. First double leaf.*

**Leaf 1, front.** [ … ] he kills the bird. And again, just as the fire
that has come out of the wood sets the wood alight again. And again, just
as when the lamb or the calf, changing its body, has become a young lion
or a young wolf, (and) is born, and then in turn eats up and destroys
cattle, oxen and hares. And just as the tongs that press on the anvil,
made themselves of noble iron, in turn break through all iron. And just as
the louse of the coat, which has come from the skin of a man, in turn
sucks the man's own blood; when the man sees it, it is driven off (?).

So he explained it. Among men, through the five gods (?), they were born
in the five kinds of plants and trees.

**Leaf 1, back.** And through the five kinds of plants and trees (?) they
were born in this senseless body. Then, because for a long time they have
been tormented for the body, have fallen sick and died, because
everywhere they have suffered bitter torments, [ … ] the pain and torment
they themselves have endured [ … ]. And they quarrel with one another and
devour (?) one another. And, striking (?) one another, they call out to one
another: "May you be oppressed (?) by famine (?), wickedly and without
end! May you fall (?) into fire and flames!" Saying such things, they
revile and strike one another. This cursing and devouring (?), hating and
striking one another, like ignorant people, like abuse and deceit (?)
[ … ]. They themselves do not understand it so.

**Leaf 2, front.** [ … ] the coming of the Burxan [ … ] book [ … ] we have
found all. Oppression and deceit are not among us. Now, O our gracious
Father! O our good-doing prince! Countless myriads of years have passed
since we were parted from you. Your gracious, fair, innocent, shining face
[ … ]; your dear, shining, living face we long and yearn to see! In your
strength we have gone unharmed, unharmed we have come! (But) the things
you commanded, all of them,

**Leaf 2, back.** we have not carried out. Now, O my gracious, royal god!
Be gracious! Your eternally perfect, innocent being (self) we would see!
The torments we have suffered for so long we would forget! For ever
loving and joyful we would be!

*(A heading in red:)* [ … ] has been written [ … ] Śākyamuni [ … ]

You (they?) will often pray such prayers: then the Great King will reveal
and show his eternally gracious, beautiful face; then all will turn (?);
for ever joyful and loving you (they?) will be!

I, Zimtu (?), will be his companion in this good joy (?). For ever, for
ever, so may it be!

In the five hundred and twenty-second year, the year of the Pig, after the
going of the divine Mani Burxan to the realm of the gods, the lord of the
Law who lives in Ötükän, the most virtuous, gracious lord of wisdom, the
divine Mār Niw Mani, [ … ] to the *mahistak* Aiyïn (?) these two [ … ]

### T II D 173b: the rescue of Ohrmizd and the making of heaven and earth

*Second double leaf. Leaf 1, front. In red: "May there be joy!"*

[ … ] he pierced. Second: the whole realm of the gods, (and) its
well-being (?), he gave. Third: the good Law he gave. Fourth: to effort,
watchfulness and following he moved them. Fifth: [ … ]

**Back.** On his right, he opened his door to the realm of the gods. Just
as water opens the door of plants and trees on the earth, so also the god
Xroštag opened his door to the god Xormuzta and the five gods. When the
god Xroštag (and?) Padvaxtag had risen up from the god Xormuzta (and) from
hell, then the god Wadžiwantag and the Mother-God (?) came quickly. They
made the god Xormuzta rise up out of hell and come out, and sent him to
the realm of the gods, (he himself) the majesty of all.

And the Mother-God and the god Wadžiwantag separated the five gods from
the god Xormuzta. And (now) they made ready to create and make the earth
and the heaven. First of all they made and created the tenfold blue heaven
in this way, all at once, just as one lays out a new orchard and a house
and its furniture; and just as one makes plants spring up at once from
new ground; just as a male child comes from a man's strength: so too the
making of this earth and of the tenfold blue heaven was like (these
things). [ … ] And eleventh, they made the zodiac, and set it up out of
(?) seven kinds of virtue. The one is to be the fetter of all the demons;
the second (is to be) for all [ … ] (end of the back).

### T II D 173: a sermon on desire

*A leaf of the same book.*

**Front.** [ … ] will not be able. His parents will not be able to speak
such words of remembrance as could enlighten that man's mind. Goods and
property will not cling to his eye (will be worth nothing to him). However
many physicians may come with their herbs, they will not be able to heal
him. And all the priests, gathering together, will bring nothing to life:
they will not be able to give children. As, by no means, does horn (?)
sprout from the horse or the ass; as able men cannot do useless things; so
men and "long-robes" (women), however much they may not eat (?) of the
power of the five gods, cannot commit shameless acts by love of the body.
Sons and daughters

**Back.** they will by no means beget. Then, if the gods' power were food
and drink, then children would be born strong and great.

That lust of sin of yours, which comes from outside mixed with food and
drink, enters the body; it unites with the lust of sin within, which is in
the male and female body. Then your lust of sin becomes as strong as when
fire kindles dry firewood; and as the fish swims in the water; as seeds or
kernels sprout in a good place: so too your lust of sin becomes strong in
the body. Then your lust of sin [fills (?)] your own body from the head to
the tip of the toe-nail [ … ]

### Parables from a sermon

*The upper part of a leaf.*

**Front.** [ … ] as when a capable man's capability finds no property (earns

useless; as a man who cannot tell apart and understand these words
[ … ] his breast like the not-dark-eyed (?) [ … ]

**Back.** [As when] fire kindles and inflames firewood; as the calf which

flees (?) from the wolf kills; and the gripping tongs, which, made of iron,
[break up the iron] [ … ]

### T Ia: a fragment of cosmogony

**Front.** [ … ] he came down to the [ … ]. Those three demons he bound to
his zodiac. With his four shining powers he came down to this earth, as
Abamu Burxan [ … ] the god Xormuzta [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] was kind of heart: how did he do it, that he killed the
demon? If anyone should ask this in doubt, give this answer: the demon,
changing his words, spoke to all the evil spirits, declaring: "The poison
taken from you I will spit (throw) at the god Xormuzta; the god Xormuzta
with this [ … ]," he said. The poison he spat struck his own head. He fell
down, and humbled himself ten-thousandfold. The demon (said): "I (will?)
the god Xormuzta [ … ]" [ … ] the demons [ … ] they were [ … ] they ate and
killed, but he, with his body, fell into the front (?) of hell.

Then the god Xormuzta, making the fire-god into an axe, split the demon's
head; and making that fire-god like a lance of seventy myriad miles, (he
struck) the demon's head with the lance's point [ … ]

### From bundle 172: a mythological text

*The upper part of two badly damaged leaves.*

**Leaf 1, front.** [ … ] marvelling [ … ] It is the gentle breeze, the wind,
the light, the water and the fire (that is, the five gods): all these have
been put on the god Äzrua (as garments) and are united with him; the
bodies of these five gods of light, all [ … ]

**Leaf 1, back.** Happy be the owner of this writing! Through his wisdom
(*vidyā*) (?), his fame and his praise among all the gods in the realm of
the gods he thus makes appear, and spreads light and splendour, as the
[sun and moon god] by his splendour [lights up our] whole [earth], the
[five] kinds of living beings [ … ]

**Leaf 2, front.** [ … ] they find. Second, through his spirit, his bodily
[ … ], which itself (consists of) those living good thoughts which arise
from the god of the majesty of the Law [ … ] himself with his army [ … ]
because of all [ … ] his head [ … ]

**Leaf 2, back.** [ … ] I have written with reverence [ … ] the god Äzrua,
who is himself the elder brother and elder sister of all the gods of the
realm of the gods, the pure majesty; the shining mind (?) (mother?), the

### T II D 171: the end of a prayer book

## Notes to this edition

- **The date in T II D 173a.** Le Coq took the "five hundred and
  twenty-second year … after the going of the divine Mani Burxan" to be the
  year 795, which would put Mani's death in 273. He thought the leaf began
  the colophon of the whole book, naming the person who had it copied (or
  translated). "Ötükän" is the sacred mountain country of the Turks.
- **The rescue of Ohrmizd** (T II D 173b): Le Coq compared al-Nadīm's
  account. *Xormuzta* (Ohrmizd) is the First Man; *Wadžiwantag* is the
  Living Spirit; the "Mother-God" (Turkish *ög täŋri*) is the Mother of Life;
  and *Xroštag* and *Padvaxtag* are the Call and the Answer. Le Coq noted
  that the zodiac is not mentioned at this point in al-Nadīm.
- **"Men and long-robes"** (the sermon on desire): Le Coq took
  "long-robes" to mean women. He compared the *Acta Archelai* 14 on
  generation as the work of food and lust.
- **The five ways** (T II D 171): the Envoys appear like Ohrmizd, the Living
  Spirit (*Wadžiwanta*), the sun-god, the moon-god, and the Maiden of Light,
  the "daughter of the god Äzrua", who changes her form.
- **Äzrua** is Zurwān, the Manichaean name, taken from Zoroastrian usage,
  for the Father of Greatness.
- **The colophon of T II D 171** names a great *možak* of Tocharistan, whom
  Le Coq thought might be the *možak* of the Karabalgasun inscription. The
  later notes by Yapγun and Arslan Mängü show that the book was used for
  recitation; *manastar hirza*, "forgive my sins", is Middle Persian.
- **Mār Ammō** was the disciple whom Mani sent to the east. Compare the
  Middle Persian story in [the smaller hymns and prayers](turfan-hymns-prayers.html#m-2-from-the-story-of-mār-ammō).

## Introduction

These leaves in Old Turkish come from Qočo (Idiqut-šähri), the Uyghur
capital near Turfan. Albert von Le Coq published them in 1911. They are
translations, he thought from Middle Persian or Sogdian, and they cover
several kinds of text: a grim legend (T II D 176); a book of sermons with
parables, a cosmogony, and a closing prayer dated 522 years after Mani's
death (T II D 173); smaller pieces of cosmogony and mythology; and a richly
coloured leaf (T II D 171) that ends a prayer book with the titles of a
Turkish prince and of a Tocharian "great *možak*". An appendix tells how
Mār Ammō, Mani's disciple, met a sorcerer at a temple.

Le Coq called his German translations "no more than an attempt", and said
the Turkish follows its originals so literally that it is often hard to
construe. Modern editions read many passages differently.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense, many of them his. The "••" that divide
the Turkish sentences are not reproduced.

## The translation

### T II D 176: the man and the corpse (a legend)

*Leaf 1, front. The story begins in the middle.*

[ … ] he saw, and thought: "This is someone of my household." He went in
and lay down beside the corpse. And because of his drunkenness and folly
he embraced the corpse and did shameless things, and was joined with the
corpse. Through his exertions the corpse burst. The blood and pus in its
loathsome body, murky and foul, were pressed out and spilled. And that
righteous man, his whole body and clothes from head to foot drenched in
blood and pus, made senseless by his shameless intent and his
drunkenness, thought in his heart: "I have become one who rejoices in
evil."

Like blood (?) the morning shone, and the sun rose. The righteous man's
drunkenness passed, and he woke from his sleep.

**Back.** Raising his head high, he went into the inside of the stupa.
In his bosom (?) the corpse lies; pus and blood flow out; everything
stinks. He looked at himself. When he saw himself all stained with blood
and drenched in uncleanness, he started up; dreadful fear seized him; he
screamed aloud. Quickly coming out of the [ … ] (the mourning robe?), he
fled as fast as he could run, so full was he of loathing and horror. That
[ … ] he tore it quickly to pieces, and threw it out, and hurried away in
grief. He came upon one of his [ … ]. He threw himself into that [ … ] of
his, and washed and cleansed himself [ … ] (end of the back).

title: "Old Turkish Manichaean texts from Qočo"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 70
summary: Uyghur Manichaean leaves from Qočo near Turfan, with a grim legend, parables of rebirth, the rescue of Ohrmizd and the making of heaven and earth, a prayer to the souls' Father dated 522 years after Mani's death, a royal prayer-book colophon, and Mār Ammō's meeting with a sorcerer.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II D 176, T II D 173a–d, T Ia, T II D 171 and others (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. I", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1911, Anhang, Abh. VI (public domain). New English translation.'

---

## Introduction

These leaves in Old Turkish come from Qočo (Idiqut-šähri), the Uyghur
capital near Turfan. Albert von Le Coq published them in 1911. They are
translations, he thought from Middle Persian or Sogdian, and they cover
several kinds of text: a grim legend (T II D 176); a book of sermons with
parables, a cosmogony, and a closing prayer dated 522 years after Mani's
death (T II D 173); smaller pieces of cosmogony and mythology; and a richly
coloured leaf (T II D 171) that ends a prayer book with the titles of a
Turkish prince and of a Tocharian "great *možak*". An appendix tells how
Mār Ammō, Mani's disciple, met a sorcerer at a temple.

Le Coq called his German translations "no more than an attempt", and said
the Turkish follows its originals so literally that it is often hard to
construe. Modern editions read many passages differently.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense, many of them his. The "••" that divide
the Turkish sentences are not reproduced.

## The translation

### T II D 176: the man and the corpse (a legend)

*Leaf 1, front. The story begins in the middle.*

[ … ] he saw, and thought: "This is someone of my household." He went in
and lay down beside the corpse. And because of his drunkenness and folly
he embraced the corpse and did shameless things, and was joined with the
corpse. Through his exertions the corpse burst. The blood and pus in its
loathsome body, murky and foul, were pressed out and spilled. And that
righteous man, his whole body and clothes from head to foot drenched in
blood and pus, made senseless by his shameless intent and his
drunkenness, thought in his heart: "I have become one who rejoices in
evil."

Like blood (?) the morning shone, and the sun rose. The righteous man's
drunkenness passed, and he woke from his sleep.

**Back.** Raising his head high, he went into the inside of the stupa.
In his bosom (?) the corpse lies; pus and blood flow out; everything
stinks. He looked at himself. When he saw himself all stained with blood
and drenched in uncleanness, he started up; dreadful fear seized him; he
screamed aloud. Quickly coming out of the [ … ] (the mourning robe?), he
fled as fast as he could run, so full was he of loathing and horror. That
[ … ] he tore it quickly to pieces, and threw it out, and hurried away in
grief. He came upon one of his [ … ]. He threw himself into that [ … ] of
his, and washed and cleansed himself [ … ] (end of the back).

### T II D 173a: from a book of sermons

*Parts of a book. First double leaf.*

**Leaf 1, front.** [ … ] he kills the bird. And again, just as the fire
that has come out of the wood sets the wood alight again. And again, just
as when the lamb or the calf, changing its body, has become a young lion
or a young wolf, (and) is born, and then in turn eats up and destroys
cattle, oxen and hares. And just as the tongs that press on the anvil,
made themselves of noble iron, in turn break through all iron. And just as
the louse of the coat, which has come from the skin of a man, in turn
sucks the man's own blood; when the man sees it, it is driven off (?).

So he explained it. Among men, through the five gods (?), they were born
in the five kinds of plants and trees.

**Leaf 1, back.** And through the five kinds of plants and trees (?) they
were born in this senseless body. Then, because for a long time they have
been tormented for the body, have fallen sick and died, because
everywhere they have suffered bitter torments, [ … ] the pain and torment
they themselves have endured [ … ]. And they quarrel with one another and
devour (?) one another. And, striking (?) one another, they call out to one
another: "May you be oppressed (?) by famine (?), wickedly and without
end! May you fall (?) into fire and flames!" Saying such things, they
revile and strike one another. This cursing and devouring (?), hating and
striking one another, like ignorant people, like abuse and deceit (?)
[ … ]. They themselves do not understand it so.

**Leaf 2, front.** [ … ] the coming of the Burxan [ … ] book [ … ] we have
found all. Oppression and deceit are not among us. Now, O our gracious
Father! O our good-doing prince! Countless myriads of years have passed
since we were parted from you. Your gracious, fair, innocent, shining face
[ … ]; your dear, shining, living face we long and yearn to see! In your
strength we have gone unharmed, unharmed we have come! (But) the things
you commanded, all of them,

**Leaf 2, back.** we have not carried out. Now, O my gracious, royal god!
Be gracious! Your eternally perfect, innocent being (self) we would see!
The torments we have suffered for so long we would forget! For ever
loving and joyful we would be!

*(A heading in red:)* [ … ] has been written [ … ] Śākyamuni [ … ]

You (they?) will often pray such prayers: then the Great King will reveal
and show his eternally gracious, beautiful face; then all will turn (?);
for ever joyful and loving you (they?) will be!

I, Zimtu (?), will be his companion in this good joy (?). For ever, for
ever, so may it be!

In the five hundred and twenty-second year, the year of the Pig, after the
going of the divine Mani Burxan to the realm of the gods, the lord of the
Law who lives in Ötükän, the most virtuous, gracious lord of wisdom, the
divine Mār Niw Mani, [ … ] to the *mahistak* Aiyïn (?) these two [ … ]

### T II D 173b: the rescue of Ohrmizd and the making of heaven and earth

*Second double leaf. Leaf 1, front. In red: "May there be joy!"*

[ … ] he pierced. Second: the whole realm of the gods, (and) its
well-being (?), he gave. Third: the good Law he gave. Fourth: to effort,
watchfulness and following he moved them. Fifth: [ … ]

**Back.** On his right, he opened his door to the realm of the gods. Just
as water opens the door of plants and trees on the earth, so also the god
Xroštag opened his door to the god Xormuzta and the five gods. When the
god Xroštag (and?) Padvaxtag had risen up from the god Xormuzta (and) from
hell, then the god Wadžiwantag and the Mother-God (?) came quickly. They
made the god Xormuzta rise up out of hell and come out, and sent him to
the realm of the gods, (he himself) the majesty of all.

And the Mother-God and the god Wadžiwantag separated the five gods from
the god Xormuzta. And (now) they made ready to create and make the earth
and the heaven. First of all they made and created the tenfold blue heaven
in this way, all at once, just as one lays out a new orchard and a house
and its furniture; and just as one makes plants spring up at once from
new ground; just as a male child comes from a man's strength: so too the
making of this earth and of the tenfold blue heaven was like (these
things). [ … ] And eleventh, they made the zodiac, and set it up out of
(?) seven kinds of virtue. The one is to be the fetter of all the demons;
the second (is to be) for all [ … ] (end of the back).

### T II D 173: a sermon on desire

*A leaf of the same book.*

**Front.** [ … ] will not be able. His parents will not be able to speak
such words of remembrance as could enlighten that man's mind. Goods and
property will not cling to his eye (will be worth nothing to him). However
many physicians may come with their herbs, they will not be able to heal
him. And all the priests, gathering together, will bring nothing to life:
they will not be able to give children. As, by no means, does horn (?)
sprout from the horse or the ass; as able men cannot do useless things; so
men and "long-robes" (women), however much they may not eat (?) of the
power of the five gods, cannot commit shameless acts by love of the body.
Sons and daughters

**Back.** they will by no means beget. Then, if the gods' power were food
and drink, then children would be born strong and great.

That lust of sin of yours, which comes from outside mixed with food and
drink, enters the body; it unites with the lust of sin within, which is in
the male and female body. Then your lust of sin becomes as strong as when
fire kindles dry firewood; and as the fish swims in the water; as seeds or
kernels sprout in a good place: so too your lust of sin becomes strong in
the body. Then your lust of sin [fills (?)] your own body from the head to
the tip of the toe-nail [ … ]

### Parables from a sermon

*The upper part of a leaf.*

**Front.** [ … ] as when a capable man's capability finds no property (earns
nothing), and he lays down all his business and goes about idle and
useless; as a man who cannot tell apart and understand these words
[ … ] his breast like the not-dark-eyed (?) [ … ]

**Back.** [As when] fire kindles and inflames firewood; as the calf which
flees (?) from the lion [ … ] makes tremble and tears; and the lamb which
flees (?) from the wolf kills; and the gripping tongs, which, made of iron,
[break up the iron] [ … ]

### T Ia: a fragment of cosmogony

**Front.** [ … ] he came down to the [ … ]. Those three demons he bound to
his zodiac. With his four shining powers he came down to this earth, as
Abamu Burxan [ … ] the god Xormuzta [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] was kind of heart: how did he do it, that he killed the
demon? If anyone should ask this in doubt, give this answer: the demon,
changing his words, spoke to all the evil spirits, declaring: "The poison
taken from you I will spit (throw) at the god Xormuzta; the god Xormuzta
with this [ … ]," he said. The poison he spat struck his own head. He fell
down, and humbled himself ten-thousandfold. The demon (said): "I (will?)
the god Xormuzta [ … ]" [ … ] the demons [ … ] they were [ … ] they ate and
killed, but he, with his body, fell into the front (?) of hell.

Then the god Xormuzta, making the fire-god into an axe, split the demon's
head; and making that fire-god like a lance of seventy myriad miles, (he
struck) the demon's head with the lance's point [ … ]

### From bundle 172: a mythological text

*The upper part of two badly damaged leaves.*

**Leaf 1, front.** [ … ] marvelling [ … ] It is the gentle breeze, the wind,
the light, the water and the fire (that is, the five gods): all these have
been put on the god Äzrua (as garments) and are united with him; the
bodies of these five gods of light, all [ … ]

**Leaf 1, back.** Happy be the owner of this writing! Through his wisdom
(*vidyā*) (?), his fame and his praise among all the gods in the realm of
the gods he thus makes appear, and spreads light and splendour, as the
[sun and moon god] by his splendour [lights up our] whole [earth], the
[five] kinds of living beings [ … ]

**Leaf 2, front.** [ … ] they find. Second, through his spirit, his bodily
[ … ], which itself (consists of) those living good thoughts which arise
from the god of the majesty of the Law [ … ] himself with his army [ … ]
because of all [ … ] his head [ … ]

**Leaf 2, back.** [ … ] I have written with reverence [ … ] the god Äzrua,
who is himself the elder brother and elder sister of all the gods of the
realm of the gods, the pure majesty; the shining mind (?) (mother?), the
pure thought [ … ] mighty [ … ]

### T II D 171: the end of a prayer book

*The end (?) of a prayer; the heading is torn off. A leaf written in many
coloured inks.*

**Front, right column.** He himself is the shining divine Mani Burxan. The
Elect, the hearer, he brings up by his wise knowledge; and as the eye is
dear to the foot, as the hand is dear to the mouth, so [ … ] to them [ … ]

*(Eighteen lines left empty, some later written over in a rough brush
hand.)*

[ … ] he was like (?): for an Elect a loving [ … ] is fitting [ … ]: all
men pray thus: "If [ … ] sin and corruption in my body and my bones [ … ]
should not have been found …"

**Front, left column.** So it will be fitting for the soul's sake to dwell
(?) without sin or fault in the shining, bright [Paradise of light]. Now he
has deigned (to speak) thus:

When the burxans and angels of Mani Burxan, of Aman (?), come, then they
appear in five ways. The first is by his gentleness, like the appearance
of the god Xormuzta. The second is by his severity (?), as is the way of
the god Wadžiwanta. *(Nine lines added later in a rough hand.)* The third
is by his beautiful form, as is the way of the shining sun-god. The fourth
is by his wise knowledge, as is the way of the prince who brings the dead
to life (?), the moon-god. And the fifth way is to change form and
appearance, as is the way of the beloved daughter of the princely king of
the gods, the god Äzrua: the radiant goddess of lightning [ … ] Wahman.

**Back, right column.** *(The heading is destroyed.)*

In the name of the exalted princely god Äzrua! It was spoken with great
joy; it was written down with deep love. Now, with the utmost zeal, it was
written in an illustrious place (?), by his awakening (?), this divine,
holy book of the Law, which [ … ] full of many, many kinds [ … ] leads the
souls to follow; which opens the mind and enlightens the breast; which
gives a right, sincere understanding, an orthodox one, in the three
times, leading to election, a living being that walks (aright), that will
lead to the shining realm of the gods; namely the divine wise knowledge,
sweeter than the drink of immortality.

month and in a victorious, happy year; in the breast of the praised (?),

I, Yapγun, a hearer who believes in both palaces of light, have recited

I, Arslan Mängü, a hearer who firmly believes in both palaces of light,

Die  hier  veröffentlichten  türkischen  manichcäisch-religiösen  Bruchstücke  sind 
zum  Teil,  wie  T.  M.  i8o  und  T.  II  D.  75a,  sehr  stark  verstümmelt;  zum

deren  Zusammenhang   unterbrochen   ist. 
Ich  kann  daher  nur  den  Versuch  einer  Übersetzung  bieten,  habe  mich 
aber  zur  Veröffentlichung  dieser  Handschriftenreste  entschlossen,  weil  einer- 
seits die  Überwindung  der  erwähnten  Schwierigkeiten  seit  dem  Erscheinen 
meiner  Arbeit  »Manichaica  I«  keiiu'rlei  Fortschritte  gemacht  hat,  anderer- 
seits, weil  ein  befreundeter  Religionsgeschichtler  mich,  des  Inhalts  der 
Bruchstücke  halber,  lebhaft  zu  diesem  Schritt  ermuntert  hat:  es  besteht 
die  Hoffnung,  daß  durch  das  Studium  der  Realien  die  Deutung  erleichtert 
und  gefordert  werden   werde. 
Da  meine  früheren  Versuche  sachlicher  Erklärungen  eine  unfreundliche 
Kritik  in  der  »Theologischen  Literaturzeitung  (191  2)«  erfahren  haben,  sehe 
ich,  obwohl  ich  eine  Berichtigung  veranlaßt  habe  (ebd.  Spalte  732),  davon 
al),  die  vorliegenden  Stücke  anders  als  durch  ihre  Übersetzung  zu  erklären, 
und  beschränke  mich  darauf,  eine  kurze  Zu.sammenfassung  des  Inhalts  zu 
geben. 
Das  stark  zerstörte  Bruchstück  T.  M.  180,  welches,  beiläufig  bemerkt, 
mit  T.  M.  419  zu  der  Ausbeute  der  Ersten  Turfan-Expedition  der  HH. 
GrC'nwekel  und  Hlth  gehört,  entliält  eine  Schilderung  des  Auftretens  des 
»falschen  Mithras«;  ob  es  sich  um  einen  bevorstehenden  Kampf  zwischen 
dem  wahren  Mithras  und  seinem  dämonischen  Nebenbuhler  handelt,  geht 
aus  der  Handschrift  nicht  mit  Sicherheit  hervor. 
Noch  stärker  zerstört  ist  das  zweite  Stück,  T.  II  I)  75a:  es  gehört  wie

ersten  Turfanreise  (Zweite  Turfan-Expedition).  Wichtig  ist  darin  der  Hinweis 
auf  »die  Kinder  (o'ilan)  der  Dämonen,  die  von  den  Himmeln  zur  Erde  nieder- 
gefallen waren«  und  die  Erwähnung  »des  Samens  jener  männlichen  Wesen«. 
Es  ist  ohne  Zweifel  ein  Stück  der  manichäischen  Kosmogonie;  wie  so  häufig 
bei  diesen  Resten,  setzt  die  Zerstörung  gerade  an  der  Stelle  ein,  von  der 
man  Aufschlüsse  erwarten   dürfte. 
Die  übrigen  Bruchstücke  enthalten  Gesänge,  von  denen  einer,  T.  M.  419, 
als  »Lied«  (wörtl.  Melodie,  küg),  die  übrigen  als  »Hymnen«  (bSS,  bäSik,  mittel- 
pers.)  bezeichnet  werden. 
Das  »Lied«  enthält  einen  Lobgesang  auf  eine  manichäische  Gottheit, 
ist  aber  deutlich  nacli  buddhistischem  Muster  verfaßt.  Der  Name  des  tür- 
kischen Verfassers  (?),  des  Fürsten  (tigin)  Aprm-c(jr  wird  wiederholt  erwähnt. 
Von  den  Hymnen  (öäi,  büäk)  befinden  sich  drei  auf  einem  Blatte,  das 
mit  einem  ebensolchen  zweiten  Blatt  zusammen  ein  wohlerhaltenes  Doppel- 
buchblatt bildet.  Dies  zweite  Blatt  enthält  einen  soghdischen  manichäischen 
Text  mit  kurzem  türkischen  Endkolophon  in  »köktürkischen«  Runen;  das 
Buch,  von  dem  noch  weitere  Blattreste  mit  iranischem  Inhalt  gefunden 
worden  sind,  dürfte  ein  liturgisches  Werk  gewesen  sein.  Die  beiden  ersten 
Hymnen  sind  vollständig,  gut  erhalten  und  inhaltlich  einfach :  sie  sind  ge- 
richtet: I  an  »den  Gott  der  Morgenröte«,  II  an  die  »Vier  großherrlichen 
Wesenheiten«.  Der  dritte  Hymnus  ist  der  wichtigste;  er  beschäftigt  sich 
in  der  Hauptsache  mit  dem  Schicksal  der  Seele  nach  dem  Tod  und  schildert 
eine  der  dann  erscheinenden  Schreckgestalten.  Leider  bricht  der  Text  zu 
früh  ab ;   die   Anzahl  der  unerklärten  Wörter  ist  bedeutend. 
Das  letzte  Bruchstück,  ein  durch  Wurmfraß  beschädigtes  Buchblatt 
(ebenfalls  die  Hälfte  eines  Doppelbuchblattes!)  entstammt  gleichfalls  einem 
liturgischen  Werke;  dieses  Buch  enthielt,  neben  mittelpersischen  Hymnen, 
auch  jene  Blätter  des  Bußgebets  der  manichäischen  auditores,  die  auf  Taf.  I 
und  II  des  in  dem  »Anhang  zu  den  Abhandlungen«  veröffentlichten  »Chu- 
astuanift«  wiedergegeben  worden  sind.  Es  scheint  ebenfalls  das  Schicksal 
der  Seele  eines  Gestorbenen  und  das  Erscheinen  einer  Schreckgestalt  zu 
Türkische Manichaica aiis Chotscho. II.

---
title: "Old Turkish hymns from Qočo: the dawn, the four majesties and the soul after death"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 71
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with a love-song to a god in Buddhist style, short hymns to the god of dawn and the four majesties, and two accounts of the soul after death, the hag-demon and the scales of judgement.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T M 180, T II D 75a, T M 419, T II D 169 and T II D 178 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. II", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1919, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 3 (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1919 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

Le Coq's second set of Old Turkish Manichaean texts from Qočo (1919) has
two badly damaged prose pieces, one on a "false Mithras" (T M 180) and one
from the cosmogony on "the children of the demons who had fallen from the
heavens to the earth" (T II D 75a), and then songs and hymns. One is a
love-song to a god, in the Buddhist manner, by a prince named Aprin Čor
Tigin (T M 419). Three short hymns stand on one leaf of a liturgical
book whose other leaf is in Sogdian (T II D 169): to the god of dawn, to
"the four majesties", and a hymn on what happens to the soul after death.
A last leaf (T II D 178), from a book that also held the hearers'
confession, describes the soul at the judgement.

Le Coq offered his German only as "an attempt at a translation", and many
words were unknown to him.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### T M 180: the false Mithras

*A piece from the middle of a larger leaf; the beginning and end are torn
away. Only scattered words can be read.*

**Front.** [ … ] two [ … ] Mithra on the earth (or: on the earth of
Mithra) [ … ] of the demon [ … ] will come, saying [ … ] I, I [ … ] the
Elect [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] to the Elect [ … ] their great [ … ] to believe, he will
[ … ] the fortune and [ … ] (the son of?) that Mani (?) [ … ]

### T II D 75a: the children of the demons

*A piece of a leaf, badly damaged by worms.*

**Front.** [ … ] in the heavy [ … ] he is lifted up [ … ] I will again [ … ]
I will be powerless [ … ] I will do this [ … ] let it not settle [ … ] "I
will not bear the torment," saying. Your lust, again, (consists of) all
those children of the demons who [fell] from the heavens [to the earth]
[ … ] of those male beings [ … ] (the rest has faded).

**Back.** *(Only known words without connection. In red ink, faint:)* [ … ]
the end of the sixth (?) [ … ] sun (and) moon [ … ]

### T M 419: the song of Aprin Čor Tigin

**Front.** The song of Aprin Čor Tigin has begun.

O you, excellent in the jewel, my good diamond thunderbolt, it is said!
You, in the diamond thunderbolt [ … ], my knowing one, my righteous one, my
shining one! [ … ] wise one! [ … ] like the splendour of the sun-god, my
dear one, my wise one! You, my fair, righteous god! You, my famous one!
You, my longing (?)! You, my fair, righteous [ … ]! God, you my Burxan! You,
my unreachable one (who cannot be found)!

Ended is the song of Aprin Čor Tigin.

[ … ] my wise one [ … ] my writer (?), my righteous one, my shining one
[ … ] my knowing one [ … ] my breast, my wise one; like the light of the
sun-god, my breast, my wise one; my fair, righteous god [ … ] my glory, my
seeing one (?); fair, righteous [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] different [ … ] you, my handsome one! [ … ] another, beloved
[ … ] beloved [ … ]

Through my [ … ] I feel care; having felt care, I long for union with my
fair-browed one! I think of my own dear one; thinking [ … ], I long to kiss
my own beloved! If I would go, my [ … ] dear one, I cannot go, you my
merciful one! If I would go in, you my little one, I cannot go in [ … ] you
my musk-scented one! By the gracious command of the gods of light, having
gained union (?) with my gentle one, let us not be parted!

You strong angels! Give (me) strength (?)! With my dark-eyed one [ … ] in
joy (?) let us sit down!

The song of Aprin Čor Tigin has ended.

### T II D 169, hymn I: to the god of dawn

*Three hymns stand in this order on one leaf of a double leaf; the other
leaf has Manichaean texts in Sogdian.*

The hymn of the god Wām (dawn).

The god of dawn has come! The god of dawn himself has come!
The god of dawn has come! The god of dawn himself has come!
Rise up, all you lords and companions! Let us praise the god of dawn!
Seeing sun-god, protect us! Visible moon-god, save us!
God of dawn! Musk-scented, shining, radiant god! God of dawn! Fivefold god
(or: five gods) of dawn!
Fivefold god of dawn! Scented, shining, radiant god of dawn! God of dawn!

(End.)

### T II D 169, hymn II: to the four majesties

A hymn to the "four great majesties".

Before God, the Light, the Strong, the Wise, we humble ourselves and pray
to him. The sun and moon god, the god of light, the majesty of the
religion, the angels of Mār Mānī we worship. O my God! Protect our body!
Purify our soul! We pray for welfare. For the gods of light let us live
unharmed! Let us be in joy!

(End.)

### T II D 169, hymn III: the soul after death

Another Turkish hymn.

We righteous, wise men, let us gather! Let us hear the book of God! Let
us offer worship to the four princely gods! Let us be set free from the
four great torments, that is: from denying the four princely gods; from
keeping the Law of God badly; from worshipping the dark demons; from
doing ten thousand evil deeds.

In the end one must die, too, and there is a falling into dark hell.
(Then), it is said, ten thousand demons come; black-misted demons hover
(?) near, it is said. Dark night presses on (the dead), it is said;
oppression (?) falls on him, it is said; sitting on his breast, she makes
him dream (?), it is said; lost (?) spirits come out, it is said. Like a
[ … ] he lays down his body (he dies), it is said. His goods are held back,
it is said.

A false (lying), hairy, grey-haired demoness comes, it is said. Her [ … ]
is like the hill-cloud; with eyebrows [ … ]; like a bloody [ … ] is her
glance, it is said; like a nail, of black colour, is her teat, it is said;
from her nose a grey cloud rises, it is said; from her throat black smoke
comes out, it is said; her breast is (made) all of ten thousand snakes; her
[ … ] is the thread-snake (?); her finger is all [ … ] (end of the leaf).

### T II D 178: the soul at the judgement

*One leaf of a double leaf with rounded corners. On both sides of the other
leaf is a Manichaean hymn in Middle Persian.*

**Front.** [ … ] says, it is said [ … ]. The deeds he himself has done
appear, it is said. The majesty of earth and water is grieved (?), it is
said. The majesty of fire and water weeps, it is said. The majesty of the
plants and trees wails aloud, it is said. The righteous official has
seized the lost soul, which appears as in a mirror. It is set down in the
scales, it is said. When the scales rise, its deed [ … ]; its ill-done deed
becomes [ … ] (end of the page).

**Back.** The coming of the lying, hairy, grey-haired demoness, and her
seizing of the lost (wandering) souls. Into the dark hell she drags them,
it is said; striking them on the head, she thrusts them in, it is said.
The demons that are in hell seize them, it is said. The [ … ] demons come,
it is said [ … ], it is said. Many souls she sees there. To pray for death
is in vain. (She begs for death, but does not find it.) (End of the page.)

## Notes to this edition

- **"It is said"** (Turkish *tiyür*) closes almost every clause of hymn III
  and T II D 178: the hymn reports what the scriptures say of death.
- **The four majesties** (hymn II, and the "four princely gods" of hymn
  III): Le Coq refers to al-Nadīm's "God, his Light, his Power and his
  Wisdom", the four-fold Father of Greatness.
- **Wām** (hymn I) is a Sogdian word for dawn or splendour; Le Coq notes
  that the title is not good Turkish.
- **The hag-demon** of hymn III and T II D 178 is the same figure in both:
  Le Coq compares "false" (*tärtrü*) with its use in the hearers' confession.
  Iranian eschatology has a similar ugly hag who meets the wicked soul.
- **"The righteous official"** (T II D 178): Le Coq compares Chinese
  Buddhist paintings of the judgement of the dead.
- **The song of Aprin Čor Tigin** (T M 419) speaks of the god as a beloved;
  Le Coq notes that it is plainly written on a Buddhist model.

+text: true
+group: extracanonical
+order: 71

+summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with a love-song to a god in Buddhist style, short hymns to the god of dawn and the four majesties, and two accounts of the soul after death, the hag-demon and the scales of judgement.
+original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)

+source: 'Turfan manuscripts T M 180, T II D 75a, T M 419, T II D 169 and T II D 178 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. II", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1919, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 3 (public domain). New English translation.'
+rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1919 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
+## Introduction
+Le Coq's second set of Old Turkish Manichaean texts from Qočo (1919) has
+two badly damaged prose pieces, one on a "false Mithras" (T M 180) and one
+from the cosmogony on "the children of the demons who had fallen from the
+heavens to the earth" (T II D 75a), and then songs and hymns. One is a
+love-song to a god, in the Buddhist manner, by a prince named Aprin Čor
+Tigin (T M 419). Three short hymns stand on one leaf of a liturgical
+book whose other leaf is in Sogdian (T II D 169): to the god of dawn, to
+"the four majesties", and a hymn on what happens to the soul after death.
+A last leaf (T II D 178), from a book that also held the hearers'
+confession, describes the soul at the judgement.
+Le Coq offered his German only as "an attempt at a translation", and many
+words were unknown to him.
+**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
+marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
+parentheses are added for sense.
+## The translation
+### T M 180: the false Mithras
+*A piece from the middle of a larger leaf; the beginning and end are torn
+away. Only scattered words can be read.*
+**Front.** [ … ] two [ … ] Mithra on the earth (or: on the earth of
+Mithra) [ … ] of the demon [ … ] will come, saying [ … ] I, I [ … ] the
+Elect [ … ]
+**Back.** [ … ] to the Elect [ … ] their great [ … ] to believe, he will
+[ … ] the fortune and [ … ] (the son of?) that Mani (?) [ … ]
+### T II D 75a: the children of the demons
+*A piece of a leaf, badly damaged by worms.*
+**Front.** [ … ] in the heavy [ … ] he is lifted up [ … ] I will again [ … ]
+I will be powerless [ … ] I will do this [ … ] let it not settle [ … ] "I
+will not bear the torment," saying. Your lust, again, (consists of) all
+those children of the demons who [fell] from the heavens [to the earth]
+[ … ] of those male beings [ … ] (the rest has faded).
+**Back.** *(Only known words without connection. In red ink, faint:)* [ … ]
+the end of the sixth (?) [ … ] sun (and) moon [ … ]
+### T M 419: the song of Aprin Čor Tigin
+**Front.** The song of Aprin Čor Tigin has begun.
+O you, excellent in the jewel, my good diamond thunderbolt, it is said!
+You, in the diamond thunderbolt [ … ], my knowing one, my righteous one, my
+shining one! [ … ] wise one! [ … ] like the splendour of the sun-god, my
+dear one, my wise one! You, my fair, righteous god! You, my famous one!
+You, my longing (?)! You, my fair, righteous [ … ]! God, you my Burxan! You,
+my unreachable one (who cannot be found)!
+Ended is the song of Aprin Čor Tigin.
+[ … ] my wise one [ … ] my writer (?), my righteous one, my shining one
+[ … ] my knowing one [ … ] my breast, my wise one; like the light of the
+sun-god, my breast, my wise one; my fair, righteous god [ … ] my glory, my
+seeing one (?); fair, righteous [ … ]
+**Back.** [ … ] different [ … ] you, my handsome one! [ … ] another, beloved
+[ … ] beloved [ … ]
+Through my [ … ] I feel care; having felt care, I long for union with my
+fair-browed one! I think of my own dear one; thinking [ … ], I long to kiss
+my own beloved! If I would go, my [ … ] dear one, I cannot go, you my
+merciful one! If I would go in, you my little one, I cannot go in [ … ] you
+my musk-scented one! By the gracious command of the gods of light, having
+gained union (?) with my gentle one, let us not be parted!
+You strong angels! Give (me) strength (?)! With my dark-eyed one [ … ] in
+joy (?) let us sit down!
+The song of Aprin Čor Tigin has ended.
+### T II D 169, hymn I: to the god of dawn
+*Three hymns stand in this order on one leaf of a double leaf; the other
+leaf has Manichaean texts in Sogdian.*
+The hymn of the god Wām (dawn).
+The god of dawn has come! The god of dawn himself has come!
+The god of dawn has come! The god of dawn himself has come!
+Rise up, all you lords and companions! Let us praise the god of dawn!
+Seeing sun-god, protect us! Visible moon-god, save us!
+God of dawn! Musk-scented, shining, radiant god! God of dawn! Fivefold god
+(or: five gods) of dawn!
+Fivefold god of dawn! Scented, shining, radiant god of dawn! God of dawn!
+(End.)
+### T II D 169, hymn II: to the four majesties
+A hymn to the "four great majesties".
+Before God, the Light, the Strong, the Wise, we humble ourselves and pray
+to him. The sun and moon god, the god of light, the majesty of the
+religion, the angels of Mār Mānī we worship. O my God! Protect our body!
+Purify our soul! We pray for welfare. For the gods of light let us live
+unharmed! Let us be in joy!
+(End.)
+### T II D 169, hymn III: the soul after death
+Another Turkish hymn.
+We righteous, wise men, let us gather! Let us hear the book of God! Let
+us offer worship to the four princely gods! Let us be set free from the
+four great torments, that is: from denying the four princely gods; from
+keeping the Law of God badly; from worshipping the dark demons; from
+doing ten thousand evil deeds.
+In the end one must die, too, and there is a falling into dark hell.
+(Then), it is said, ten thousand demons come; black-misted demons hover
+(?) near, it is said. Dark night presses on (the dead), it is said;
+oppression (?) falls on him, it is said; sitting on his breast, she makes
+him dream (?), it is said; lost (?) spirits come out, it is said. Like a
+[ … ] he lays down his body (he dies), it is said. His goods are held back,
+it is said.
+A false (lying), hairy, grey-haired demoness comes, it is said. Her [ … ]
+is like the hill-cloud; with eyebrows [ … ]; like a bloody [ … ] is her
+glance, it is said; like a nail, of black colour, is her teat, it is said;
+from her nose a grey cloud rises, it is said; from her throat black smoke
+comes out, it is said; her breast is (made) all of ten thousand snakes; her
+[ … ] is the thread-snake (?); her finger is all [ … ] (end of the leaf).
+### T II D 178: the soul at the judgement
+*One leaf of a double leaf with rounded corners. On both sides of the other
+leaf is a Manichaean hymn in Middle Persian.*
+**Front.** [ … ] says, it is said [ … ]. The deeds he himself has done
+appear, it is said. The majesty of earth and water is grieved (?), it is
+said. The majesty of fire and water weeps, it is said. The majesty of the
+plants and trees wails aloud, it is said. The righteous official has
+seized the lost soul, which appears as in a mirror. It is set down in the
+scales, it is said. When the scales rise, its deed [ … ]; its ill-done deed
+becomes [ … ] (end of the page).
+**Back.** The coming of the lying, hairy, grey-haired demoness, and her
+seizing of the lost (wandering) souls. Into the dark hell she drags them,
+it is said; striking them on the head, she thrusts them in, it is said.
+The demons that are in hell seize them, it is said. The [ … ] demons come,
+it is said [ … ], it is said. Many souls she sees there. To pray for death
+is in vain. (She begs for death, but does not find it.) (End of the page.)
+## Notes to this edition
+- **"It is said"** (Turkish *tiyür*) closes almost every clause of hymn III
+  and T II D 178: the hymn reports what the scriptures say of death.
+- **The four majesties** (hymn II, and the "four princely gods" of hymn
+  III): Le Coq refers to al-Nadīm's "God, his Light, his Power and his
+  Wisdom", the four-fold Father of Greatness.
+- **Wām** (hymn I) is a Sogdian word for dawn or splendour; Le Coq notes
+  that the title is not good Turkish.
+- **The hag-demon** of hymn III and T II D 178 is the same figure in both:
+  Le Coq compares "false" (*tärtrü*) with its use in the hearers' confession.
+  Iranian eschatology has a similar ugly hag who meets the wicked soul.
+- **"The righteous official"** (T II D 178): Le Coq compares Chinese
+  Buddhist paintings of the judgement of the dead.
+- **The song of Aprin Čor Tigin** (T M 419) speaks of the god as a beloved;
+  Le Coq notes that it is plainly written on a Buddhist model.

Phü.-hist.  Klasse..    1912.    Abh.  V.

Zum  Druck  eingereicht  am  gleichen  Tage,  ausgegeben  am   19.  April  1913. 
In  seinen  Tableaux  historiques  de  l'Asie  S.  124  hat  uns  Klaproth  schon 
1826  ein  Bild  von  der  Civilisation  der  Uiguren  entworfen,  das  auch  heute 
noch,  nacli  so  mannigfacher  Bereicherung  unseres  Wissens  auf  diesem  Felde, 
als  wesentlich  richtig  bezeichnet  werden  muß.  Die  Zusammenfassung  am 
Schlüsse  seiner  Ausführungen  ist  auch  jetzt  noch  die  beste  Charakteri- 
sierung der  uigurischen  Civilisation.  Was  die  Forschung  seitdem  geleistet 
hat,  ist  gewissermaßen  nur  die  Ausmalung  der  von  ihm  schon  entworfenen 
Umrisse. 
»Ein  chinesischer  Reisender,  der  am  Ende  des  10.  Jahrhunderts  in 
Si-tschou  war,  fand  in  dieser  Stadt  mehr  als  fünfzig  Buddhatempel,  meist 
auf  Befehl  chinesischer  Kaiser  errichtet.  In  diesen  Tempeln  bewahrte  man 
das  Gesetzesbuch  auf  und  chinesische  Werke,  wie  das  Tonwörterbuch  der 
Thang-Dynastie,  das  Vokabular  Yü-pien  und  die  Kommentare  zu  den  King 
oder  klassischen  Büchern.  In  anderen  Teilen  der  Stadt  sah  man  öffentliche 
Bibliotheken,  wo  sich  die  Erlasse  des  Kaisers  Thai-tsung,  des  Gründers 
der  Thang-Dynastie,  befanden.  Es  gab  auch  Tempel  der  Religion  des  Mo  ni 
oder  Manes  [!]',  der  Priester  aus  Pho  szü  oder  Persien,  d.h.  Anhänger 
des  Zoroaster,  und  andere,  wo  jeder  sein  Gesetz  befolgte,  und  welche  in 
den  Büchern  der  Buddhisten  mit  dem  Namen  , äußere  Lehren'  bezeichnet 
werden.     Die  Sprache  des  Landes  hieß  damals  ui-gu-el  oder  uigur  usw.  .  .  . 
1  Also  schon  1826  die  richtige  Erklärung  des  Wortes.  Der  sichere  Blick  Klaproths 
verdient  hervorgehoben  zu  weiden,  wenn  man  sieht,  wie  noch  50  Jahre  später  Schott, 
der  übrigens  die  chinesischen  beiden  Zeichen  richtiger  Ma-ni  las,  zur  Übersetzung  Mani- 
chäer  ein  Fragezeichen  setzt.  Erst  1897,  durch  Deveria  undMarquart,  wurde  die  immer 
wieder  angezweifelte  Gleichsetzung  endgültig  bewiesen.  —  Auch  bezüglich  der  rothaarigen 
und  blauäugigen  Centralasiaten  hat  Klaproth  in  der  Sache  wenigstens  Recht  behalten, 
wenn  auch   seine  Etymologien   beute  nur  noch  als  Spielereien  angesehen   werden  können.

4  F.W.  K.  Müller: 
Man  ersieht  aus  dieser  Erzählung,  daß  die  eigentlich  sogenannten 
Uiguren  in  dieser  Epoche  eine  (ivilisation  chinesischen,  indischen 
und  abendländischen   Ursprungs  besaßen.« 
Die  hier  angeführte  Stelle  stammt  aus  dem  Gesandtschaftsberichte  des 
Wang  Yen-tö,  der  nachmalig  noch  von  Stan.  Julien  und  Schott'  be- 
arbeitet worden  ist. 
Letzterer  besonders  hat  versucht,  ein  anschauliches  Bild  von  dem  Leben 
und  Treiben  an  dem  Hofe  des  Uigurenfürsten  in  der  Sommerresidenz  Pe-thing 
zu  entwerfen. 
»Am  siebenten  Tage  der  Ankunft  war  großer  Empfang.  Eine  An- 
zahl Hofleute  schlug  den  Takt  der  Begrüßungen  auf  Tafeln  aus  Klingstein, 
während  König  und  Königskinder  beiderlei  Geschlechts  um  die  Reihe  vor- 
traten und  mit  gen  Osten  gewendetem  Gesicht,  den  Huldigungsgruß  dar- 
bringend, die  für  sie  bestimmten  Geschenke  an  sich  nahmen.  Dann  gab 
es  ein  festliches  Gelage  mit  Saitenspiel  und  theatralischen  Aufführungen  bis 
zum  Abend.  Des  andern  Tages  machte  man  eine  Lustfahrt  auf  einem 
kleinen  See,  während  von  allen  Ufern  her  Musik  ertönte.  Am  dritten  Tage 
besuchte  der  Chakan  mit  seinen  Gästen  einen  Buddhatempel,  welcher  vor 
mehr  als  drei  Jahrhunderten  (.  .  640)  erbaut  war.« 
»Also«  —  sagt  Schott  —  »feierliche  Vorstellung,  Festmahl,  Theater, 
Lustfahrt  mit  Musik,  und  endlich  Besuch  eines  der  Religion  geheiligten 
Gebäudes,  als  sollte  dem  Saus  und  Braus  zweier  Tage  am  dritten  eine  Art 
Aschermittwochbuße  nachfolgen.  Zur  vollständigen  Analogie  mit  abend- 
ländischen Sitten   fehlte   nur   eine  Truppenschau   oder   ein  Scheintreft'en.«

essante Einblicke  in  die  merkwürdigen  Mischungen  von  Völkern,  Sprachen 
und  Kulturen  an  diesem  mittelasiatischen  Hofe  ermöglichen.

input.content:
---
title: "The Mahrnāmag: preface and contents of a Manichaean hymnbook"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 72
summary: The Middle Persian preface of a hymnbook from Turfan, blessing the Uyghur khan and his court, telling how the book was begun in the 546th year after Mani's birth and finished long after, and listing the first lines of its hymns.
original_language: Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan manuscript M 1 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by F. W. K. Müller, "Ein Doppelblatt aus einem manichäischen Hymnenbuch (Mahrnāmag)", Abhandlungen der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1912, Phil.-hist. Klasse, Abh. V (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Müller's 1912 German, with his transcription in view; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

M 1 is a nearly complete double leaf from a Manichaean hymnbook
(*mahrnāmag*, "book of hymns") in Middle Persian. The first leaf is the
preface: a long blessing on the reigning Uyghur khan, his family and his
court, with dozens of names and titles in Turkish, Sogdian, Persian and
Chinese, followed by an account of how the book came to be written. The
second leaf is part of the table of contents: the first lines of the
hymns, in alphabetical order, in four sections.

The account of the book's making is the most important part. It was begun
"in the year five hundred and forty-six after the birth of the Envoy of
Light", and in the year 162 after the death of Mār Šād Ohrmizd, but the
scribe could not finish it, and it lay unfinished "for many years" in a
building of the fortress until the preacher Yazd-āmad found it and had it
completed.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from F. W. K. Müller's German
of 1912. Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Müller marked as guesses are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense. The table of contents gives
only the first words of each hymn, which end in "…" in the manuscript.

## The translation

### Leaf 1, front: the blessing on the khan and his house

*Heading: "Invocation of the hearers".*

[May they send] health and wholeness, the two "glories" and the two
blessednesses, to these our rulers, the lords: first of all to the most
blessed of those born, the shining "limb" of the Envoy of Light, the pious
hearer *Ai Tängridä Qut Bulmïš Alp Bilgä*, khan of the Uyghurs, the
protector (?) of the apostles, the patron of the righteous and pure (the
Elect); and also to his offspring and his royal line, the princes and
princesses: first of all to Yultuzbai Tegin, Ügä Peröz Tegin, Xasar Tegin,
Vazurgān Tegin, Tatar Apa Tegin, Zireft Tegin and Nev Tegin, these
princes;

and to the lords, the mighty: Savag Tutuq, Čïq Tutuq; and the *čigšis*,
the *tiräks*; and also Il-Ügäsi Kadoš, the *niyōšagbed* (master of the
hearers), the shining "limb" of the Envoy of Light; and to the
Il-Ügäsis: Ötür Ügä, Savčï Buga (?) Tarxan Ügä, Bilig Köngül Sangun Ügä,
Batur Sangun Ügä, Tai Buga (?) Tarxan Ügä, Nizük Sangun Ügä, these lords,
the mighty. And also those whose names I have not mentioned (?): may they
live and prosper for ever, Amen!

And also the lord of Panjkand (Pentapolis), Beg Künki Taisangun Sirtuš;
Yägän Apa, the shining hearer; Türlüg Apa Sansïz Pačag; and the hearers
Mašïān Mahārāj, Ärklig Zāryūd, Türk [ … ].

Also the lord of Čīnānčkand, Tapïγlïγ Sangun; Vagšemāx Tapmïš Tarxan;
Isïq Ingi Ičräki; Vanōmāx Tontarxan; Körtlä Čur Tusuč; Yaγlaqar Inal;
Vanōšer Amal; Orungu Yaramïš; Iznačū Pūtyān; Gāv Pāx Isïγ; Iznačū Indun;
Dašāpat Yišōvarz; Simāk Māxyān; Tupa Fušï Bägräk Čur Bändäk Aspaste.

Also Äküčik Sirtuši Yïdduq Čur, Nigōšak (hearer) Tarxan; Kāšī Xšēd (the
lord of Kashgar?); Lifūtūšī Nigōšakpat (master of the hearers); Parvānč
Žaβγu (the *yabγu* of Parvān); Liūläng Xūmār Čur; Yišōvarz Bagerez; and
Xarakul La Čur; Mahāyān; Kāvfarn; Dačāpat; Freštvarz Čapïš; Tsü-si-läng
Šemgōn; Ūtam Nōimāx Xazān; Zvānak Wage-zvān; Denfrād-šadak; Vagšefarn;
Wagefarn; Bagebirat.

Also the lord of the fortress, Ičräki Itmïš Zim-tai-ši; Uyγur Tapmïš;
Lit Bir Uyγur Tapmïš; Yaβγu Taγarmï Čapïš; Ulugfuši; Tangfuši; Lafuši;
Ončur Yišōyān; Asag Tulïš Yïnal; Tamgan Tarxan; and Satōyān Nigōšakpat;
Rōxšyān Biāmanvarz Čur; Iznačū Rēzyān; Iltutguvānčik; Liük Lata; Lāzih;
Māxfarn the physician; Xutpāyan the interpreter; Pauk (?) Panxuan; Tsu
Panxuan; Pārak Bōg; Lāfarn; Zernvāk (Gold-voice) Yāhm Yāki Togarak (the
Tocharian?) Čuftgui Fatak.

The lord Isïγ Tarxan; Sinaamgä (?) Nigōšakpat; Yargan Anzirki [ … ]

### Leaf 1, back: the officials and the women hearers

*(The list continues with further officials, among them a physician and
scribes, and then:)* the women, the hearers: [ … ] the leader of the women
hearers [ … ]; *(and after a further list of names, among them Qut Xatun,
Qutluγ Qïz Tolun, Farnwām, and many names ending in -wām and Xatun:)* these
pious hearers, brothers and sisters, great and small: may the angels
themselves protect them in body and soul for ever! Amen, Amen! So may it
be!

*(Five lines left empty.)*

### The making of the book

In the year five hundred and forty-six after the birth of the Envoy of
Light, [that is,] now, in the year [ … ] *(left blank)* after he was
raised up in power, and in the year one hundred and sixty-two after the
raising up (the death) of Mār Šād Ohrmizd, the wise, it was that this
hymnbook was begun, which is full of living words and beautiful songs.

The scribe who began to write it at the command of the spiritual heads was
not able to finish writing it. Because he could not [ … ], he wrote a few
hymns, but he did not bring it to an end. Unfinished, it lay in that place
for many years, kept in a dwelling of the fortress.

Then I, Yazd-āmad, the preacher, when I saw it lying there, [ … ] again
(gave it) to my dearest son, the beloved Nīxvarīg-rōšan ("seed of light"
?), to finish it: so that it might become in the faith a means (?) of
increase, a hymnbook in the hands of the children of the faith, the new
disciples, so that the spirits might be taught by it, and gain teaching,
insight, instruction and skill from it [ … ].

By the blessing of Yazd [ … ] Mār Aryānšāh, the new teacher (?), and the
good omen; and by the good fortune of Mār Dōšist, the deacon; and by the
good guidance (?) of [ … ], the presbyter; and by the diligence of
Yazd-āmad, the wise preacher; and further and more by the zeal [and] care
of Nīxvarīg-rōšan, who was the most eager in it with a warm heart and a
loving mind: they have, nights and days, together with the scribes [ … ]
that I, on account of this writing, I, Nīxvarīg-rōšan, the servant, the
scribe in the preparing, arranging and writing [ … ] (end of the second
page).

## Notes to this edition

- **The khan** of the preface bears the throne-name *Ai Tängridä Qut
  Bulmïš Alp Bilgä*. Müller distinguished him from the khan who first
  brought Manichaeism to the Uyghurs (Bögü Khan, who reigned 759–780 and
  is called "emanation of Mani" in another fragment, T II D 135); the khan
  here is called "the shining limb of the Envoy of Light".
- **The date.** Five hundred and forty-six years after the birth of Mani
  (born 216) is the year 762, the year the Uyghurs adopted Manichaeism.
  The year "after he was raised up in power" was left blank by the scribe.
  Mār Šād Ohrmizd was a head of the eastern Manichaean church.
- **Panjkand and Čīnānčkand**: Müller took Panjkand to be the "Pentapolis"
  (the five cities of the Beshbalïq region) and Čīnānčkand to be the
  "Chinese town" (Qočo).
- **The section titles** of the table of contents: the first red end-title
  that survives marks the songs "on the passing away", that is, laments for
  the dead. The hymns run alphabetically by their first letter in the
  Manichaean script within each section, so the English order follows the

## Notes to this edition

- **The khan** of the preface bears the throne-name *Ai Tängridä Qut
  Bulmïš Alp Bilgä*. Müller distinguished him from the khan who first
  brought Manichaeism to the Uyghurs (Bögü Khan, who reigned 759–780 and
  is called "emanation of Mani" in another fragment, T II D 135); the khan
  here is called "the shining limb of the Envoy of Light".
- **The date.** Five hundred and forty-six years after the birth of Mani
  (born 216) is the year 762, the year the Uyghurs adopted Manichaeism.
  The year "after he was raised up in power" was left blank by the scribe.
  Mār Šād Ohrmizd was a head of the eastern Manichaean church.
- **Panjkand and Čīnānčkand**: Müller took Panjkand to be the "Pentapolis"
  (the five cities of the Beshbalïq region) and Čīnānčkand to be the
  "Chinese town" (Qočo).
- **The section titles** of the table of contents: the first red end-title
  that survives marks the songs "on the passing away", that is, laments for
  the dead. The hymns run alphabetically by their first letter in the
  Manichaean script within each section, so the English order follows the
  manuscript, not the English alphabet.
- **Names.** The spellings of personal names follow Müller's readings, in
  simplified form. Many are uncertain, and modern editions read some of
  them differently.

## Notes to this edition

- **The khan** of the preface bears the throne-name *Ai Tängridä Qut
  Bulmïš Alp Bilgä*. Müller distinguished him from the khan who first
  brought Manichaeism to the Uyghurs (Bögü Khan, who reigned 759–780 and
  is called "emanation of Mani" in another fragment, T II D 135); the khan
  here is called "the shining limb of the Envoy of Light".
- **The date.** Five hundred and forty-six years after the birth of Mani
  (born 216) is the year 762, the year the Uyghurs adopted Manichaeism.
  The year "after he was raised up in power" was left blank by the scribe.
  Mār Šād Ohrmizd was a head of the eastern Manichaean church.
- **Panjkand and Čīnānčkand**: Müller took Panjkand to be the "Pentapolis"
  (the five cities of the Beshbalïq region) and Čīnānčkand to be the
  "Chinese town" (Qočo).
- **The section titles** of the table of contents: the first red end-title
  that survives marks the songs "on the passing away", that is, laments for
  the dead. The hymns run alphabetically by their first letter in the
  Manichaean script within each section, so the English order follows the
  manuscript, not the English alphabet.
- **Names.** The spellings of personal names follow Müller's readings, in
  simplified form. Many are uncertain, and modern editions read some of
  them differently.
