Manuskriptfragment in türkischer Sprache 
aus Turfan (Chinesisch-Turkistan). 
Von Dr. phil. A. von Le Coq. 
f\’’orgelegt von Hm. F.W. K. am 11 . November 1909 [s. oben S. 1136 ].) 
Hierzu Taf. XIII und XIV. 
Das christliche Fragment T. II, B. I. 
Der großen Ausbeute an chnstJichen Manu.skripten, -welche meiner 
Expedition ün Sommer 1905 in der alten Siedelung bei Bulaylq (nörd¬ 
lich von Turfan) zuteil wurde, entstammt auch dieses Fragment. 
Es ist ein ziemlich wohlerhaltenes Blatt in europäischer Buch¬ 
form ; das Format ist 13^- x 9^ cm. Das Papier ist grob und von 
gelbbrauner Farbe; die Linien sind in grauer Tinte gezogen. 
Die imschöne Schrift zeigt die in unseren Texten sonst nicht 
vorkommende Eigentümlichkeit, daß zuweilen der Buchstabe »n me- 
diale« ^ durch einen darübergesetzten Punkt ^ vom »a« ^ unter¬ 
schieden wird. 
Der Inhalt ist christlich, aber anscheinend apokryph und eine 
wörtliche Übersetzung aus dem Syrischen. 
Das manichäische Fragment T. II, D, 178 . 
(Hieran Tat XIV.) 
Dieses Handschriftenfragment stammt ebenso wie das bereits ver¬ 
öffentlichte Blatt' aus einem Gewölbe des nordwestlichen Teiles der 
manichäischen Gebäudegruppe JT in Idiqut-Schähri (Kao-cang, Chotscho), 
der Hauptstadt des üigui’enreichs. 
Es ist ein Blatt eines in westländischer Weise hergestellten Buches, 
von welchem außerdem noch drei Doppelblätter und ein sehr gut er¬ 
haltenes einzelnes Blatt am selben Orte gefunden wurde. Das Papier 
ist vortrefflich, es ist von gelblichweißer Farbe und im Format 28 cmx 
Sitziing.sber. d. Bi*rl. .\kad. d. Wiss. XIX, 1908, *. .April. 
I 
A. VON Le Coq: Ein chi-Lstliches und ein inanichSisdies MS.-Fragment. 1203 
12-i-cin zugeschnittcii. Bei dem heute publizierten Fragment ist die Höhe 
der Seite durch Wurmfraß auf 26.04 cm reduziert. Die Liniierung und 
die diese rechts und links begrenzenden Randstriche sind in mattkarmin- * 
roter Tusche ausgeführt. Die Schrift ist mit der Rohrfeder und, dem 
Duktus nach zu scliließen, augenscheinlich von rechts nach links (nicht 
von oben nach unten) geschrieben. Da alle drei der Doppelblatter in 
ganz regelmäßiger Verteilung zwei verschiedene Handschriften ent¬ 
halten, von denen die eine steife, eng aneiuandergedrängte Buchstaben,

Der Duktus der Schrift ist altertümlich, ebenso die Orthographie,
die jedoch in ihrer Schreibweise nicht konsequent ist. So sehen wir
Auch sonst kommen Eigenheiten vor — ob aus Nachlässigkeit
oder ob dem Dialekt entsprechend, ist heute noch nicht festzustellen.
gegeben (in einem noch nicht publizierten Text ist letzteres sogar die
so scharf unterschieden, als es in anderen Manuskripten üblich ist; mr
sind daher im Zweifel, ob bis, kisi, äsidip zu lesen ist oder bis, kiSi, äSidip.
Die Frage, ob der vorliegende Dialekt die Verschiedenheit der Laute
dieser Texte dem Leser auf; sie kann aber heute noch nicht mit Sicher¬
heit gelöst werden. Höchst auffallend ist die Erscheinung, daß der
wird; er tritt in Endungen, Pronominal- und anderen Suffixen mit einer
gewissen Regelmäßigkeit auf. So finden wir (zum Teil in dem hier
veröffentlichten, zum Teil in den dazugehörigen, aber noch nicht pu¬
blikationsfähigen Blättern) die Formen
1. tartap für tarlxp,

Kine Reihe anderer Formen, die dieselbe Eigentümlichkeit zeigen,
könnte noch aufgeführt werden. Die Form des Genitivs wird durch
die Unvollkommenheit der Schläft verdunkelt. Er wird auf , , md 4
*nmg* lesen muß oder ob man etwa ang (äng) zu setzen hat. Jeden¬
köktürkischen Inschriften zu werfen, deren Sprache der Dialekt unseres
Fragments nahesteht.
Der Inhalt ist bedeutsam. Dies Fragment enthält nämlich eine
Episode aus der Buddhalegende; es bringt uns einen Teil der Er¬
für buddhistisch halten, wenn nicht schon Form xmd Ausstattung de.s
Buches, dem alle diese Blätter entstammen, sowie der Inhalt einiger
dieser Blätter dieser Auffassung gebieterisch widerspräche. Gute alte
buddhistische Schriften sind nämlich niemals in auf westländische Weise
gehefteten Büchern, sondern bisher nur in indischen Pothibüchern, Buch-
roUen und Faltbüchern in unseren Besitz gelangt. Auch kommen die
Interpunktionszeichen der Manichäer, schwarze mit Mennigrot umran¬
dete Punkte, niemals in buddhistischen Manuskripten vor. Weit wich¬
tiger als dieses mehr äußerliche Zeugnis ist jedoch der Inhalt der an¬
deren, zum selben Buch gehörigen Blätter, nämlich jener, welclie von den¬
selben Schreibern geschriebene Texte enthalten, in denen vom Messias
mSixa, vom (manichäischen) Evangelium
selbst (mit einer wichtigen Datiemng) imd von iranischen Gottheiten
die Rede ist. Ich möchte daher unser Blatt als einen Beweis dafür be¬
trachten, daß auch der Buddhismus in dem sjmkretistischcn Religions¬
system des Mani (jedenfalls in diesen Gegenden) einen wichtigen Platz
eingenommen hat.
In diesem Zusammenhang scheint ein in dem Text und der Über¬
schrift, des hier publizierten Fi-agments öfters wiederkehrendes Wort
S. 13 und 14, gegenüber Kadloff, Vorislamitisdie Schriftarten der Türken S. 835,

input.content:
---
title: "The Bodhisattva prince, and Manichaean pieces in runic script"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 73
summary: A Manichaean Old Turkish leaf telling how the Bodhisattva prince met an old man, a source of the Barlaam and Josaphat legend, with hymn and story fragments in Turkic runic script from Turfan.
original_language: Old Turkish and Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II D 178e, T M 339, T M 330 and T M 342 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Köktürkisches aus Turfan" and "Ein christliches und ein manichäisches Manuskriptfragment in türkischer Sprache aus Turfan", Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1909, pp. 1047–1061 and 1202–1218 (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1909 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

In 1909 Le Coq published two short sets of Turfan texts.

The first is a leaf (T II D 178e) from the same Manichaean book as other
Old Turkish leaves from Qočo. It tells the episode of the Buddha legend in
which the Bodhisattva prince, riding out with his groom Chandaka, sees an
old man for the first time. Le Coq argued that the book was Manichaean,
not Buddhist: it is bound in the western way, uses the Manichaean
punctuation, and its other leaves, by the same scribes, speak of the
Messiah, the Manichaean Gospel and Iranian gods. He suggested that the
Manichaeans, not the Christians, first brought the story of the Bodhisattva
prince to the West, where it became the legend of *Barlaam and Josaphat*.

The second set is written in Turkic runic script on paper: a Middle Persian
hymn with Turkish rubrics, some Middle Persian scraps, and a double leaf in
Turkish (T M 342) from a story.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### T II D 178e: the Bodhisattva prince and the old man

**Front.** *(Heading:)* The book of Chandaka's answers.

Then the Bodhisattva prince [ … ], drawing his horse up by the rein, stood
still. Looking at Chandaka, he asked: "This [one], so ugly, lying and
rolling about (?): what kind of man is this?" he asked.

Chandaka answered him with reverence: "O prince, this man was once a
youth, a healthy, young and handsome youth like you. Now he has grown old
and sick; he has fallen ill and lies there so ugly."

Then the Bodhisattva said: "[ … ] we too, living long, [ … ] so [ … ] there
is nothing [ … ] become ashes [ … ]" *(the next four lines are destroyed).*

**Back.** *(Heading, in black:)* The Bodhisattva prince, from Chandaka.

Having heard these words, turning back his rein, in care and great
distress he went (back) himself into his capital. Going in, saying a word
to no one, he sat down, loving, grieving and brooding. His father the king
and his mother the queen, having heard (this), both came; whatever they
asked their son, he gave no answer. Then Śuddhodana the king said to all
his officials and nobles, sternly: "[ … ]," he said. "Pursue (?) [ … ]
going; every [ … ], every people [ … ] the people [ … ]" *(two lines
destroyed; end of the back).*

### T II T 20: a hymn to the Maiden of Light, in runic script

*An incomplete leaf of a book bound in the western way. The text is in
Middle Persian with Turkish rubrics, in black and red; the heading of the
back is in blue.*

**Front.** *(Heading, in black:)* Enlightenment [ … ] mind (?) [ … ] to the
shining Moon-god [ … ] in blessing [ … ] the former enlightenment [ … ]
forgive my sins! [ … ] God; Maiden of Light; (the) five soul-gathering
angels.

**Back.** *(Heading, in blue:)* It has begun: the Maiden [ … ]

[ … ] Ended is (the hymn of the) enlightenments.

*(Three lines left empty.)*

Maiden of Light: hymn (?) [ … ] praise and blessing [ … ] (end of the back).

### T M 339 and T M 330: Middle Persian scraps

*The upper parts of two leaves of one manuscript (T M 339a and b), and a
lower part of a leaf (T M 330), each with coloured headings and flowers.
Only scattered letters and words survive, which Le Coq printed without a
translation.*

### T M 342: from a story, in Turkish

*A double leaf of a book bound in the western way, in a large clear hand.*

**First (?) leaf, front.** [ … ] he thought: "[If it] is [ … ] water, I
will drink it; if it is food that has been made and prepared, I will eat
it" [ … ]

**First leaf, back.** *(Heading in blue, the beginning destroyed.)* [ … ]
inclined to act (?) [ … ] what kind of demon [ … ] what evil spell (?) did
he devise [ … ] tasteless (?) [ … ] he? all (?) [ … ]

**Second leaf, front.** *(Heading in black, destroyed.)* [ … ] they quarrelled.
Then the first said thus: "I [ … ] I [ … ] everywhere [ … ] a mighty star
he has become." Then the second man said thus: "All [ … ]"

**Second leaf, back.** *(Heading in black, destroyed.)* Again they wished
(?) this word [ … ]; they did not agree to find the earth together (?); and
to praise the star, the man said thus: "I [ … ] the star so mighty have I
called (?) [ … ]"

## Notes to this edition

- **The Bodhisattva legend.** The groom Chandaka and King Śuddhodana are
  the figures of the Buddha's own story; in *Barlaam and Josaphat* the
  prince likewise meets an old man and a sick man and returns home troubled.
  Müller added a note to Le Coq's article on the name *Bodisav* and its
  relation to the name *Josaphat*.
- **The Christian fragment** published with it (T II B 1, from Bulayïq) is
  an apocryphal Christian text in Turkish and is not Manichaean, so it is
  not given here.
- **Runic script.** These are among the few texts in Turkic runes written on
  paper; Le Coq published them in part for the new letter forms they show.

## Introduction

In 1909 Le Coq published two short sets of Turfan texts.

The first is a leaf (T II D 178e) from the same Manichaean book as other
Old Turkish leaves from Qočo. It tells the episode of the Buddha legend in
which the Bodhisattva prince, riding out with his groom Chandaka, sees an
old man for the first time. Le Coq argued that the book was Manichaean,
not Buddhist: it is bound in the western way, uses the Manichaean
punctuation, and its other leaves, by the same scribes, speak of the
Messiah, the Manichaean Gospel and Iranian gods. He suggested that the
Manichaeans, not the Christians, first brought the story of the Bodhisattva
prince to the West, where it became the legend of *Barlaam and Josaphat*.

The second set is written in Turkic runic script on paper: a Middle Persian
hymn with Turkish rubrics, some Middle Persian scraps, and a double leaf in
Turkish (T M 342) from a story.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### T II D 178e: the Bodhisattva prince and the old man

**Front.** *(Heading:)* The book of Chandaka's answers.

Then the Bodhisattva prince [ … ], drawing his horse up by the rein, stood
still. Looking at Chandaka, he asked: "This [one], so ugly, lying and
rolling about (?): what kind of man is this?" he asked.

Chandaka answered him with reverence: "O prince, this man was once a
youth, a healthy, young and handsome youth like you. Now he has grown old
and sick; he has fallen ill and lies there so ugly."

Then the Bodhisattva said: "[ … ] we too, living long, [ … ] so [ … ] there
is nothing [ … ] become ashes [ … ]" *(the next four lines are destroyed).*

**Back.** *(Heading, in black:)* The Bodhisattva prince, from Chandaka.

Having heard these words, turning back his rein, in care and great
distress he went (back) himself into his capital. Going in, saying a word
to no one, he sat down, loving, grieving and brooding. His father the king
and his mother the queen, having heard (this), both came; whatever they
asked their son, he gave no answer. Then Śuddhodana the king said to all
his officials and nobles, sternly: "[ … ]," he said. "Pursue (?) [ … ]
going; every [ … ], every people [ … ] the people [ … ]" *(two lines
destroyed; end of the back).*

### T II T 20: a hymn to the Maiden of Light, in runic script

*An incomplete leaf of a book bound in the western way. The text is in
Middle Persian with Turkish rubrics, in black and red; the heading of the
back is in blue.*

**Front.** *(Heading, in black:)* Enlightenment [ … ] mind (?) [ … ] to the
shining Moon-god [ … ] in blessing [ … ] the former enlightenment [ … ]
forgive my sins! [ … ] God; Maiden of Light; (the) five soul-gathering
angels.

**Back.** *(Heading, in blue:)* It has begun: the Maiden [ … ]

[ … ] Ended is (the hymn of the) enlightenments.

*(Three lines left empty.)*

Maiden of Light: hymn (?) [ … ] praise and blessing [ … ] (end of the back).

### T M 339 and T M 330: Middle Persian scraps

*The upper parts of two leaves of one manuscript (T M 339a and b), and a
lower part of a leaf (T M 330), each with coloured headings and flowers.
Only scattered letters and words survive, which Le Coq printed without a
translation.*

### T M 342: from a story, in Turkish

*A double leaf of a book bound in the western way, in a large clear hand.*

**First (?) leaf, front.** [ … ] he thought: "[If it] is [ … ] water, I
will drink it; if it is food that has been made and prepared, I will eat
it" [ … ]

**First leaf, back.** *(Heading in blue, the beginning destroyed.)* [ … ]
inclined to act (?) [ … ] what kind of demon [ … ] what evil spell (?) did
he devise [ … ] tasteless (?) [ … ] he? all (?) [ … ]

**Second leaf, front.** *(Heading in black, destroyed.)* [ … ] they quarrelled.
Then the first said thus: "I [ … ] I [ … ] everywhere [ … ] a mighty star
he has become." Then the second man said thus: "All [ … ]"

**Second leaf, back.** *(Heading in black, destroyed.)* Again they wished
(?) this word [ … ]; they did not agree to find the earth together (?); and
to praise the star, the man said thus: "I [ … ] the star so mighty have I
called (?) [ … ]"

## Notes to this edition

- **The Bodhisattva legend.** The groom Chandaka and King Śuddhodana are
  the figures of the Buddha's own story; in *Barlaam and Josaphat* the
  prince likewise meets an old man and a sick man and returns home troubled.
  Müller added a note to Le Coq's article on the name *Bodisav* and its
  relation to the name *Josaphat*.
- **The Christian fragment** published with it (T II B 1, from Bulayïq) is
  an apocryphal Christian text in Turkish and is not Manichaean, so it is
  not given here.
- **Runic script.** These are among the few texts in Turkic runes written on
  paper; Le Coq published them in part for the new letter forms they show.

+Middle Persian with Turkish rubrics, in black and red; the heading of the
+back is in blue.*

+he has become." Then the second man said thus: "All [ … ]"

398 SiUnng der phil.-hist. Classe v. 2. April 1908. — Mifth. v. 19. Mär*. 
Ein manichäisch-uigurisclies Fragment aus 
Idiqut-Schahri. 
Von A. VON Le Coq. 
(Vorgelegt von Hrn. F.W. K. Mütxkb am 19 . März 1908 [s. oben S. 327 ].) 
Hierzu Taf. HI. 
Unter den manichäischen Schriften in soghdischer und türkischer 
Sprache, welche ich im Jalire 1905 in der Ruinengruppe K von Idiqut- 
Schahri entdeckte, befand sich auch das vorliegende türkische Manu¬ 
skriptfragment manichäisch-religiösen Inhalts. Zum ersten Male sehen 
wir hier ein derartiges Werk in uigurischer Schrift: alle früher be¬ 
kannten türkischen Manichaica sind in jener modifizierten Estrangelo- 
schrift geschrieben, welche auf Mänl zurückgefuhrt wird und über die 
in den Sitzungsberichten 1904 S. 348 ff. zum ersten Male von dem 
Entdecker berichtet worden ist. 
Der Inhalt ist eine Schilderung von Kämpfen, welche ein »zru 5 c 
bur%an« genanntes Wesen gegen Dämonen und Zauberer besteht; 
der Schauplatz ist die heilige Stadt der Manichäer, das ehrwürdige 
Babylon. 
Man wird kaum fehlgehen, wenn man diesen »zru. 4 c burx,an« 
mit dem Apostel der Iranier Zarathustra identifiziert; sein Vorkommen 
in einer manichäischen Legende beweist, daß die Manichäer, wenig- 
sten.s in Turkistan, nicht nur, wie schon bekannt, einzelne Gnmd- 
gedanken der iranischen Lichtreligion, sondern auch die Gestalt des 
Propheten derselben in ihren Kultus herübergenommen haben. 
Obwohl das hauptsächliche Interesse des Bruchstücks in diesem 
literarischen Nachweise besteht, ist doch auch die äußere Beschaffen¬ 
heit des Fragments imd besonders die Spi-ache, die es uns bewahrt 
hat, nicht ohne Wichtigkeit. 
Wie leicht ersichtlich, bildet das uns erhaltene halbe Blatt 
folgende Seiten.
Das Papier ist gut, glatt und von braungelblicher Farbe, die
Schrift eine schöne deutliche uigurische Kursive, in glünzendschwarzer
Tinte wahrscheinlich mit der Rohrfeder ausgeführt. Auf der Vorder¬
an den Rand geschrieben.
Unser Fragment dürfte der Tliang-Periode (rund 600—900) zu¬
zurechnen sein.
Die Sprache ist altes Türkisch* und stimmt mit der in den andern
manichäischen und in den buddhistischen Manuskripten überlieferten
überein.
Die Erzählung ist belebt imd würde bei einem weniger frag-
mentarisclien Erhaltungszustand nur geringe Schwierigkeiten bieten;
die Veröffentlichung erfolgt u. a., um den sprachlichen Stoff einem
größern Kreise zugänglich zu machen. Sobald das Studium unsrer
Texte ein reicheres Vokabular erschlossen haben wird, sollen weitere
Publikationen türkischer Manichaica erfolgen.
Im Anschlüsse teile ich eine aus mehreren mit manichäischen
Lettern geschriebenen Manuskripten ausgezogene Wörterliste mit, um
damit einen Beitrag zur Kenntnis des Konsonantismus der alten tür¬
kischen Sprache zu liefern. Die manichäischen Buchstaben lassen
nämlich irgendwelche Zweifel über den Lautwert eines jeden Kon¬
sonanten nicht bestehen. Die sich ergebenden Werte scheinen am
besten mit den von V. Thomsen gewonnenen Resultaten übereinzu¬
stimmen.
Viele der aufgeführten Wörter sind wohlbekannt, die Bedeutungen
der andern werden sich allmählich ergeben. Auf ihren Vokalismus
kann hier noch niclit eingegangen werden, da über diesen erst das
Studium der in indischen Alphabeten (Brähmi und Tibetisch) geschrie¬
benen und die Vokale klar wiedergebenden türkischen Manuskripte®
unanfechtbaren Aufschluß zu geben vermag.
‘ Im Gegeusat* zur indischen Buciiform (pof/ii) und dem chinesischen Buch
(Holle oder Fallbuch).
* Kin anderes Manuskript, welches zusammen mit dem vorliegenden gefunden
in dem letzthin [hier 1907 S.958] veröffentlichten Kolophon eines buddhistischen Buches,
• Aus meinen im Jahre 1905 in den Ruinen von Singim AgTz und Toyoq ge¬
machten Funden.

input.content:
---
title: "Zarathustra in Babel: a Manichaean Uyghur fragment"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 74
summary: Half a leaf of an Old Turkish Manichaean legend in which "Zrušč Burxan", the prophet Zarathustra, fights demons and sorcerers in the city of Babel.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'A manuscript fragment from ruin K, Idiqut-šähri (Qočo) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Ein manichäisch-uigurisches Fragment aus Idiqut-Schahri", Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1908, pp. 398–414 (archive.org `in.gov.ignca.26822`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1908 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

This half leaf, found by Le Coq at Qočo in 1905, was the first Manichaean
work known to be written in the Uyghur script rather than the Manichaean
one. It tells of battles that a being called *Zrušč Burxan* fights against
demons and sorcerers in Babel, the holy city of the Manichaeans. Le Coq
identified *Zrušč Burxan* with Zarathustra, the prophet of the Iranians,
whom the Manichaeans counted among the Envoys of Light before Mani. He
dated the leaf to the Tang period (about 600–900).

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

**Front.** [ … ] (his) wise Law [ … ] the strong apostles (angels), who to
him [ … ] (?) [ … ] saying. The great one among those demons fled and
appeared (?) [ … ] was a tree (?). The great one among those demons, at
that tree (?) [ … ] seized the apostles, dragged them off and had them
slaughtered; the leaf of that tree (?) fell to the earth.

At that time the people who were in the city of Babel became hostile;
taking stones for the sorcerer [ … ] turned back towards them, their heads
[ … ] spoke so: "You [ … ]"

**Back.** He sat down on the top of that tree (?); in his heart he thought
so: "I will throw myself down, I will fall, I will kill Zrušč Burxan,"
so he thought.

At that time the sorcerers in the city of Babel took bow and arrow; [the
arrow], glancing back (?), struck his own vein of life. In this way the
demon died. The great one among the sorcerers was filled with shame.

Zrušč [Burxan] rose up from the place where he had been, and went to the
court of the city of Babel; so [ … ] (the rest is lost).

## Notes to this edition

- ***Zrušč Burxan***: *burxan* is the Turkish word for a buddha or prophet,
  used in Manichaean texts for the Envoys of Light. Le Coq took *zrušč* to
  be a form of Zarathustra's name. Mani taught that Zarathustra in Persia,
  the Buddha in India and Jesus in the West had come before him.
- **Babel** is called the holy city of the Manichaeans: Mani was born in

content.content:
Di 
’ie vorliegenden türkischen Texte manichäisch-religiösen Inhalts bilden, abgesehen von zwei schwierigen 
astronomisch-kalendarischen Blättern und einer geringen Anzahl kleinerer Fragmente, den Rest unserer Aus¬ 
beute an Fundstücken dieser Kategorie in türkischer Sprache. Ein beträchtlicher Teil dieser Reste einer 
merkwürdigen, in den Sammlungen der anderen Länder nur schwach vertretenen Literatur wurde von der 
ersten Expedition (Grönweokl-Huth) geborgen; alle Bruchstücke entstammen der Oase von Turfan. 
Eine Reihe, von meist kleineren Bruchstücken ist ohne TTbersetzung geblieben, zum Teil, weil der Sinn 
sieh ohne weiteres von selbst ergibt, zum Feil, weil das Vorkommen unbekannter Wörter in stark beschädigten 
zusammenhangslosen Stücken mir die Erschließung nicht erlaubte. 
Schweren Herzens habe ich mich entschlossen, mit dieser Veröffentlichung hervorzutreten, und alle hier 
gegebenen T'bersetzungen sind als erste Deutungsversuche zu betrachten. Aber da wiederholte Bemühungen 
im Laufe vieler Jahre die Erkenntnis nur wenig gefordert haben, ist es bei der Wichtigkeit de» Stoffes eine 
Pflicht, anderen Mitarbeitern die Teilnahme an diesen Forschungen zu ermöglichen. 
Abgesehen nämlich von dem sprachlichen Material, das dem Turkologen eine reiche Auslaute bringt, 
bieten diese Schriften eine Fülle von religions- und kulturgeschichtlichen Hinweisen. Nie darf außer acht 
gelassen werden, in wie wirksamer Weise gerade dieser Synkretismus den Osten dem Westen, den Westen 
dem fisten nähergobracht und zur gegenseitigen Befruchtung genötigt hat. Besonders war er und nicht etwa 
das östliche Christentum der'Frager indisch-buddhistischer Legenden nach den Westlanden 1 und hellenistischer, 
mesopotamiseber und iranischer Gedanken nach dem fernen Osten. 
So darf es uns nicht wundernehmen, daß ein leider nur kleines Bruchstück (Nr. 14) uns das Vorkommen 
der Fabeln des Äsop Del den Uiguren in Turfan beweist*; ein anderes Fragment (Nr. 1) erwähnt in einer 
Aufzählung manichäischer Gottheiten den Götternamen Siin. wobei ich nicht zu entscheiden wage, ob man an 
den babylonischen Mondgott oder aber an ein chinesisches Wort zu denken hat. 
Auch die kleinen und kleinsten Bruchstücke werden, wie ich hoffe, dazu beitragen, unsere Kenntnis 
der Realien und der Geschichte des Manichäismus in Ostturkistan durch die darin erwähnten Personen- und 
< >rtsnamen, Speisevorschriften u. a. in. in etwas zu bereichern. 
Neben den interessanten Bruchstücken Nr. 3, das kosmogonischen oder esehatologischen Inhalts ist (Be¬ 
zwingung der htwiäma ), Nr. 4, das uns von der Göttin anram berichtet, und Nr. 9. dem großen Hymnus- 
Fragment, in dem Maui als »neuer Ta//, netter Monat, neues Jahr* angerufen wird, verdient Nr. 8 besondere 
Aufmerksamkeit. L'nter dieser Nummer hat es sich ermöglicht, eine Reihe verschiedener, an verschiedenen 
Orten gefundener Handschriftenreste zu vereinen zu einem ziemlich umfangreichen Bruchstück, in einer an¬ 
scheinend älteren Version, jenes fast buddhistisch anmutenden chinesischen Textes, den die Herren Chavannis 
und Pelliot im Jahre 1912 unter dem Fitei • l n traitr manichrrn retroure rn l'hinr* im Journal asiatit/ue ver¬ 
öffentlicht haben. Ohne die Kenntnis dieses Werkes wäre die Zusammenstellung mir nicht möglich gewesen. 
Stark buddhistisch beeinflußt zeigen sich unter unseren Texten die Nummern 39 (Erwähnung des Anan/la) 
und 40, welch letztere auch durch die von den Stiftern gewählte Buchform den Eindruck eines buddhistischen 
Werkes hervomift. Es ist nämlich das erste (und bisher einzige) Mal, daß wir einen manichäischcn, in ma- 
nichäischen Lettern geschriebenen Text in der Form eines indischen Buchbündels (pothT) vor uns sehen. 
Das erste Blatt zeigt auf dem Obvers eine Miniatur, die einen sitzenden oder knienden electus unter 
einem Baum dnrstellt, unter ihm sind zwei sitzende (oder kniende) menschliche Figuren, augenscheinlich die 
frommen Stifter, nbgehildct.

astronomisch-kalendarischen Blättern und einer geringen Anzahl kleinerer Fragmente, den Rest unserer Aus¬ 
beute an Fundstücken dieser Kategorie in türkischer Sprache. Ein beträchtlicher Teil dieser Reste einer 
merkwürdigen, in den Sammlungen der anderen Länder nur schwach vertretenen Literatur wurde von der 
ersten Expedition (Grönweokl-Huth) geborgen; alle Bruchstücke entstammen der Oase von Turfan. 
Eine Reihe, von meist kleineren Bruchstücken ist ohne TTbersetzung geblieben, zum Teil, weil der Sinn 
sieh ohne weiteres von selbst ergibt, zum Feil, weil das Vorkommen unbekannter Wörter in stark beschädigten 
zusammenhangslosen Stücken mir die Erschließung nicht erlaubte. 
Schweren Herzens habe ich mich entschlossen, mit dieser Veröffentlichung hervorzutreten, und alle hier 
gegebenen T'bersetzungen sind als erste Deutungsversuche zu betrachten. Aber da wiederholte Bemühungen 
im Laufe vieler Jahre die Erkenntnis nur wenig gefordert haben, ist es bei der Wichtigkeit de» Stoffes eine 
Pflicht, anderen Mitarbeitern die Teilnahme an diesen Forschungen zu ermöglichen.

bieten diese Schriften eine Fülle von religions- und kulturgeschichtlichen Hinweisen. Nie darf außer acht 
gelassen werden, in wie wirksamer Weise gerade dieser Synkretismus den Osten dem Westen, den Westen 
dem fisten nähergobracht und zur gegenseitigen Befruchtung genötigt hat. Besonders war er und nicht etwa

input.content:
---
title: "The Sermon of the Light-Nous in Old Turkish"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 41
summary: Leaves from four Uyghur books at Qočo with an Old Turkish version of the Sermon of the Light-Nous (the Chinese Traité), on the five limbs of the soul, the days and nights in the body, the twelve kingships and the signs of the Elect, with a fragment of an Iranian legend.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II D 119, T M 300, T M 423a–e and T I α 2 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2, text no. 8 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

The *Sermon of the Light-Nous* survives in Chinese as the
[Traité](traite.html), and parts of it in Parthian and Sogdian. Le Coq
found that a number of Old Turkish leaves from Qočo, from four different
books, contain another version of it. He placed them against the pages of
Chavannes and Pelliot's edition of the Chinese, and noted that the Turkish
often differs a good deal from the Chinese and is meant for the Elect. One
leaf (T M 423d) in the same book has instead part of a lively Iranian
legend, so the book was probably a collection of important writings for the
Elect.

The section numbers in the headings below refer to the sections of the
Traité on this site.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "a first attempt at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words
Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added
for sense.

## The translation

### T II D 119: the five limbs and their five kinds of knowledge (compare Traité §10)

*A badly damaged leaf in Manichaean script.*

**Front.** [ … ] from his limb [ … ] (?) letting the knowledge of love
spring up, he puts it on the god of the gentle breeze. From his limb "the
mind" letting the knowledge of piety spring up, he puts it on the god of
wind. From his limb "the thoughts" letting the knowledge of patience spring
up, he puts it on the god of water. From his limb "insight" letting wise
knowledge spring up, he puts it on the god of fire.

And as the first (the foremost) of all words these have been called on:
(1) the god of the gentle breeze, (2) the god of wind, (3) the god of
light, (4) the god of water, (5) the god of fire; (6) the knowledge of
love, (7) the knowledge of piety, (8) the knowledge of keeping the
commandments (?), [ … ] knowledge, [ … ] (11) being pious in word and
speech, (12) giving wise knowledge [to others?], (and 13) thirteenth, the
god of the majesty of the Law. These [ … ] so [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] this is one shining day with its twelve good hours, which
[ … ] puts on (imparts to) all the Elect, [like] the gods in the realm of
the gods with [ … ].

And the second shining day is itself the twelve kingships, which resemble
the god of the majesty of the Law (and) the shining sun-god with his twelve
divine maidens. (Namely:) (1) ruling and exercising power, (2) wise
knowledge, (3) conquering, (4) rejoicing, (5) keeping the commandments,
(6) being truthful, (7) being faithful, (8) being patient, (9) being
upright, (10) doing good deeds, (11) being of even heart, (12) being shining
and radiant. This is the second shining day with its twelve good hours,
which have emanated from the god of the majesty of the Law, just as the
sun-god has emanated from that great god.

And that [third?] shining day is itself the power of the five gods, which
[is] set free from the body of the sun-like Elect [ … ] this [ … ] power of
the five gods [ … ]

### T M 300: when the old man fights the new (compare Traité §§8–9)

*A leaf with the top torn off; Uyghur script.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] should come near (?) [ … ]. (If) the power of the five
gods passing over from this body should not be spoiled, [ … ] will be. And
it happens that [ … ] fight with the new man. If (then) that man loses his
understanding and his sense, then the sign of it is this: he loses his
patience; he [becomes] one who knows haste (rashness?) and violence [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] the power of the (five) gods he sends joyfully to the
realm of the gods. Then (it is), or becomes, [ … ] of his soul [ … ] And
there is such a time, (that is, it happens) that from his [ … ] fight with
(his) new man. If (then) that man loses and lays aside his knowledge (his
understanding) and his sense, the sign of it will be this: his wisdom
dwindles (loses its savour); he goes about without wisdom; the power of
the five gods passing over from this body [is] bound [ … ]

### T M 423: the days and nights in the body, and the twelve kingships (compare Traité §§13–15)

*Five leaves of a book bound in the western way, in Uyghur script, on
paper taken from a Chinese book-roll. The leaves were stuck together and
out of order.*

**T M 423c, front.** [ … ] his limbs (?) [ … ] are these: (1) the soul,
(2) the understanding, (3) the mind, (4) the thought, (5) insight; (6) the
knowledge of love, (7) the knowledge of faith. Their place, where they must
be set, is: these good kinds of knowledge (?) of yours.

And this third shining day resembles and is like the sun-god. And its
twelve hours are these: the twelve divine maidens.

The two dark nights are these: the first night is this dark body itself,
and its twelve hours are these, (namely) the five limbs of the visible
[ … ] body: (1) bones, (2) sinews, (3) veins, (4) flesh, (5) skin; and the
five invisible, intangible evil kinds of knowledge, which are these: (1)
the knowledge of destruction,

**Back.** (2) the knowledge of anger, (3) shameless knowledge, (4) the
knowledge of haste (quarrelling?), (5) unwise knowledge [ … ] the shameless
demon. And the second dark night is [ … ] the deadly thought. And its
twelve hours are those twelve dark glories (lordships).

And the shining days rose up to resist the dark nights and fight them. And
the shining day conquered; it destroyed the dark night, again like the
earlier battle of the god Xormuzta.

And after this the princes and kings exercise power and rule, each in his
own kingdom. The first is (1) the shining glory (lordship), the second (2)
wise

**T M 423b, front.** knowledge, the third (3) conquering, the fourth (4)
rejoicing, the fifth (5) following the commandments (?), the sixth (6)
(being) truthful, the seventh (7) believing, the eighth (8) being patient,
the ninth (9) being upright, the tenth (10) (being) one who does good, the
eleventh (11) being of even heart, the twelfth (12) the light. These twelve
hours spread and flourish in the heart. And [ … ] itself perfect (?),
purified (?) [ … ]. And those in the heart they brought out and made to
appear. And whatever man should plant and sow these twelve

input.content:
---
title: "A penitent's hymn to Mani in Old Turkish"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 75
summary: Leaves of an Uyghur Manichaean hymnbook from Qočo in which a penitent prays to his god, the Saviour and physician, for release from demons and the "sons of hell", and hails him as "our new day, our new month".
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II D 78a–k (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2, text no. 9 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

Le Coq's no. 9 is a set of damaged double leaves (T II D 78a–k) from an
Uyghur book of European form, written with a careless brush on coarse brown
paper, found in ruin K at Qočo. They hold a long hymn of prayer, spoken by a
penitent to "my God", who is the Saviour, the master-physician, the father
who lights up the mind. Le Coq called it "the great hymn fragment, in which
Mani is called on as *new day, new month, new year*". Only the first five
pieces (i–v) are well enough preserved to translate; for the rest (vi–xi)
Le Coq printed the Turkish words that survive, mostly without German.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "a first attempt at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words
Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added
for sense.

## The translation

### i. T II D 78a

**Front.** [ … ] for your choice praises, for your divine piety I myself
would gain fullness! Why? I am yours! Beside you (through you?) I have
fallen into confusion (?)! To you I direct my plea [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] my self! You my [ … ]! You, the prince who purifies my
soul! You, the god who brings joy to my living self! You, the father who
lights up my mind! Now end my fear, and free me from doubts! My God!
Gracious and [ … ]

**Second leaf, front.** [ … ] from those who do evil set (me) free! From
those laden with sin part (me) and save (me)! From the sons of hell, who
are all evil and spread nothing but evil. My God! Guard (me) from these
devouring demons (and) the many kinds of poisonous [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] My God! To you I direct my plea; before your face I pray!
You are the master-physician! You are the teacher of the well-disposed! You
are the one who gladdens, through your love, those you love! Now make my
head (eager) for learning! The evil-doing Sumnu [ … ]

### ii. T II D 78b

**Front.** [ … ] mighty in prayer [ … ] divine [orchard] [ … ] good mind
[ … ] is the great Law.

**Back.** [ … ] love (?) [ … ] you (?) [ … ] are (?) [ … ] my soul from the
dark [ … ]

**(Front, continued.)** [ … ] You, you are the faultless (?), understanding,
wise knowledge. Grant graciously that I may come to your salvation! My God!
Always, without ceasing, bring me to my senses! Deign to make me
understand [ … ]

**Second leaf, front.** [ … ] now [ … ] down [ … ] My God! You [ … ] shining,
strong, good-doing, gracious God! Now have mercy on me! From now on I will
cause no confusion! Scattered before you (lying at your feet?), I will not
again set out (offerings?) for the demons [ … ]

**(Back, continued.)** [ … ] from the lands of the grey-haired demoness of
death save me! From the son (sons?) of the evil-doing Sumnu purify me! Lead
me into your fragrant garden, breathing musk!

**Back.** [ … ] you [ … ] are the faultless, loving, perfectly wise
knowledge! Now deign to love me, my God! Forgive my sins! End my
transgressions! Purify my wretchedness! Now, through your gracious [ … ],
good reward [ … ]

### iii. T II D 78c

**Front.** [ … ] soul [ … ] your [ … ] my strong God! To your majesty (to your
salvation) [ … ] graciously [ … ] I pray and beg! With great and merciful
mind, have mercy on us, my God! Our living self begs towards you [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] therefore [ … ] we [ … ] My God! [ … ] narrow (?) [ … ] you
are one to be revered by all, to be remembered by all (?)! Your great ones
and your shining sons, all, and your chosen apostles [ … ]

**Second leaf, front.** [ … ] five [ … ] thirty [ … ] the god of the majesty
of the Law [ … ] because of [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] (of the) god (of the majesty of the Law?) [ … ] song (?)
[ … ] First [ … ] the Elect [ … ] preaching (?) much [ … ] care and painful
brooding because of the five gods [ … ] sees perfectly [ … ] he showed. We
(our?) [ … ] law and ordinances; blessing, monkhood, purity [ … ] is a
needful song (?). That which is in the mixed (impure, hardened?) mind [ … ]

### iv. T II D 78d

**Back.** [ … ] your knowledge [ … ] folding (laying together) my hands, I
rise to praise you! The wickedness and sin that is in my heart [ … ]

**Second leaf.** [ … ] your shining, chosen self, your watchful mind,
mighty in prayer, your beautiful, shining, jewel-hard [ … ]

[ … ] light (and sun) [ … ] whoever believes and works in God's radiance
(?) [ … ], that man [ … ] in the Law [ … ]

[ … ] praised [ … ] king, who parts us from all false teachings of the Law;
the great, shining [ … ] in our hearts [ … ] we [ … ]

### v. T II D 78e

**Back.** [ … ] you are [ … ]. Through their living insight I myself will
rise up again! (So) I pray and beg [ … ] towards your eternal kingdom! Our
new day, (our) new month, (our) living [ … ] new shining [ … ]

### vi–xi. T II D 78f–k

*Small and badly damaged pieces of further double leaves. Le Coq printed
the surviving Turkish words, mostly without a translation. Among them can be
made out: "my God", "you are mighty", "your majesty", "we pray to you, my
God", "Mani Burxan", "for ever", "living", "you are the true Law", and a
line in which every phrase ends "you are … in all".*

## Notes to this edition

- **"Our new day, our new month"** (v): the same images as in the
  Middle Persian hymns of the new moon and the full moon to Jesus and Mani
  ([M 176](turfan-fragments-2.html)) and Le Coq's description of this hymn,
  "new day, new month, new year".
- **Sumnu** (i, ii) is a demon's name that Le Coq left unexplained; "the
  grey-haired demoness of death" is the hag of the hymns on the soul after
  death ([Old Turkish hymns](turkish-manichaica-2.html)).
- **"The master-physician"**: the same title is given to Jesus and to Mani
  in the Chinese Hymnscroll ("King of Physicians").

input.content:
---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: gods, cosmos and sermons"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 76
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo and Turfan, with a list of the gods of light, the waxing and waning of the moon, the demon pinned under the mountains, a teacher's sermon on the body as a stormy sea, the day of death, sayings of Jesus on alms, the four thoughts about food, and Mani's teaching on the Maiden of Light.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 1–7 (T M 139, 140, 141, 147, 175, T III T V 49, T M 298, T II D 172a, 173b–c and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

These are the first seven groups of texts in Le Coq's last volume of Old
Turkish Manichaica (1922). Most are small and damaged, and Le Coq called
all his translations "first attempts at interpretation". No. 6 comes from
the same book of sermons as the leaves T II D 173 in his first volume (see
[Old Turkish texts from Qočo](turkish-manichaica-1.html)); no. 7 from the
same book as T II D 176.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German. Gaps are
marked [ … ]; words Le Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in
parentheses are added for sense. Where Le Coq gave no German for a leaf,
that is said.

## The translation

### No. 1: a hymn naming the gods of light

*Pieces of several leaves of one book (T M 139, 141, 140 with 147, T III T V
49, T M 175), in Manichaean script; one piece from the foothills north of
Turfan.*

**T M 141.** [ … ] set free the chosen ones! Drive away the darkness!
Destroy the demons! Let the Elect rejoice! [ … ] The eternal god Zurwān,
the living self (life) [ … ]

Because the darkness has been scattered, the evil-doers have all, many
times, fallen into confusion; all those who have gone astray have come to
grief. Because they did not know the good-doing God, they will tremble and
burn in the flaming hell. Why? (Because they did not know) the (saving?)
way that leads upward [ … ]

**T M 140 and 147.** [ … ] day [ … ] the shining moon-god; the goddess, the
Maiden of Light; the mighty Siin; Srōšahrāy the god; the two strong shining
(gods), the sun-god and the moon-god; those Seven, and the twelve
helmsman-gods; the twelve good hours; and the good [ … ] god; the five
radiant ones, who bring the good fruit of victory; with all the arhats of
the majesty of the Law born before; the Caller(-god and?) the
Voice-giver, brothers; the three wheels, (namely) the gods of wind, water
and fire [ … ]

**T III T V 49 (continuing T M 141).** (The eternal) god (Zurwān) is the
living self, and that splendour [ … ] and to all the princes [ … ] and the
Father of Life [ … ] the chosen ones [ … ] the light has come; because the
darkness has been scattered, the evil-doers [ … ] He gave the teaching for
the majesty of the religion. We have understood our shining (?) earth; we
have understood and known that our bodies and our souls, above and below,
in the light and in the darkness [ … ] He made shine for the shining [ … ]
lovely Law [ … ] on the whole earth [ … ]

*(The back repeats the passage "all the evil-doers have many times fallen
into confusion … in the flaming hell … the way that leads upward … the good
guide". T M 175 has the same text as T M 139 and 141, too broken to
translate; among its words are "Zurwān" and "the shining gods".)*

### No. 2: the palaces of the sun and moon

*The lower part of a leaf of European form, about a third missing; Uyghur
script.*

[ … ] thirty [ … ] four (fourteen?) [ … ] the shining power that gives
[ … ] is this. The radiance of light in the palace of the moon-god springs
up for the sun (?). At each [ … ] the palace of the moon-god to the palace
of the sun-god; on the twenty-ninth (day of the month) the two palaces
meet. From the palace of the sun-god, the sun-god, the Mother-God and the
god Wadžiwanta [ … ]

[ … ] Xormuzta, the god, [ … ] enters the palace of the moon-god and settles
there. In each month on two days the moon-god goes his way without taking
his shining power; again he turns; on the thirtieth and the fifteenth of
the month he does not take (it). This is why he does not take it: the
power of the light should remain (cloudy?) like dregs in those strong
demons. If [ … ]

### No. 3: the demon pinned under the earth

*A leaf, badly damaged; the writing of the back partly rubbed out. Uyghur
script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] presses [ … ]. The land lying to the east [ … ] presses on that old
(?) demon's head. Whatever mountains and their plants, rocks and sand are
there [ … ] the land lying to the west presses [ … ]. His two shoulders are
pressed down by the lands lying to the south and the north. His trunk (?)
is pressed down by Mount Sumeru. In pairs, those eight mountains press on
his joints. The great, mighty, snowy (?) [ … ] of the god Wadžiwanta
presses on that demon. If that spell were not there [ … ] so [ … ] for the
sake of the earth-demons.

Then the god Wadžiwanta in the tenfold heaven girded up his robe, and put
on the water-god like armour (or) like a robe; that robe [ … ] the eyes of
all (?) the demons [ … ] with a loud voice they screamed and roared. The
demons [ … ] all [ … ] the earth [ … ] he filled [ … ]

### No. 4: the body is like the sea (T M 298)

*Part of a leaf; several lines missing at top and bottom. Uyghur script.
Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] they become dark, gloomy, robbed of understanding.

And the [ … ] of the *mahistak* [ … ] deigned to speak thus: "What now
[ … ] you. My dear son and my (younger) brothers! Strive (in the faith),
then, so that you may always be awake to this one victorious god of the
majesty of the Law, who has appeared over you! And this body, which
surrounds you (is upon you): look at it and judge it so: it is made and
created wholly out of deceit and illusion, falsehood and leading astray.
Within it are many powers, senses, kinds of knowledge and thoughts, which
seethe and are in constant motion! Its appearance is just like the great
ocean, Samudra, where there is much uproar and confusion. And in everything,
as when the wind stands towards the sea [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] it turns back that uproar and surge towards the east. And
as when the wind stands from the south, it carries those disturbances
towards the north and turns them round. And as when the north wind rules,
it turns that uproar of water, the masses of foam, confusion, surge and
swell, and brings them back towards the south. Just as in that sea, when a
south wind rules, uproar, confusion and surge appear within it, so again
(in) this body, which [ … ]"

### No. 5: a good life, and the day of death

*A leaf; at least one line lost at the top. Manichaean script. Found at
Qočo.*

[ … ] visible in kingdom and king [ … ] companions, nobles, princes [ … ] as
if to be revered [ … ] more fitting for the people [ … ] it was fortunate in
your house. So it was needful, if his heaven above should have become very
hard. If he had not used up the livelihood he had brought, (and) had lived
long on earth, then he would have had many blessed joys with you, and
would have completed the good deed that serves (?) the soul. Outside he
would have walked happily with all the noble ones [ … ] whoever acts so
[ … ] not to be found [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] thousand [ … ] with dreadful death [ … ] even if he himself
should be victorious, (he does) not (escape) dying [ … ] Why? So: [the day
of death] fears and shrinks from (nothing); it lets no one hear or notice
it; like the thief, it comes unnoticed. As a lion [ … ] the ox, (or) a wolf
falls on the sheep: so that day of death, to whomever it comes, destroys
all; without mercy it kills (them)! It does not fear kings and emperors
[ … ] bride and bridegroom [ … ] it does not spare old men and old women
[ … ] it has no pity [ … ] those born [ … ]

### No. 6: from a book of sermons

*Leaves of the book to which T II D 173 belongs (T II D 173b, 2; 173c, 1
and 2), in late Sogdian script.*

**T II D 173b, 2, front.** [ … ] if he should be [ … ], let him do good deeds
through the power of alms. And Mšiha (the Messiah) Burxan called those who
believe and give alms, and the people who pray with their soul, the
well-disposed, for their good mind. He deigned to say thus: "Without ever
being stingy towards the shining Law, hide your hidden (treasure), trusting
with your treasure-heart, without doubting." And he deigned to say thus:
"Whoever toils and labours for the sake of the body, his reward (wages) is
the finding (the gain) (that he will) die and perish for the body. But
whoever sows good seed for the sake of his soul, by its reward he will not
die for ever, but will find (himself) in the realm of the gods." Again he
deigned to say thus: "That [ … ] property and possession of yours [ … ] a
very [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] treasure! [ … ] believe: the reward for one loaf of yours,
one vessel of your water, will not go far off (come late), (but) it is
ready!" And in the great book he deigned to say thus: "Those hearers are not
all alike. There are also perfect hearers. There are (truly) such: they are
well-disposed. There are (also) such: they are people who love the Law."

And the rising of the soul to the zodiac, and its rolling about, and its
(going) into another body, unlike [ … ], and different from one another:
there is much (of this). Just as among the fetters, bonds and chains of a
sinful man there are heavy (or) light ones [ … ]

**T II D 173c, 1.** [ … ] he deigned to keep his blessing and his prayer.
The second thought is this: the food eaten, which into that body [ … ] The
[third] thought again, they say: "My body of flesh is a very important
[ … ], mighty thing; to give it that food and drink at the right time is
needful. Why would it do no harm?" (?) The fourth thought is called this:
it is fighting and struggling for ever with the evil passions. Why?
Because your evil passions are very like and very pleasing to the fleshly
body, they become so strong, just as fire kindles dry firewood. (Therefore)
it is needful always to take food and drink at their (set) time, so that
the passions may not become strong and may not harm your body. So, when
(someone) settles down at the resting-place (?), he must consider and weigh
these words with his whole heart.

And the disciples spoke their doubt to their teacher thus: "For what

if to be revered [ … ] more fitting for the people [ … ] it was fortunate in
your house. So it was needful, if his heaven above should have become very
hard. If he had not used up the livelihood he had brought, (and) had lived
long on earth, then he would have had many blessed joys with you, and
would have completed the good deed that serves (?) the soul. Outside he
would have walked happily with all the noble ones [ … ] whoever acts so
[ … ] not to be found [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] thousand [ … ] with dreadful death [ … ] even if he himself
should be victorious, (he does) not (escape) dying [ … ] Why? So: [the day
of death] fears and shrinks from (nothing); it lets no one hear or notice
it; like the thief, it comes unnoticed. As a lion [ … ] the ox, (or) a wolf
falls on the sheep: so that day of death, to whomever it comes, destroys
all; without mercy it kills (them)! It does not fear kings and emperors
[ … ] bride and bridegroom [ … ] it does not spare old men and old women
[ … ] it has no pity [ … ] those born [ … ]

### No. 6: from a book of sermons

*Leaves of the book to which T II D 173 belongs (T II D 173b, 2; 173c, 1
and 2), in late Sogdian script.*

**T II D 173b, 2, front.** [ … ] if he should be [ … ], let him do good deeds
through the power of alms. And Mšiha (the Messiah) Burxan called those who
believe and give alms, and the people who pray with their soul, the
well-disposed, for their good mind. He deigned to say thus: "Without ever
being stingy towards the shining Law, hide your hidden (treasure), trusting
with your treasure-heart, without doubting." And he deigned to say thus:
"Whoever toils and labours for the sake of the body, his reward (wages) is
the finding (the gain) (that he will) die and perish for the body. But
whoever sows good seed for the sake of his soul, by its reward he will not
die for ever, but will find (himself) in the realm of the gods." Again he
deigned to say thus: "That [ … ] property and possession of yours [ … ] a
very [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] treasure! [ … ] believe: the reward for one loaf of yours,
one vessel of your water, will not go far off (come late), (but) it is
ready!" And in the great book he deigned to say thus: "Those hearers are not
all alike. There are also perfect hearers. There are (truly) such: they are
well-disposed. There are (also) such: they are people who love the Law."

And the rising of the soul to the zodiac, and its rolling about, and its
(going) into another body, unlike [ … ], and different from one another:
there is much (of this). Just as among the fetters, bonds and chains of a
sinful man there are heavy (or) light ones [ … ]

**T II D 173c, 1.** [ … ] he deigned to keep his blessing and his prayer.
The second thought is this: the food eaten, which into that body [ … ] The
[third] thought again, they say: "My body of flesh is a very important
[ … ], mighty thing; to give it that food and drink at the right time is
needful. Why would it do no harm?" (?) The fourth thought is called this:
it is fighting and struggling for ever with the evil passions. Why?
Because your evil passions are very like and very pleasing to the fleshly
body, they become so strong, just as fire kindles dry firewood. (Therefore)
it is needful always to take food and drink at their (set) time, so that
the passions may not become strong and may not harm your body. So, when
(someone) settles down at the resting-place (?), he must consider and weigh
these words with his whole heart.

And the disciples spoke their doubt to their teacher thus: "For what
reason, in the book of the Great Gospel, is the moon-god praised and
blessed first, and only (afterwards) the great princely king of the gods,
Zurwān the god?" Their teacher deigned to speak thus: [ … ] *(the answer is
lost).*

**T II D 173c, 2.** [ … ] their (his) own remaining [ … ], their seed, their
grain, must be thought of, if one gives good alms for all good law. Why?
That (man's) left-behind treasure and property shall not perish [ … ]
sinful towards God [ … ] hard [ … ] gone [ … ] Summer [ … ] and winter
[ … ] it is right (?). Just as all [ … ] there are [ … ] of vanishing and
coming [ … ] if one should hurry, all together pours out and scatters [ … ]
in gain and profit (and more), limb and bone [ … ] to gather in time
[ … ]; their living self (to) death is right (?). To be well, to be sick, to
grow old, is right (?). And of all kinds of food and drink [ … ]

*A small leaf in Manichaean script.* [ … ] should give, who should think of
it [ … ] in the Law and in the faith; in ruin, in rich possessions, or
[ … ] of deeds of the fleshly body [ … ] in the hearers the divine knowledge
of love is not found. Let those hearers not think so [ … ] towards God and
the Law [ … ]

### No. 7: Mani's teaching on the Maiden of Light

*A double leaf of the same book as T II D 176 (T II D 172a and others), in
Manichaean script.*

**I.** [ … ] this maiden for another [ … ] you throw yourself in with all
[ … ] you replace, very [ … ] second [ … ] a fresh green tree [ … ] fragrant
[ … ] *(six lines torn away)* [ … ] with all your heart [ … ] keep [ … ] let
it be [ … ] sent [ … ] thus [ … ] you hear! [ … ] tell: in early (times),
in past time, a great city [ … ] for all goods perfect [ … ]

**II.** [ … ] And again: just as a master washer [ … ] the king's robe [ … ]
just as one throws (it) into flowing water that is not [ … ] and cleans it
with the hand [ … ] *(eight lines torn away)* [ … ] as one [trains] a horse
fit for the king [ … ] sows seed in a place, and again so [ … ] much [ … ]
suffers pain, later (but) [ … ] at the time [ … ] then joys [ … ]

**III.** [ … ] has become perfect [ … ] that blessed living self you send with
joy on the true way, to the true place (?), since you have been called for
that. [ … ] souls [ … ] Father, the divine Mani, deigned to say thus:

"My beloved youth (son)! First consider those detailed (?) words and
interpretations which I have set before you. That Maiden of Light, the
Mother(-God), the shining Wind, our prince (and) king of the gods Zurwān
the god, (and) the second [ … ] light itself, which itself is the deity
Kanig Rōšan (the Maiden of Light), is the god who gathers the dead.
Third, the shining [ … ] of the majesty of the Law, which itself is that
prince of the whole Law [ … ] of those three princely [ … ], their coming
and descending, and their virtue, strength in prayer and piety, and how,
after their coming, it is imparted (put on) to all these treasures [ … ]
was. This wise knowledge I have told you and set before you through many
parables, many interpretations and testimonies, with the words of all these
strong ones; and also at what time these princely gods came and appeared,
who are that Yišō Kanig (Jesus the Maiden), Wahman Rōšan, the deity [ … ];
this wise knowledge, which is itself that Maiden of Light [ … ]"

## Notes to this edition

- **Siin** (no. 1): Le Coq could not decide whether this name of a god is
  the Babylonian moon-god Sin or a Chinese word.
- **The moon's waxing and waning** (no. 2): in Manichaean teaching the moon
  fills with the light gathered from the world and empties it into the sun
  each month.
- **The demon under the mountains** (no. 3): the Living Spirit
  (*Wadžiwanta*) holds the defeated demons down under the earth and the
  mountains, with Mount Sumeru on the trunk.
- **Mšiha Burxan** (no. 6) is the Messiah, Jesus. "One loaf … one vessel of
  your water" recalls Matthew 10:42 ("a cup of cold water").
- **The question about the moon-god and Zurwān** (no. 6) shows that the
  Great Gospel (Mani's Living Gospel) was read in Turkish communities.
- **Kanig Rōšan** (no. 7) is the Maiden of Light, here identified with
  "wise knowledge"; Yišō is Jesus, and Wahman Rōšan the Light-Nous.

input.content:
---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: hymns, parables and Aesop"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 77
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with hymns to the "new day, new month, new year" and to the shining soul, a warning against false Elect, the parable of the astrologer, the tree of wisdom, the book of the fairy queen, and a fable of Aesop.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 10–14 (T II D 175, T II D 181, T I α 1 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

These are Le Coq's nos. 10 to 14 in his 1922 volume: two short hymns, a
leaf on alms and false Elect from the same book as the hearers' confession
(the [Xwāstwānīft](xwastwanift.html)), several leaves of a book of parables
(*brama*), and the start of his group of colophons and miscellaneous pieces,
which includes a scrap of the fables of Aesop in Turkish.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
sense.

## The translation

### No. 10: "You are the new day"

*A small double leaf; one leaf has Middle Persian text, the other Turkish.
Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] to empty [ … ] My God! (You are) the new (day), the new,
shining (month), the new, praised year! You are the new, mighty, shining
God! And, my God, when you came forth from the realm of the gods, my God,
your [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] (through) the sight [ … ] of (your) shining, beautiful face
we have become full of joy. You are the princely, strong, shining God,
mighty in prayer! And, my God, (that which is) above [ … ]

### No. 11: "O shining soul"

*The lower part of a leaf; Manichaean script, the lines in carmine. Found at
Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] to gather wood [ … ] stuffed in [ … ] smoking [ … ] glowing
*(hymn)* [ … ] become charcoal; cooked [ … ] (the soul?) does not die at
all, he says. You, how can you?! O shining soul! *Śrī!* Whoever does not
build and give a house to the homeless arhat (Elect), they set him, it is
said, in a [ … ] set with spikes (?). He finds the spikes, (and they) come
out of his head. *Śrī!*

**Back.** [ … ] does not spread. Your sinews [ … ] parting from your bones
[ … ]. The soul never dies, they say. O shining soul! *(hymn)* How will you
be able (to)! O shining soul! Pure alms let us give! O shining soul! With
pure alms let us do reverence! O shining soul! *(hymn)* Whoever does not
prepare and give food to the hungry, thirsty Elect [ … ]

### No. 12: against false Elect

*A leaf from the same book as the leaves of the hearers' confession
(Xwāstwānīft) T II D 178. Manichaean script. Found in ruin K at Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] do not eat; hide and conceal (it) surely; let no other man
see (it). The false teachers, who go astray, wander off and are perverse
through three [ … ] words, claim the name of Elect, and, deceiving and
cheating, take alms. They themselves will go to hell, and take the giver
along after them.

The Āz demon, the shameless devil of greed, the dark demons, make many men
go astray, and fasten them to the [ … ] son. They suffer the pains of birth
and death; they are destroyed by the fire of greed, and cannot satisfy it;
the shining soul

**Back.** they do not improve. If one thinks of (this) with care, (then)
we are a happy people [ … ] become (for?) the hour of passing away (?).
Let us revere and beseech the shining, pious Elect! Let us not torment
their mind and their wisdom! [ … ] according to what we can bear (as far as
we are able), let us give alms! [ … ] not to the Āz demon! Let us give
(our) goods as alms! The white-robed Elect [ … ] let us beseech! Our Father
Zurwān [ … ]

### No. 13: from a book of parables

*Several leaves of one book, in a careless Uyghur hand. Found in ruins α
and K at Qočo.*

**T II D 175, 1, front.** *(Red title, destroyed.)* [ … ] earth [ … ] is the
[ … ] eternal realm of the gods. On this earth you walk in sorrow, pressed
down, exposed to contempt. On that earth you will walk without sorrow, in
wide freedom. And whoever on this earth in wide freedom [ … ]

**Back.** *(Red title, destroyed.)* [ … ] has been born [ … ] That astrologer
[ … ] had become pious, as he had said. And one day that astrologer spoke
with reverence to the king thus: "Majesty! I have looked at your star (and)
thought (about it) [ … ] I know and understand [ … ]"

-title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: hymns, parables and Aesop"
-text: true
-group: extracanonical
-order: 77

-summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with hymns to the "new day, new month, new year" and to the shining soul, a warning against false Elect, the parable of the astrologer, the tree of wisdom, the book of the fairy queen, and a fable of Aesop.
-original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)

-source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 10–14 (T II D 175, T II D 181, T I α 1 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'

-## Introduction
-These are Le Coq's nos. 10 to 14 in his 1922 volume: two short hymns, a
-leaf on alms and false Elect from the same book as the hearers' confession
-(the [Xwāstwānīft](xwastwanift.html)), several leaves of a book of parables
-(*brama*), and the start of his group of colophons and miscellaneous pieces,
-which includes a scrap of the fables of Aesop in Turkish.
-**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
-called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
-Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
-sense.
-## The translation
-### No. 10: "You are the new day"
-*A small double leaf; one leaf has Middle Persian text, the other Turkish.
-Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.*
-**Front.** [ … ] to empty [ … ] My God! (You are) the new (day), the new,
-shining (month), the new, praised year! You are the new, mighty, shining
-God! And, my God, when you came forth from the realm of the gods, my God,
-your [ … ]
-**Back.** [ … ] (through) the sight [ … ] of (your) shining, beautiful face
-we have become full of joy. You are the princely, strong, shining God,
-mighty in prayer! And, my God, (that which is) above [ … ]
-### No. 11: "O shining soul"
-*The lower part of a leaf; Manichaean script, the lines in carmine. Found at
-Qočo.*
-**Front.** [ … ] to gather wood [ … ] stuffed in [ … ] smoking [ … ] glowing
-*(hymn)* [ … ] become charcoal; cooked [ … ] (the soul?) does not die at
-all, he says. You, how can you?! O shining soul! *Śrī!* Whoever does not
-build and give a house to the homeless arhat (Elect), they set him, it is
-said, in a [ … ] set with spikes (?). He finds the spikes, (and they) come
-out of his head. *Śrī!*
-**Back.** [ … ] does not spread. Your sinews [ … ] parting from your bones
-[ … ]. The soul never dies, they say. O shining soul! *(hymn)* How will you
-be able (to)! O shining soul! Pure alms let us give! O shining soul! With
-pure alms let us do reverence! O shining soul! *(hymn)* Whoever does not
-prepare and give food to the hungry, thirsty Elect [ … ]
-### No. 12: against false Elect
-*A leaf from the same book as the leaves of the hearers' confession
-(Xwāstwānīft) T II D 178. Manichaean script. Found in ruin K at Qočo.*
-**Front.** [ … ] do not eat; hide and conceal (it) surely; let no other man
-see (it). The false teachers, who go astray, wander off and are perverse
-through three [ … ] words, claim the name of Elect, and, deceiving and
-cheating, take alms. They themselves will go to hell, and take the giver
-along after them.
-The Āz demon, the shameless devil of greed, the dark demons, make many men
-go astray, and fasten them to the [ … ] son. They suffer the pains of birth
-and death; they are destroyed by the fire of greed, and cannot satisfy it;
-the shining soul
-**Back.** they do not improve. If one thinks of (this) with care, (then)
-we are a happy people [ … ] become (for?) the hour of passing away (?).
-Let us revere and beseech the shining, pious Elect! Let us not torment
-their mind and their wisdom! [ … ] according to what we can bear (as far as
-we are able), let us give alms! [ … ] not to the Āz demon! Let us give
-(our) goods as alms! The white-robed Elect [ … ] let us beseech! Our Father
-Zurwān [ … ]
-### No. 13: from a book of parables
-*Several leaves of one book, in a careless Uyghur hand. Found in ruins α
-and K at Qočo.*
-**T II D 175, 1, front.** *(Red title, destroyed.)* [ … ] earth [ … ] is the
-[ … ] eternal realm of the gods. On this earth you walk in sorrow, pressed
-down, exposed to contempt. On that earth you will walk without sorrow, in
-wide freedom. And whoever on this earth in wide freedom [ … ]
-**Back.** *(Red title, destroyed.)* [ … ] has been born [ … ] That astrologer
-[ … ] had become pious, as he had said. And one day that astrologer spoke
-with reverence to the king thus: "Majesty! I have looked at your star (and)
-thought (about it) [ … ] I know and understand [ … ]"
-**T II D 175, 2, leaf 1, front.** *Title: "Parable (brama)".* Then the god of
-the majesty of the Law comes, with the three gods that he himself is,
-(as?) [ … ] pious mercy [ … ] to that soul. He speaks many kinds of [ … ]
-words of remembrance (?). Then he sends it to the judge of the dead. By
-the fruit of the good deeds it has done itself, it finds there victory and
-gain [ … ]
-*In red:* Ended is this parable of the astrologer.
-"[ … ] good deeds I did not do many times," he said. "Why? From those alms
-I gave, from the good deeds I did, I have found as fruit (reward) the
-shining realm of the gods." [ … ] Tušist the god [ … ]
-*In red:* Ended is this book, the parable of the astrologer.
-*In red:* Here begins the parable of [ … ]
-**Leaf 1, back.** [ … ] book. The bark of the excellent tree of wisdom (is)
-watchfulness (and) understanding, wisdom (and) care for the release of the
-power of the five gods. The calm, gentle mind endures heavy pain. This so
-[ … ] And bear the unchosen (?), unshakable [ … ]. To be wretched, to be
-merciful [ … ] stained with red blood [ … ]
-**Leaf 2.** [ … ] to circle (?). This is the third hymn (?). And one *baqïr*
-in weight is: being patient (?). Two *baqïr* in weight is: being watchful.
-Seven parts = [ … ]; one part = the root of the knowledge of insight; two
-parts = the flower of the Law; seven *baqïr* in weight = the seed of
-Srōšahrāy; one single ounce = the leaf of fine nature and conduct; one part
-**T II D 181, leaf 1.** *Title: "The book of the fairy queen".* [ … ] as far as
-Gandhāra (?) [ … ] for the religion [ … ] those who hide (bury) [things]
-from one another [ … ] And at that time I [ … ] went, the two of us, to the
-castle of that fairy queen [ … ] all [ … ] I spoke [ … ] then [ … ]
-**Back.** *Title: "The splendour (?) of the fairies".* [ … ] in guilt and sin
-[ … ] I have given [ … ] to free (themselves) [ … ] Then [from the] sin
-[ … ] I have purified: this to me [ … ] he begged; if [ … ]
-**Leaf 1, second side.** [ … ] wise words [ … ] way, the Buddha way. These
-three [ … ] And three [ … ] the divine self, which itself is this [ … ]; the
-wise self; second, the visible [ … ] self; third, the self of miraculous
-power. In this [ … ] divine self [ … ]
-**Leaf 2.** [ … ] way, the Buddha way, this [ … ] Third: this mind's [ … ]
-so [ … ] if it is as has been said [ … ] that moon (?) [ … ] has been, in
-all torment and confusion. Then [ … ] thinking, cannot so act [ … ] of the
-mind, shining, pure [ … ] understood [ … ]
-### No. 14: a fable of Aesop
-*From Le Coq's group of colophons, pieces naming historical persons, Aesop
-and food rules. The upper part of a large leaf of European form; Manichaean
-script. Found in ruin α at Qočo.*
-**Front.** *Title, in red: "Of the (wise) Yosipas (Aesop)".* [ … ] is needed.
-At this word they all laughed and praised Aesop, and spoke thus: "Be
-joyful, Aesop!" When Aesop said, "Why?", (they answered:) "We are all very
-glad! For this reason our [ … ] (and) its strength is small; all our
-knowledge [ … ]" Aesop thus [ … ] will speak [ … ]
-**Back.** *Title, in red: "Good, fair (book)".* "If one drives it to be killed,
-it roars." Aesop spoke thus: "That is why the sheep does not cry out!" Why?
-"One by one they tie its legs, throw it down and shear its wool." Just as
-when, for the sake of [ … ], one ties the legs [ … ] but the pig [ … ]
-## Notes to this edition
-- ***Śrī*** and ***baš*** (no. 11): Le Coq thought *baš* a form of the word
-  for "hymn", and left open whether *śrī* invokes the Indian goddess of
-  fortune.
-- ***baqïr*** (no. 13) is a small weight; Le Coq gives it as about a tenth
-  of an ounce.
-- **Tušist** (no. 13) may be Tušita, the Buddhist heaven, here taken as the
-  name of a god.
-- **Aesop** (no. 14): Le Coq identified *Yosipas* with Aesop through the
-  Syriac and Arabic fables of "Sophos", and compared a fable in Landsberger's
-  edition, *Die Fabeln des Sophos* (1859), no. 66. The pig and the sheep are
-  the animals of that fable.

input.content:
---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: the Iduq-qut's enthronement and other pieces"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 78
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with the church's blessing on the enthronement of an Iduq-qut of Qočo, a hymn on a god who came down with the mahistak Noydar, a blessing for a možak's community, and fragments on hell, the sun-god's battle and a fish left on dry sand.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 15–19 (T M 417 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

These pieces belong to Le Coq's group of colophons and leaves naming
historical persons. The most important (no. 15, T M 417) is a blessing
spoken by the Manichaean community of Qočo when a new *Iduq-qut*, the
Uyghur ruler of Qočo, took the throne after the death of his predecessor.
Lines of it had already been printed by F. W. K. Müller in *Uigurica*
(1908). The other pieces are a short hymn on a god who came down from
heaven and brought a *mahistak* named Noydar, a blessing on a *možak* and
his community, and fragments of sermons.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
sense. The numbering of the smaller pieces follows the order in which Le
Coq printed them.

## The translation

### No. 15 (T M 417): the blessing on the new Iduq-qut

*A large leaf, 28.5 × 17 cm, in Manichaean script; the top line and the
upper inner edge destroyed. Found at Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] shining. Because he has deigned (to set) like the sun-god,
in the capital [ … ] first of all the whole two shining communities [ … ],
the youths (?) (and) the Elect; outside in the province, the nobles living
in the blessed land, the princesses, the god-like princes, the Il-ügäs, the
envoys and all those of name; his people, high and low, who act like birds
[ … ] like dogs, cattle and two-footed ones (?); from the blue heaven above
down to the king of the earth-god: we, the souls and spirits, rejoicing
with all our heart, have reverently wished for this day of fortune. Because
the majesty of Il-Ötükän has deigned to give strength, because we have all
reverently found the whole happiness of the heart, therefore, my divine
one, from the heart, with loving mind and great love, we reverently speak
blessings and ask for joy!

The bestowing of the title, which we have performed, with the divine,
illustrious name on our divine king, the Iduq-qut; his gracious taking of
his seat on the golden throne, on the jewelled throne; his becoming
majestic and fortunate: may it come to pass! May the four shining kings of
the gods come, the burxans mighty in prayer who are in the ten directions!

**Back.** [ … ] the souls who have been set free [ … ], having completed
their own affairs, have gone to the realm of the gods. "That (throne?)
shall not remain empty," saying [ … ]; so he deigned to sit on that
throne. All the burxans, strong in prayer, as if of one face (?), changing
name and form, appeared to save (set free) the souls.

When our prince the Iduq-qut deigned (to set) like the sun-god, we, the
whole poor, wholly common people, were grieved and troubled. As, in the
place of the sun-god, the shining moon-god deigns to appear shining, so our
prince the Iduq-qut deigns to appear in the place of Awlawč. It was (his)
pleasure (the command) to sit down on the golden throne.

May the princely majesty of Il-Ötükän, the majesty of the former wise
prince-fathers and of the princes, the majesty of this illustrious throne,
settle on our divine prince the Iduq-qut! From the seven and the twelve
mighty rulers may strength and help come; may fair, longed-for, many-
coloured light and splendour settle on the majesty of our brave, virtuous,
high and mighty prince! And on his whole kingdom and all its order [ … ]

### A hymn on the god who came down (with the *mahistak* Noydar)

*A leaf of European form, 17 × 10.6 cm; one line (or more) missing at the
bottom. Uyghur script. Found at Qočo. The title reads "Noydar the
mahistak" and the start of the first line a few words not understood.*

**Front.** Here begins [ … ] at the lack (absence) [ … ]. Our shining,
radiant god, mighty in magic, came down from the realm of the gods. When
he came down from the realm of the gods, he brought the god Tvai (?) with
him. Through the coming of the god Tvai (?), he took away our souls (bound
for) hell [ … ] Because (he) [ … ]

**Back.** Because (he) deigned to free and enlighten (us), we have been
saved from the place from which no one returns. Because he set up the Law
of the Burxan, we have been freed from (weeping and) lamenting. Clothed
with the majesty of the Law (?), our king himself has brought Noydar, the
*mahistak*.

### A blessing for the *možak* and his community

*The edge of a leaf, damaged at the sides, 6.5 × 7.2 cm; Manichaean
script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] the Burxan; our divine [ … ] the divine *možak* [ … ] all [ … ] the
Elect [ … ], the princesses, the *tarqan*s, the princes, the statesmen
[ … ], my divine one! On this day, in the blessed month, [with] joy [ … ]
may there be his favour, without danger, without oppression, without
