-title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: the Iduq-qut's enthronement and other pieces"
-text: true
-group: extracanonical

-summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with the church's blessing on the enthronement of an Iduq-qut of Qočo, a hymn on a god who came down with the mahistak Noydar, a blessing for a možak's community, and fragments on hell, the sun-god's battle and a fish left on dry sand.
-original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)

-source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 15–19 (T M 417 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
-rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
-## Introduction
-These pieces belong to Le Coq's group of colophons and leaves naming
-historical persons. The most important (no. 15, T M 417) is a blessing
-spoken by the Manichaean community of Qočo when a new *Iduq-qut*, the
-Uyghur ruler of Qočo, took the throne after the death of his predecessor.
-Lines of it had already been printed by F. W. K. Müller in *Uigurica*
-(1908). The other pieces are a short hymn on a god who came down from
-heaven and brought a *mahistak* named Noydar, a blessing on a *možak* and
-his community, and fragments of sermons.
-**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
-called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
-Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
-sense. The numbering of the smaller pieces follows the order in which Le
-Coq printed them.
-## The translation
-### No. 15 (T M 417): the blessing on the new Iduq-qut
-*A large leaf, 28.5 × 17 cm, in Manichaean script; the top line and the
-upper inner edge destroyed. Found at Qočo.*
-**Front.** [ … ] shining. Because he has deigned (to set) like the sun-god,
-in the capital [ … ] first of all the whole two shining communities [ … ],
-the youths (?) (and) the Elect; outside in the province, the nobles living
-in the blessed land, the princesses, the god-like princes, the Il-ügäs, the
-envoys and all those of name; his people, high and low, who act like birds
-[ … ] like dogs, cattle and two-footed ones (?); from the blue heaven above
-down to the king of the earth-god: we, the souls and spirits, rejoicing
-with all our heart, have reverently wished for this day of fortune. Because
-the majesty of Il-Ötükän has deigned to give strength, because we have all
-reverently found the whole happiness of the heart, therefore, my divine
-one, from the heart, with loving mind and great love, we reverently speak
-blessings and ask for joy!
-The bestowing of the title, which we have performed, with the divine,
-illustrious name on our divine king, the Iduq-qut; his gracious taking of
-his seat on the golden throne, on the jewelled throne; his becoming
-majestic and fortunate: may it come to pass! May the four shining kings of
-the gods come, the burxans mighty in prayer who are in the ten directions!
-**Back.** [ … ] the souls who have been set free [ … ], having completed
-their own affairs, have gone to the realm of the gods. "That (throne?)
-shall not remain empty," saying [ … ]; so he deigned to sit on that
-throne. All the burxans, strong in prayer, as if of one face (?), changing
-name and form, appeared to save (set free) the souls.
-When our prince the Iduq-qut deigned (to set) like the sun-god, we, the
-whole poor, wholly common people, were grieved and troubled. As, in the
-place of the sun-god, the shining moon-god deigns to appear shining, so our
-prince the Iduq-qut deigns to appear in the place of Awlawč. It was (his)
-pleasure (the command) to sit down on the golden throne.
-May the princely majesty of Il-Ötükän, the majesty of the former wise
-prince-fathers and of the princes, the majesty of this illustrious throne,
-settle on our divine prince the Iduq-qut! From the seven and the twelve
-mighty rulers may strength and help come; may fair, longed-for, many-
-coloured light and splendour settle on the majesty of our brave, virtuous,
-high and mighty prince! And on his whole kingdom and all its order [ … ]
-### A hymn on the god who came down (with the *mahistak* Noydar)
-*A leaf of European form, 17 × 10.6 cm; one line (or more) missing at the
-bottom. Uyghur script. Found at Qočo. The title reads "Noydar the
-mahistak" and the start of the first line a few words not understood.*
-**Front.** Here begins [ … ] at the lack (absence) [ … ]. Our shining,
-radiant god, mighty in magic, came down from the realm of the gods. When
-he came down from the realm of the gods, he brought the god Tvai (?) with
-him. Through the coming of the god Tvai (?), he took away our souls (bound
-for) hell [ … ] Because (he) [ … ]
-**Back.** Because (he) deigned to free and enlighten (us), we have been
-saved from the place from which no one returns. Because he set up the Law
-of the Burxan, we have been freed from (weeping and) lamenting. Clothed
-with the majesty of the Law (?), our king himself has brought Noydar, the
-*mahistak*.
-### A blessing for the *možak* and his community
-*The edge of a leaf, damaged at the sides, 6.5 × 7.2 cm; Manichaean
-script. Found at Qočo.*
-[ … ] the Burxan; our divine [ … ] the divine *možak* [ … ] all [ … ] the
-Elect [ … ], the princesses, the *tarqan*s, the princes, the statesmen
-[ … ], my divine one! On this day, in the blessed month, [with] joy [ … ]
-may there be his favour, without danger, without oppression, without
-grief, without care, without harm! May he hold (us) in his care and guard
-(us) in every danger and adversity, by night and day! Many [ … ] of soul
-and body [ … ] that [ … ] himself divine [ … ]
-### From a sermon: the throne in the fire-god's heaven, and the body
-*A leaf badly damaged at the edges, 23.1 × 13 cm; Manichaean script,
-apparently of the same book as T M 170 and 176. Found in ruin K at Qočo.*
-**Front.** [ … ] if (they) go astray [ … ] they (will) fall into hell [ … ]
-very hard [ … ] he deigned (to say) [ … ] teacher [ … ] Paradise [ … ] he
-named Paradise [ … ] in the realm of the gods of the fire-god [ … ]
-throne [ … ] he deigned [ … ] If so [ … ]
-[ … ] naked [ … ] covering (?) [ … ] many enemies [ … ] his life, his heart
-(liver) [ … ] he cannot stand and stay [ … ] seeing so [ … ] his body [ … ]
-brides and bridegrooms [ … ] for the stinking body [ … ]
-**Back (continued).** [ … ] on (this) earth, in a kingdom, in a city, he
-endured many kinds of oppression. For your sake he set forth the two
-Laws. If your foundation and root should not be there, then that kingdom,
-that city, that earth is without colour, without beauty, without [ … ],
-without strength [ … ] colour, strength [ … ] called [ … ] chosen (?)
-[ … ] my disciples [ … ] this [ … ] sin [ … ]
-### From a cosmogony: the sun-god against the demons
-*The upper part of a leaf, 12.5 × 12 cm; Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.
-The heading is in red and blue.*
-**Front (?).** *We have sinned [ … ].* "He comes to fight," saying. The
-sun-god thought so: "He has resisted (?). That is why he has [ … ]." He
-knew the wickedness of the devil. "(I?) will strike the demons and
-(fasten them) to the zodiac," saying. The (ten)fold (heaven) [ … ] he made
-rise [ … ]
-**Back.** *(The four?) great things.* [ … ] (if) water should go down, (and)
-plants (?); if the end (foot) of that water [ … ], and should reach the
-great sand, and the water should stick in the sand in front, that fish, as
-if its skin (its coat?) had stayed behind on the dry sand [ … ] sun [ … ]
-the sun-god [ … ]
-## Notes to this edition
-- **The Iduq-qut** (no. 15) was the title of the Uyghur rulers of Qočo.
-  The blessing compares the death of the former ruler with the setting of
-  the sun and the new ruler with the moon that shines in its place;
-  *Awlawč* is apparently the name of the predecessor. Il-Ötükän is the
-  sacred homeland of the Turks, here personified as a "majesty".
-- **"The seven and the twelve"** (no. 15) are the planets and the signs of
-  the zodiac, here as the "mighty rulers" whose favour is wished on the
-  prince.
-- **Noydar the *mahistak***: a church official of the third rank (the
-  *mahistag*, "elder"); the god *Tvai* is not identified (Le Coq's reading is
-  uncertain).
-- **"The two Laws"** (the sermon fragment) are perhaps the Law of the Elect
-  and the Law of the hearers.

---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: rules, the lamb, and Mani in the Uyghur land"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 79
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with rules for the Elect and the hearers on chastity and fast days, Mani's commandments, a saying on the flesh of the sinless lamb, a prayer for a Tängrikän ruling Qočo and its twenty-two cities, and a prayer to Mani who came to the Uyghur land.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 20–25 (T M 148, 165, 177, T M 176, T II D 62 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

More of Le Coq's colophons and miscellaneous pieces (1922): rules of
conduct and fast days, a leaf on the commandments Mani gave his Elect, a
leaf in which the disciples are told to eat "the flesh of the innocent,
sinless lamb" without breaking its bones, prayers for a ruler (*Tängrikän*)
of Qočo and its twenty-two cities, and a prayer to Mani "who, when we came
to the Uyghur land, [gave] us strength and fortune".

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
sense. The pieces are given in the order in which Le Coq printed them.

## The translation

### Rules of conduct and fast days

*A leaf destroyed on three sides, 16.5 × 10.5 cm; Manichaean script. Found
at Qočo.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] water [ … ] he shall guard (?). And from fornication the
shining ones and the long-robed ones [ … ]; again, whoever is long-robed,
from the man [ … ]; again, guarding their bodies, they shall flee
altogether. Again, a man one shall not strike [ … ], one shall not bind and
[ … ]; [ … ] the soul one shall call good. And the good-(doing) shining
Elect one shall revere with shining food and shining drink [ … ] lies,
transgression and sin [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] weeps (?) [ … ] or if he does (it) [ … ]; to whom he does
(it) on the eleventh (day?), or if he does it on the day of Ohrmizd; or if
he does it on the great or the small fast-day; or if he does it on a
*qaming* (any?) day, then the gods [ … ] of the good deed [ … ] whoever does
[ … ] deeds to men [ … ]; and [ … ] his soul like [ … ] (two-, four-?) footed
beings [ … ] slave and slave-girl [ … ] should be [ … ]

### Mani's commandments

*The middle of a leaf, 10 × 11.5 cm; Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] shining and clear [ … ] its (their) torment on it
entirely [ … ] when they [ … ]. How at the coming of the shining, divine
Mani, the Burxan, he became Elect, and handed over to them the shining Law.
He handed over to them the command of tormenting abstinence and the five
commandments. First of all he gave (strength and energy) for piety [ … ]
God [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] male [ … ] "on shameless things you shall not think [ … ]
you shall be [ … ]," he deigned to say. "Fourth," he said this: "Dried
blood you shall not eat. That dried blood itself [ … ]"

### The flesh of the sinless lamb

*The bottom edge of a leaf, 14.5 × 8.5 cm; Manichaean script. Found at
Qočo. In the margin, in Uyghur script and upside down: "he lived on his
knees".*

[ … ] he made appear; twelve kinds of very different signs he showed; the
shining, bright Law (religion) of the Magi he established [ … ] he made.
Six days, six nights [ … ] he deigned [to say]: "Eat the flesh of the
innocent, sinless, dear lamb, but do not break its bones!" Saying so, he
handed over to his disciples the seal of the commandments, which you [ … ]

### A prayer for the Tängrikän

*The lower part of a leaf, 14.5 × 10 cm; Manichaean script. Found at
Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] radiant [ … ] our shining [ … ] mighty in prayer [ … ] our
Tängrikän, the great [ … ]: in the capital, for the sake of the religion;
in the province, for the sake of the whole kingdom, he has tormented his
jewel-like noble body in service [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] became [ … ] all [ … ] plants [ … ] all sprouted [ … ] became
alike (?). Therefore the fortune and the (guardian) spirit of the kingdom
of Qočo and of the twenty-two cities [ … ], (namely?) our lovely Tängrikän,
his high majesty very [ … ]

### A piece on the Moon-god and the Toquz Oγuz

*The edge of a leaf, 10.7 × 9.5 cm; Uyghur script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] for the sake of [ … ] died; by his dying (?) set free [ … ] scattered
like barley [ … ] the people [ … ] grief [ … ] scattered much [ … ] the
soul [ … ] the moon-god [ … ] came down [ … ]

[ … ] his banner, his drum (signs of rule!) [ … ] stayed (in the realm?) of
the Toquz Oγuz [ … ] has been set up. The majesty of the Law [ … ] came down
[ … ] in the middle of the river [ … ] my God! The five [ … ] through [ … ]
knowledge [ … ]

### A prayer to Mani, who came to the Uyghur land

*The lower part of a leaf, 9 × 9.1 cm; Uyghur script. Found in ruin K at
Qočo.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] Mani the Apostle, the [Burxan], we beseech as if
blindly. Because Mani the Apostle [ … ] us, when we came to the Uyghur land,
[gave] us strength and fortune [ … ], we beseech him as if blindly! [ … ]
the eternally praised Apostle (angel) [ … ] the strong gods for ever [ … ]
we beseech! [ … ] my God! [ … ] in us [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] the apostles [ … ] the victorious spirit of the
*tvcyan qoz* (?) I will hold. Without grief and sorrow may you live, and
end in well-being! May your praised Law (last) for all eternity! Ended is
[ … ] *tiuda* [ … ]

## Notes to this edition

- **The day of Ohrmizd** (the rules): the first day of the Iranian month,
  named after Ohrmizd; the great and small fast-days are the Manichaean
  fasts. Le Coq's reading of the word for "Ohrmizd" (*Vurmazt*) is a little
  uncertain.
- **"The five commandments"**: the commandments of the Elect. The ban on
  "dried blood" agrees with the Elect's rule against eating flesh and
  blood.
- **"The flesh of the innocent, sinless lamb … do not break its bones"**:
  compare Exodus 12:46 and John 19:36, said of the Passover lamb and of
  Jesus. The speaker, who "made appear twelve kinds of signs" and
  established "the Law of the Magi", is not named in what survives.
- **Qočo and the twenty-two cities**: the Uyghur kingdom of Qočo
  (the West Uyghur kingdom) and its towns; the *Tängrikän* is its ruler.
- **The Toquz Oγuz** ("Nine Oγuz") are the Uyghur tribal confederation.

[ … ] deeds to men [ … ]; and [ … ] his soul like [ … ] (two-, four-?) footed
beings [ … ] slave and slave-girl [ … ] should be [ … ]

**Front (?).** [ … ] shining and clear [ … ] its (their) torment on it
entirely [ … ] when they [ … ]. How at the coming of the shining, divine
Mani, the Burxan, he became Elect, and handed over to them the shining Law.

commandments. First of all he gave (strength and energy) for piety [ … ]
God [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] male [ … ] "on shameless things you shall not think [ … ]
you shall be [ … ]," he deigned to say. "Fourth," he said this: "Dried
blood you shall not eat. That dried blood itself [ … ]"

*The bottom edge of a leaf, 14.5 × 8.5 cm; Manichaean script. Found at
Qočo. In the margin, in Uyghur script and upside down: "he lived on his
knees".*

[ … ] he made appear; twelve kinds of very different signs he showed; the
shining, bright Law (religion) of the Magi he established [ … ] he made.
Six days, six nights [ … ] he deigned [to say]: "Eat the flesh of the
innocent, sinless, dear lamb, but do not break its bones!" Saying so, he
handed over to his disciples the seal of the commandments, which you [ … ]

*The lower part of a leaf, 14.5 × 10 cm; Manichaean script. Found at
Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] radiant [ … ] our shining [ … ] mighty in prayer [ … ] our
Tängrikän, the great [ … ]: in the capital, for the sake of the religion;
in the province, for the sake of the whole kingdom, he has tormented his
jewel-like noble body in service [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] became [ … ] all [ … ] plants [ … ] all sprouted [ … ] became

*The lower part of a leaf, 9 × 9.1 cm; Uyghur script. Found in ruin K at
Qočo.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] Mani the Apostle, the [Burxan], we beseech as if
blindly. Because Mani the Apostle [ … ] us, when we came to the Uyghur land,

we beseech! [ … ] my God! [ … ] in us [ … ]

**Back (?).** [ … ] the apostles [ … ] the victorious spirit of the
*tvcyan qoz* (?) I will hold. Without grief and sorrow may you live, and

  named after Ohrmizd; the great and small fast-days are the Manichaean
  fasts. Le Coq's reading of the word for "Ohrmizd" (*Vurmazt*) is a little
  uncertain.
- **"The five commandments"**: the commandments of the Elect. The ban on
  "dried blood" agrees with the Elect's rule against eating flesh and
  blood.

  (the West Uyghur kingdom) and its towns; the *Tängrikän* is its ruler.
- **The Toquz Oγuz** ("Nine Oγuz") are the Uyghur tribal confederation.

---
title: "Old Turkish Manichaean fragments from Qočo, III: the Manistan, colophons and Ānanda"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 80
summary: Uyghur Manichaean pieces from Qočo, with a saying that this made earth is not eternal, a blessing on the hearers gathered in the Manistan, a colophon naming an Uyghur khan and his court, a fragment on the drying world, and a dialogue in which the monk Ānanda asks the Burxan who falls into the three evil ways.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur)
source: 'Turfan manuscripts in Le Coq''s nos. 26–39 (T M 164, 174, 279, 278, 288, T I D 1, T M 137 and others) (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Türkische Manichaica aus Chotscho. III", Abhandlungen der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 1922, Phil.-hist. Klasse Nr. 2 (archive.org `AbhandDerPreussAkadDerWissen1922`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Le Coq's 1922 German; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

The last group of smaller pieces in Le Coq's 1922 volume. They include a
saying that "this earth is a made earth … not eternal", a long blessing
read over the hearers gathered in the *Manistan* (the Manichaean monastery),
a colophon in which a scribe named Aïduq records who asked for the book, a
fragment comparing the world to a drying river, and a dialogue, much in the
Buddhist manner, in which the monk Ānanda questions the Burxan about the
evil ways of rebirth.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Le Coq's German, which he
called "first attempts at interpretation". Gaps are marked [ … ]; words Le
Coq marked as uncertain are marked (?); words in parentheses are added for
sense. The pieces are given in the order in which Le Coq printed them.

## The translation

### "This earth is not eternal"

*The middle of a leaf, 8 × 7.6 cm; Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] goes [ … ] thousand thousand, ten thousand ten thousand [ … ] men
[ … ] kings and [ … ] [on this] earth we have been born. Before, it did not
exist: it is a made earth; this earth is by no means eternal. The eternal
earth, heaven [ … ] who the seven [ … ] is not (here?) [ … ]

### A blessing on the hearers in the Manistan (T M 164 and 174)

*A leaf, the side edges and bottom damaged, 19 × 13.5 cm; Manichaean
script, in an unusual spelling. Found at Qočo.*

**Front (?).** [ … ] may the host of lightning-flame come to the divine king,
and still more, above all [ … ] and the noble *tarqan* princesses [ … ] the
*beg*, the *tutuq* and the *čigši*. Then the noble hearers, men and women,
well inclined to their souls [ … ] Xormuzta the god [ … ] piety [ … ] for the
good deed [ … ]: may perfect attainments of salvation (take place) for your
souls and your bodies! May your living without sorrow (your whole life
long), your being glad and happy, come to pass! May the reward (fruit) for
all (the torments you have suffered) come daily, quickly, from the shining
princes of the gods, and long upon your smooth cheeks (?)! [ … ] And house
and court [ … ] three good causes [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] the *tarqan*s, the *qunčuy*s and others; the noble hearers,
men and women, well inclined to the soul, all [having come … ]. On this
happy day you have gathered at the divine, shining *Manistan*, and [ … ]
have become. The divine Mani [ … ] raises (carries) [ … ] Then [ … ] may it
be! The four (?) [ … ] Yišō Kanig Wahman [ … ] the deity, [ … ] guarding
the Law (?) [ … ] the salvation (majesty) of the Burxan, which has come
down many times. And [ … ] throne (?) [ … ] may they give fortune, welfare
and energy! First (above all) may the Law, then may the kingdom stay far
and wide with our divine princely khan, perfect in both kinds of good! Long
[ … ] (may) his fortune [be?] wholly blessed!

### A colophon of the scribe Aïduq

*A fragment of a leaf or roll written on one side (a colophon?); Uyghur
script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] Wahman (?) [ … ] (inner) direction; the majestic [ … ] who has found
fortune from the moon-god [ … ], who has seized the kingdom by his bravery
and virtue, the great, wise, divine [ … ] rules [ … ]; his beloved son
[ … ]; Tüzlüg Bäg [ … ]; the Il-Ügäsi Bars [ … ] himself wished and asked
for [this] writing, (that) the fled (departed) soul might a little resemble
(?) the name of the beloved son Yorčuq Inal [ … ]. I, Aïduq, the scribe
[ … ]

### A fragment from a roll

*The edge of a text written on the back of a Chinese book-roll, 28.2 × 7.5
cm; Uyghur script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] well-being, joy [ … ] after, freedom [ … ] may it not [ … ]. And [ … ]
the apostles [ … ] the holy [ … ] the apostles [ … ] my divine one [ … ] the
divine one himself [ … ] may it be [ … ] the apostles [ … ] within [ … ]
may they be [ … ] beginning, the god [ … ] the two [ … ]

### The drying river

*The middle of a leaf, 9.7 × 5.3 cm; Manichaean script. Found at Qočo.*

[ … ] strikes with [ … ] by no means can they bring (it) to life. Righteous
and wise men, weep no more! Grief, care and weeping [ … ] all, of every
kind [ … ] settles again; tomorrow it dries up, it goes to its own place.
That rain-water (?) dries up. And as when the dew [ … ] falls and the earth
becomes wet, and (then) the blue-black wind [ … ] if [ … ]

### Ānanda and the Burxan (T M 137)

*A leaf, much damaged, the bottom torn away, 24 × 15.6 cm; Uyghur script.
Found in ruin α at Qočo.*

**Front.** [ … ] evil-doing [ … ] love [ … ] for the sake of living beings
[ … ] deceit (?) [ … ] you: listen carefully! On this I will preach,"
he deigned to say. "I [ … ] (two?) kinds of men [ … ], calling them
virtuous (?), calling them wise, I praise. [ … ] That living being does
good from birth, until the day of death [ … ] sin and evil deeds [ … ] a
good, wise man. [The second is] without wisdom from birth [ … ] doing [evil]
deeds and [ … ]

**Back.** [ … ] does not go in," he said. Ānanda, the monk, again
reverently asked thus: "My God! If it is so, which living beings fall into
the three evil ways?" The divine Burxan answered: "Whoever has done sin and
evil deeds and does not feel boundless fear and remorse, that living being
falls into the three evil ways." And again Ānanda: "I, through the great
merciful knowledge [ … ] evil deeds [ … ] the son of man [ … ]"

## Notes to this edition

- **The *Manistan*** is the Manichaean monastery or meeting-house; the
  blessing names the ruler's court and the noble hearers, men and women,
  in the same way as the Middle Persian preface of the
  [Mahrnāmag](mahrnamag.html).
- **"The fled soul … the beloved son Yorčuq Inal"**: the colophon seems to
  have been written in memory of a dead son, for the good of his soul.
  Le Coq notes that a scribe of the same name, Aïduq, wrote the colophon of
  T II D 171 ([Old Turkish texts from Qočo](turkish-manichaica-1.html)).
- **Ānanda and the Burxan**: Ānanda is the Buddha's disciple; the dialogue
  follows Buddhist models, and Le Coq counted it among the most strongly
  Buddhist-influenced Manichaean texts. "The three evil ways" are the
  Buddhist bad rebirths (hell, hungry ghosts, animals).

input.command:
python -I - <<'EOF'
p='docs/texts/turkish-manichaica-3e.md'; t=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
sec='''### A Manichaean book in Indian form (no. 40)

*A small book of loose leaves in the Indian manner (pothī), in Manichaean
script with unusual spellings, found in the rubble of a guard-house on the
wall of Qočo. Le Coq describes it but gives its text only in transcription,
without a translation.*

The top leaf has a miniature: an Elect (or a cleric) sitting or kneeling
under a tree, with something hanging behind him from a branch; before him
a kind of altar, desk or throne, on which a green bird (?) can faintly be
seen; he sits on a carpet patterned with water. Below, two kneeling figures
dressed in white, probably the donors, with a turned wooden censer between
them. Le Coq thought the whole late in date and plainly influenced by
Chinese painting.

The other side of the leaf begins with an invocation in red and black
letters to "my father, Mani the Burxan". Le Coq took the whole to be a
hymn, and noted that it is the first Manichaean text in Manichaean script
known in the form of an Indian book, with many purely Buddhist terms

*A small book of loose leaves in the Indian manner (pothī), in Manichaean

without a translation.*

The top leaf has a miniature: an Elect (or a cleric) sitting or kneeling
under a tree, with something hanging behind him from a branch; before him
a kind of altar, desk or throne, on which a green bird (?) can faintly be
seen; he sits on a carpet patterned with water. Below, two kneeling figures
dressed in white, probably the donors, with a turned wooden censer between
them. Le Coq thought the whole late in date and plainly influenced by
Chinese painting.

The other side of the leaf begins with an invocation in red and black
letters to "my father, Mani the Burxan". Le Coq took the whole to be a
hymn, and noted that it is the first Manichaean text in Manichaean script
known in the form of an Indian book, with many purely Buddhist terms
(*nom ärdini*, "jewel of the Law"; *višaya*; *nirvana*; *samsara*). He saw in
it a sign that, in later times at least, Manichaeans living among Buddhists

content.content:
KIN  MANICHAISCHES  BUCH -FRAGMENT 
AUS  CHOTSCHO. 
(Hierzu  Tafel  IV.) 
Das  vorliegende  Manuskript  bildet  einen  Teil  des  ziemlich  um- 
fangreichen Fundes  manichäischer  Handschriften,  der  meiner  Expedition 
am  12.  Januar  1905  in  einem  Gewölbe  der  Gebäude-Gruppe  K  in  der 
Ruinen-Stadt  Chotscho  (Idiqut-Schährl,  bei  dem  modernen  Flecken 
Qara-Chodscha  nahe  Turfan)  zufiel. 
Es  ist  ein,  leider  sehr  stark  beschädigter,  Teil  eines  kleinen, 
in  europäischer  ^yeise  gehefteten  Buches  und  besteht  aus  zwei,  beim 
Fund  stark  miteinander  verklebten,  doppelten  Buchblättern,  von  denen 
jedes  einzelne  etwa  6'/>  cm  breit  ist.  Die  frühere  Länge  der  Blätter 
läßt  sich  nicht  mehr  bestimmen:  sie  beträgt  heute  an  der  am  besten 
erhaltenen  Stelle  noch  etwa  12'/.,  cm.  Die  Zeilen  sind  mit  schwarzer 
Tinte  (Tusche)  gezogen  und  an  den  Seiten  durch  senkrechte,  karmin- 
rote Striche  abgegrenzt. 
Die  Intei-punktionszeichen  sind  nicht,  wie  in  den  meisten  unserer 
manichäischen  Handschriften  kleine,  schräggestellte,  um  einen  oder 
zwei  schwarze  Punkte  gezogene  rote  Ovale,  sondern  die  in  bud- 
dhistischen MSS.  häufigeren,  einem  Doppelkomma  gleichenden  Zeichen. 
Obwohl  die  beiden  Doppelblätter  unzweifelhaft  demselben  Buch 
angehörten,  ist  es  weder  möglich,  festzustellen,  in  welcher  Eeihenfolge 
sie  geheftet  waren,  noch  wie  viel  Blätter  zwischen  ihnen  fehlen. 
Die  Schrift  ist  jene  wahrscheinlich  in  ziemlich  später  Zeit 
(8.  Jahrb.?)  entstandene  Variante  oder  Entwickelung  der  soghdischen 
Schrift,  die  von  den  Türken  der  Turfan-Oase  angenommen  wurde  und 
uns  unter  dem  Namen  der  Uigurischen  Schrift  bekannt  ist;  der  Schreiber 
hat  zuweilen  auf,  zuweilen  zwischen  die  sorgfältig  gezogenen  Linien 
geschrieben.  Als  Eigenheit  sei  erwähnt,  daß  der  Buchstabe  ï,  i  des 
öfteren  nicht  mit  den  darauf  folgenden  Lettern  verbunden  wird  (qoi-n; 
in;  m{a)yj-stal(). 
Die  Sprache  ist  altertümlich,  denn  sie  zeigt  die  in  den  kök- 
türkischen    Runen -Inschriften    häufigen    Gerundien    auf    -pan,    -jjcùi 
■  Thomsen-Festschrift.  10 
146  A.  von  Le  Coq, 
(harïpan,  Jc{ä)lq)än);  auch  das  Verbum  irihuäh,  das  in  unseren  Texten 
bisher  gefehlt  hat,  aber  öfter  in  den  Runen -Inschriften  wiederkehrt, 
hat  sicli  in  diesem  Text  erhalten. 
Bei  dem  äußerst  fragmentaren  Zustand  des  Manuskripts  ist  aber 
leider  das  sprachliche  Interesse  nur  gering;  die  hier  und  da  einzeln 
stehengebliebenen  Wörter  will  ich  nicht  zu  übersetzen  versuchen,  ich 
beschränke  mich  darauf,  ihr  Vorkommen  zu  verzeichnen. 
Auch  der  Inhalt  wäre  ziemlich  belanglos,  wenn  nicht  mehrere 
Zeilen,  und  außer  diesen  Zeilen  mehrere  Namen  deutlich  genug  erhalten 
wären,  um  das  Manuskript  als  Bruchstück  einer  historischen  Ab- 
handlung erkennen  zu  lassen.  Solche  Schriften  gehören  zu  den  größten 
Seltenheiten;  sie  lehren  uns,  daß  unter  den  Manichäern  Turkistans 
die  Aufzeichnung  geschichtlicher  Ereignisse  gepflegt  wurde.  Da  ein  in 
diesem  Text  vorkommender  Passus  die  Person  des  '  weisen  Tonyuquq  ', 
ein  anderer  die  des  manichäischen  Apostels  dieser  Grenzländer  zu 
betreffen  scheint,  möge  die  Transkription,  von  einigen  Anmerkungen 
begleitet,  hier  folgen.

---
title: "Bögü Khan and the Uyghur court: two pieces from the Thomsen Festschrift"
text: true
group: extracanonical
order: 81
summary: An Old Turkish history fragment in which the Uyghur khan Bögü comes to Qočo and takes counsel with a možak about settling three mahistaks, and a Middle Persian blessing on a khan called "the emanation of Mani" and his court.
original_language: Old Turkish (Uyghur) and Middle Persian
source: 'Turfan manuscripts T II K bundle D 173 and T II D 135 (Berlin), as read and translated into German by A. von Le Coq, "Ein manichäisches Buch-Fragment aus Chotscho", and F. W. K. Müller, "Der Hofstaat eines Uiguren-Königs", in Festschrift Vilhelm Thomsen zur Vollendung des siebzigsten Lebensjahres (Leipzig 1912), pp. 145–154 and 207–213 (archive.org `festschriftvilhe00thom`) (public domain). New English translation.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from the 1912 German of Le Coq and Müller; not checked against a modern edition)."
---

## Introduction

Two short pieces published in 1912 in honour of Vilhelm Thomsen, who
deciphered the Old Turkic inscriptions.

**Le Coq's book fragment** is from a small Manichaean book in Uyghur script
found at Qočo in 1905. It is badly damaged, but enough names survive to show
that it was a work of history, one of the very few known from the
Manichaeans of Turkestan. It names the Uyghur khan Bögü coming to Qočo and
holding counsel "with the *možak*" about the settling of three *mahistaks*
"in the year of the Sheep", and it quotes "the wise Tonyuquq", the famous
Turkic statesman. Le Coq identified the khan with Bögü Khan (reigned
759–780), who made Manichaeism the religion of the Uyghur state, and
suggested that the year of the Sheep is 767.

**Müller's piece** (T II D 135) is the back of a leaf from the opening of a
Manichaean book in Middle Persian; on the front was a miniature of armed
warriors around a larger figure. The text blesses the "great ruler", a khan
whose Turkish titles end "the emanation of Mani", and his court, rank by
rank. Müller identified this khan, too, with the khan who brought
Manichaeism to the Uyghurs.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from the German of Le Coq and
Müller. Gaps are marked [ … ]; words they marked as uncertain are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### Le Coq's fragment: Bögü Khan at Qočo

*Two double leaves of a small book of European form, stuck together when
found; the order of the leaves is not certain.*

**Double leaf I, leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] inside [ … ] hurrying out to meet
the hundred, Tai Ügä Qutadmïš (title and name) [ … ] (and) the brothers (?)
[ … ]-ant, all went in [ … ] the [ … ] Tigin Ügä [ … ] wish [ … ]

**Page 2.** The divine [ … ] Uyghur khan Bögü, coming to Qočo, because of
the settling of three *mahistaks* (to be made) in the (cyclical) year of
the Sheep, held counsel with the *možak* [ … ] Fifth [ … ] five [ … ]

**Leaf 2, page 1.** [ … ] The wise Tonyuquq spoke thus: "The kingdom (prince?)
of the Turks has perished [ … ] has become," he said.

**Page 2.** [ … ] he gave. Third: his daughter, the princess Qadïr (?), he
gave to the *iltäbär* of the Uyghurs. Fourth: his daughter [ … ]smil Saγ[ … ]
he gave to the Bilgä [Khan?]. [ … ] Bilgä [ … ]

**Double leaf II (?), leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] he was. Far [ … ] his younger
brother was called khan. Having gone back [ … ] they spoke so, with
reverence, to Si[ … ] Tigin: "You now [ … ] if he goes [ … ]"

**Page 2.** *(The writing has faded except for the words "comes down",
"may he sit", "may he stand", "my God, shining …".)*

**Leaf 2.** [ … ] forward [ … ] he went; the cities lying outside [ … ]
became [ … ]. From in front, the Barašlï (?) people from outside, scattered
from (the region or city of) Su-chou [ … ] Kül Sangun [ … ]

### Müller's T II D 135: the blessing on the khan, "the emanation of Mani"

*Back of a leaf from the opening of a Manichaean book; the text in black and
red. The beginning is lost.*

**First column.** [May the angels] with their own, the helpers, themselves
protect and guard the whole community of the hearers; first of all the
great ruler, the great majesty, the good, the blessed, worthy of the two
blessednesses, the two lives and the two lordships, of body and of soul;
the ruler of the East, the keeper of the religion and helper of the
righteous; the shining hearer, the wearer of the diadem, the ruler of
praised and blessed name, *Ulug Ilig Tängridä Qut Bulmïš Ärdämin Il Tutmïš
Alp Qutlug Külüg Bilgä*, khan of the Uyghurs, the emanation of Mani [ … ]

**Second column.** And also the [ … ] great protectors (?) and generals of
the blessed ruler. First of all the Il-Ügäsi Nigōšakpat (master of the
hearers), the Il-Ügäsi Yägän Säväg Tutuq, the Il-Ügäsi Ötür Buila Tarxan.
And also those (titled) *tutuq*: Tapmïš Qutlug Tutuq, Čüg Tutuq; and those
(titled) *čigši*: Waga Čigši, Yägän Öz Čigši, Tudun Čigši, [ … ] Čangši, Kül
Sangun Tiräk, Inanču Bilgä Tiräk. And also the *buila*s: Tapmïš Buila
Tarxan, Ašpädä (Ašpara?) Buila. May they all live unharmed, and at the end
may they receive the reward of the pious for ever. [So] may it be!

And further the palace officials of name, who do their service before the
pious ruler: first of all Ötür Buila Tarxan, Qutlug Ičräki [ … ], Tapmïš,
Ina[nču] [ … ], Qutlug [ … ] (the rest is lost).

## Notes to this edition

- **"The emanation of Mani"** (Middle Persian *zahag ī Mānī*): Müller
  explained *zahag* as "emanation, birth", a fitting honorific for the Turkish
  patron of the Manichaean church. He identified the khan with the one named
  on the Karabalgasun inscription who brought Manichaeism to the Uyghurs
  (the khan Mou-yü, reigned 759–780).
- **Bögü Khan and the year of the Sheep**: Le Coq noted that if the khan is
  Bögü, the year of the Sheep could be 767, and that the three *mahistaks*
  need not have been the first Manichaeans settled in the Uyghur state,
  since the khan is already on friendly terms with the *možak*.
- **Tonyuquq** was the adviser of the early Turkic khans, known from his
  own runic inscription.
- **The ranks** in T II D 135 are, after the ruler: the Il-Ügäsi, the
  *tutuq*, the *čigši*, the *tiräk* and the *buila*, then the *ičräki*
  (palace officials). Müller compared the different order in the preface of
  the [Mahrnāmag](mahrnamag.html); several titles are Chinese loanwords.
- Müller ended his article with a greeting to Thomsen "in the sounds of the
  Persian and Turkish followers of Mani": "unharmed, without sorrow, …
  for long years … always remain glad, live long!"

## Introduction

Two short pieces published in 1912 in honour of Vilhelm Thomsen, who
deciphered the Old Turkic inscriptions.

**Le Coq's book fragment** is from a small Manichaean book in Uyghur script
found at Qočo in 1905. It is badly damaged, but enough names survive to show
that it was a work of history, one of the very few known from the
Manichaeans of Turkestan. It names the Uyghur khan Bögü coming to Qočo and
holding counsel "with the *možak*" about the settling of three *mahistaks*
"in the year of the Sheep", and it quotes "the wise Tonyuquq", the famous
Turkic statesman. Le Coq identified the khan with Bögü Khan (reigned
759–780), who made Manichaeism the religion of the Uyghur state, and
suggested that the year of the Sheep is 767.

**Müller's piece** (T II D 135) is the back of a leaf from the opening of a
Manichaean book in Middle Persian; on the front was a miniature of armed
warriors around a larger figure. The text blesses the "great ruler", a khan
whose Turkish titles end "the emanation of Mani", and his court, rank by
rank. Müller identified this khan, too, with the khan who brought
Manichaeism to the Uyghurs.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from the German of Le Coq and
Müller. Gaps are marked [ … ]; words they marked as uncertain are marked
(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.

## The translation

### Le Coq's fragment: Bögü Khan at Qočo

*Two double leaves of a small book of European form, stuck together when
found; the order of the leaves is not certain.*

**Double leaf I, leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] inside [ … ] hurrying out to meet
the hundred, Tai Ügä Qutadmïš (title and name) [ … ] (and) the brothers (?)
[ … ]-ant, all went in [ … ] the [ … ] Tigin Ügä [ … ] wish [ … ]

**Page 2.** The divine [ … ] Uyghur khan Bögü, coming to Qočo, because of
the settling of three *mahistaks* (to be made) in the (cyclical) year of
the Sheep, held counsel with the *možak* [ … ] Fifth [ … ] five [ … ]

**Leaf 2, page 1.** [ … ] The wise Tonyuquq spoke thus: "The kingdom (prince?)
of the Turks has perished [ … ] has become," he said.

**Page 2.** [ … ] he gave. Third: his daughter, the princess Qadïr (?), he
gave to the *iltäbär* of the Uyghurs. Fourth: his daughter [ … ]smil Saγ[ … ]
he gave to the Bilgä [Khan?]. [ … ] Bilgä [ … ]

**Double leaf II (?), leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] he was. Far [ … ] his younger
brother was called khan. Having gone back [ … ] they spoke so, with
reverence, to Si[ … ] Tigin: "You now [ … ] if he goes [ … ]"

**Page 2.** *(The writing has faded except for the words "comes down",
"may he sit", "may he stand", "my God, shining …".)*

**Leaf 2.** [ … ] forward [ … ] he went; the cities lying outside [ … ]
became [ … ]. From in front, the Barašlï (?) people from outside, scattered
from (the region or city of) Su-chou [ … ] Kül Sangun [ … ]

### Müller's T II D 135: the blessing on the khan, "the emanation of Mani"

*Back of a leaf from the opening of a Manichaean book; the text in black and
red. The beginning is lost.*

**First column.** [May the angels] with their own, the helpers, themselves
protect and guard the whole community of the hearers; first of all the
great ruler, the great majesty, the good, the blessed, worthy of the two
blessednesses, the two lives and the two lordships, of body and of soul;
the ruler of the East, the keeper of the religion and helper of the
righteous; the shining hearer, the wearer of the diadem, the ruler of
praised and blessed name, *Ulug Ilig Tängridä Qut Bulmïš Ärdämin Il Tutmïš
Alp Qutlug Külüg Bilgä*, khan of the Uyghurs, the emanation of Mani [ … ]

**Second column.** And also the [ … ] great protectors (?) and generals of
the blessed ruler. First of all the Il-Ügäsi Nigōšakpat (master of the
hearers), the Il-Ügäsi Yägän Säväg Tutuq, the Il-Ügäsi Ötür Buila Tarxan.
And also those (titled) *tutuq*: Tapmïš Qutlug Tutuq, Čüg Tutuq; and those
(titled) *čigši*: Waga Čigši, Yägän Öz Čigši, Tudun Čigši, [ … ] Čangši, Kül
Sangun Tiräk, Inanču Bilgä Tiräk. And also the *buila*s: Tapmïš Buila
Tarxan, Ašpädä (Ašpara?) Buila. May they all live unharmed, and at the end
may they receive the reward of the pious for ever. [So] may it be!

And further the palace officials of name, who do their service before the
pious ruler: first of all Ötür Buila Tarxan, Qutlug Ičräki [ … ], Tapmïš,
Ina[nču] [ … ], Qutlug [ … ] (the rest is lost).

## Notes to this edition

- **"The emanation of Mani"** (Middle Persian *zahag ī Mānī*): Müller
  explained *zahag* as "emanation, birth", a fitting honorific for the Turkish
  patron of the Manichaean church. He identified the khan with the one named
  on the Karabalgasun inscription who brought Manichaeism to the Uyghurs
  (the khan Mou-yü, reigned 759–780).
- **Bögü Khan and the year of the Sheep**: Le Coq noted that if the khan is
  Bögü, the year of the Sheep could be 767, and that the three *mahistaks*
  need not have been the first Manichaeans settled in the Uyghur state,
  since the khan is already on friendly terms with the *možak*.
- **Tonyuquq** was the adviser of the early Turkic khans, known from his
  own runic inscription.
- **The ranks** in T II D 135 are, after the ruler: the Il-Ügäsi, the
  *tutuq*, the *čigši*, the *tiräk* and the *buila*, then the *ičräki*
  (palace officials). Müller compared the different order in the preface of
  the [Mahrnāmag](mahrnamag.html); several titles are Chinese loanwords.
- Müller ended his article with a greeting to Thomsen "in the sounds of the
  Persian and Turkish followers of Mani": "unharmed, without sorrow, …
  for long years … always remain glad, live long!"

New English translation.'

+## Introduction
+Two short pieces published in 1912 in honour of Vilhelm Thomsen, who
+deciphered the Old Turkic inscriptions.
+**Le Coq's book fragment** is from a small Manichaean book in Uyghur script
+found at Qočo in 1905. It is badly damaged, but enough names survive to show
+that it was a work of history, one of the very few known from the
+Manichaeans of Turkestan. It names the Uyghur khan Bögü coming to Qočo and
+holding counsel "with the *možak*" about the settling of three *mahistaks*
+"in the year of the Sheep", and it quotes "the wise Tonyuquq", the famous
+Turkic statesman. Le Coq identified the khan with Bögü Khan (reigned
+759–780), who made Manichaeism the religion of the Uyghur state, and
+suggested that the year of the Sheep is 767.
+**Müller's piece** (T II D 135) is the back of a leaf from the opening of a
+Manichaean book in Middle Persian; on the front was a miniature of armed
+warriors around a larger figure. The text blesses the "great ruler", a khan
+whose Turkish titles end "the emanation of Mani", and his court, rank by
+rank. Müller identified this khan, too, with the khan who brought
+Manichaeism to the Uyghurs.
+**This translation is a draft.** It is made from the German of Le Coq and
+Müller. Gaps are marked [ … ]; words they marked as uncertain are marked
+(?); words in parentheses are added for sense.
+## The translation
+### Le Coq's fragment: Bögü Khan at Qočo
+*Two double leaves of a small book of European form, stuck together when
+found; the order of the leaves is not certain.*
+**Double leaf I, leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] inside [ … ] hurrying out to meet
+the hundred, Tai Ügä Qutadmïš (title and name) [ … ] (and) the brothers (?)
+[ … ]-ant, all went in [ … ] the [ … ] Tigin Ügä [ … ] wish [ … ]
+**Page 2.** The divine [ … ] Uyghur khan Bögü, coming to Qočo, because of
+the settling of three *mahistaks* (to be made) in the (cyclical) year of
+the Sheep, held counsel with the *možak* [ … ] Fifth [ … ] five [ … ]
+**Leaf 2, page 1.** [ … ] The wise Tonyuquq spoke thus: "The kingdom (prince?)
+of the Turks has perished [ … ] has become," he said.
+**Page 2.** [ … ] he gave. Third: his daughter, the princess Qadïr (?), he
+gave to the *iltäbär* of the Uyghurs. Fourth: his daughter [ … ]smil Saγ[ … ]
+he gave to the Bilgä [Khan?]. [ … ] Bilgä [ … ]
+**Double leaf II (?), leaf 1, page 1.** [ … ] he was. Far [ … ] his younger
+brother was called khan. Having gone back [ … ] they spoke so, with
+reverence, to Si[ … ] Tigin: "You now [ … ] if he goes [ … ]"
+**Page 2.** *(The writing has faded except for the words "comes down",
+"may he sit", "may he stand", "my God, shining …".)*
+**Leaf 2.** [ … ] forward [ … ] he went; the cities lying outside [ … ]
+became [ … ]. From in front, the Barašlï (?) people from outside, scattered
+from (the region or city of) Su-chou [ … ] Kül Sangun [ … ]
+### Müller's T II D 135: the blessing on the khan, "the emanation of Mani"
+*Back of a leaf from the opening of a Manichaean book; the text in black and
+red. The beginning is lost.*
+**First column.** [May the angels] with their own, the helpers, themselves
+protect and guard the whole community of the hearers; first of all the
+great ruler, the great majesty, the good, the blessed, worthy of the two
+blessednesses, the two lives and the two lordships, of body and of soul;
+the ruler of the East, the keeper of the religion and helper of the
+righteous; the shining hearer, the wearer of the diadem, the ruler of
+praised and blessed name, *Ulug Ilig Tängridä Qut Bulmïš Ärdämin Il Tutmïš
+Alp Qutlug Külüg Bilgä*, khan of the Uyghurs, the emanation of Mani [ … ]
+**Second column.** And also the [ … ] great protectors (?) and generals of
+the blessed ruler. First of all the Il-Ügäsi Nigōšakpat (master of the
+hearers), the Il-Ügäsi Yägän Säväg Tutuq, the Il-Ügäsi Ötür Buila Tarxan.
+And also those (titled) *tutuq*: Tapmïš Qutlug Tutuq, Čüg Tutuq; and those
+(titled) *čigši*: Waga Čigši, Yägän Öz Čigši, Tudun Čigši, [ … ] Čangši, Kül
+Sangun Tiräk, Inanču Bilgä Tiräk. And also the *buila*s: Tapmïš Buila
+Tarxan, Ašpädä (Ašpara?) Buila. May they all live unharmed, and at the end
+may they receive the reward of the pious for ever. [So] may it be!
+And further the palace officials of name, who do their service before the
+pious ruler: first of all Ötür Buila Tarxan, Qutlug Ičräki [ … ], Tapmïš,
+Ina[nču] [ … ], Qutlug [ … ] (the rest is lost).

+- **Tonyuquq** was the adviser of the early Turkic khans, known from his

+- **The ranks** in T II D 135 are, after the ruler: the Il-Ügäsi, the

China^s zu ihm, ich glaube, es war der Fürst der Tagazgaz 8*®), 
mit der Meldung: In meinen Ländern sind dreimal mehr^^) 
Muslimen als in deinen Ländern Anhänger meiner Religion, 
und schwor ihm, wenn !er einen von diesen todte, so werde 
er für ihn die ganze Gemeinde todten, die Moscheen zer- 
stören und in allen Ländern Leute aufstellen, die den Mus- 
limen auflauerten und sie umbrächten. Da liess der Herrscher 
Yon.Chur&sän von ihnen ab und liess sich von ihnen die Kopf- 
steuer zahlen*®^). In den Staaten des Islam sind ihrer nur 
wenige. In der Stadt des Heils ^Bagdad) habe ich von ihnen 
unter der Regierung des Mu'izz-ad-daula*®*) ungefähr drei- 
hundert kennen gelernt; in der gegenwärtigen Zeit aber sind

•dieser Zeit*or). 
Al-Dscha'd ben Darham*®®) ist derselbe, von dem Mar- 
wfin ben Mulbammad seinen Beinamen erhielt, so dass er 
Marw&n al-Dscha^di genannt wurde. Er war der Erzieher 
desselben und seines Sohnes und verführte jenen zum JJn- 
glauben *<>®). Hischäm ben ^Abdalmalik todtete Dscha^d unter 
seinem Chali&te, nachdem er ihn lange in der Gewalt des 
Ch&lid ben 'Abdallah al-Kasrl gefangen gehalten hatte**^). 
Man erzählt, dass die Familie des Dscha'd an Hischam eine 
Bittschrift übergab, worin sie über ihre Hilflosigkeit und die 
lange Gefangenschaft des Dscha'd klagte ^^^). Ist er denn 
noch am Leben? erwiderte Hischam und schrieb an Chälid 
mit dem Befehl ihn zit todten, was an einem Opferfest auch 
wirklich geschah, indem er ihn anstatt der Opfer todten liess,

---
title: "Mani's books and letters: al-Nadīm's list"
text: true
group: scripture
order: 95
summary: The list of Mani's books, the chapters of his Book of Mysteries, and the titles of seventy-six letters by Mani and the leaders after him, from al-Nadīm's Fihrist (10th century).
original_language: Arabic
source: 'Ibn al-Nadīm, Kitāb al-Fihrist (987), chapter on the Manichaeans, as translated into German by G. Flügel, Mani, seine Lehre und seine Schriften (Leipzig 1862), pp. 102–105 (archive.org `maniseinelehreu00manegoog`) (public domain). New English translation from Flügel''s German.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from Flügel's 1862 German; not checked against the Arabic or a modern translation)."
---

## Introduction

Ibn al-Nadīm, a Baghdad bookseller, finished his *Fihrist* ("Catalogue")
in 987. Its chapter on the Manichaeans, based on Manichaean sources and on
his own meetings with Manichaeans in Baghdad, is one of the main witnesses
to Mani's teaching. This page gives the part that lists Mani's books, the
chapters of the *Book of Mysteries*, and the titles of the letters "which
Mani and the leaders after him wrote". For most of the books, this list and
a few quotations are all that survive.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Gustav Flügel's German of
1862, which is in the public domain. Flügel's notes, which discuss the
readings of the Arabic names, are not reproduced. Words he marked as
uncertain are marked (?); "…" marks a title or chapter list left blank in
the Arabic.

## The translation

### The names of the books written by Mani

Mani wrote seven books, one in Persian and six in Syriac. At their head
stands:

**I. The Book of Mysteries**, which contains the following chapters:

1. On the Daisanites (the followers of Bardaisan).
2. On the testimony of Hystaspes against the Beloved.
3. On the testimony of Jacob against himself.
4. On the son of the poor widow, who in Mani's meaning is the crucified
   Messiah, whom the Jews crucified.
5. On the testimony of Jesus against himself, in relation to the Jews.
6. The beginning of the testimony of Yamīn after his victory.
7. On the seven spirits.
8. On the teaching of the four perishable spirits.
9. On laughter.
10. On the testimony of Adam about Jesus.
11. On falling away from the religion.
12. On the teaching of the Daisanites about the soul and the body.
13. A polemic against the Daisanites about the living soul.
14. On the three ditches.
15. On the preservation of the world.
16. On the three days.
17. On the prophets.
18. On the resurrection.

These are the chapters that the Book of Mysteries contains.

**II. The Book of the Giants**, containing …

**III. The Book of Precepts for the Hearers**, with a chapter of precepts
for the Elect (?).

**IV. The Book Šābuhragān.** This book contains the chapters: 1. On the
dissolution of the hearers. 2. On the dissolution of the Elect (?). 3. On
the dissolution of the sinners.

**V. The Book of Bringing to Life**, containing …

**VI. The Book Pragmateia**, containing …

### The titles of the letters which Mani and the leaders after him wrote

1. The letter on the two principles.
2. The letter on the elders.
3. The greater letter to the Indians.
4. The letter on the armour of righteousness.
5. The letter on just judgement.
6. The letter to Kaškar.
7. The greater letter to Futtaq.
8. The letter to Armenia.
9. The letter to Amūliyā the unbeliever.
10. The letter to Ctesiphon. One leaf.
11. The letter on the ten words.
12. The teacher's treatise on social ordinances.
13. The letter of Wahman on the seal of the mouth.
14. The letter of Xabarhāt on consolation.
15. The letter of Xabarhāt on …
16. The letter to the Amhasam (?) of Ctesiphon.
17. The letter of Yaḥyā (John) on fragrance.
18. The letter of Xabarhāt on …
19. The letter to Ctesiphon on the hearers.
20. The letter to Fāfī.
21. The smaller letter on the right way.
22. The letter of Sīs, of double meaning.
23. The greater letter to Babylon.
24. The letter to Sīs and Futtaq, on the forms.
25. The letter on Paradise.
26. The letter of Sīs on time.
27. The letter of Saʿyūs on the tithe.
28. The letter of Sīs on the pledges.
29. The letter on administration.
30. The letter of Abā the disciple.
31. The letter of Ibrai to Rahā.
32. The letter of Abā on love.
33. The letter of Maisān on the day.
34. The letter of Abā on …
35. The letter of Baḥrāyā on the terrifying form.
36. The letter of Abā on the mention of fragrance.
37. The letter of ʿAbdīšōʿ on the more distant relatives.
38. The letter of Baḥrāyā on social ordinances.
39. The letter to Šāʾil (Šatīl?) and Sakanī.
40. The letter of Ubayyā on the different kinds of tax on property.
41. The letter of Qudāyā on the dove.
42. The letter of Afqūriyā on time.
43. The letter of Zakū on time.
44. The letter of Suhrāb on the tithe.
45. The letter on the hermit's cell and the fruit ʿArāb, from which the
    beads of rosaries are made (?).
46. The letter of Suhrāb on the Persians.
47. The letter to Abrāhīyā.
48. The letter to Abū Yasām the surveyor.
49. The letter to Abrāhīyā the unbeliever.
50. The letter on baptism (washing).
51. The letter of Yaḥyā on the dirhams.
52. The letter of Afaʿand on the four kinds of tithe.

Besides these, the following letters are also mentioned:

53. The letter of Afaʿand on the first blessedness.
54. The letter of Yanū (Linus?) on the cushions.
55. The letter of Yuḥannā on the administration of alms.
56. The letter to the hearers on fasting and the keeping of vows.
57. The letter to the hearers on the great fire.
58. The letter to Ahwāz on property that may be freely sold.
59. The letter to the hearers on Yazdānbaxt's interpretation of dreams.
60. The first letter to the Persian woman Mēnoq.
61. The second letter to Mēnoq.
62. The letter on the tithe and the different kinds of alms.
63. The letter to Ardašīr and Mēnoq.
64. The letter to Salām and ʿAnṣarā.
65. The letter to Ḥaṭṭā.
66. The letter of Xabarhāt on property that may be freely sold.
67. The letter of Abrāhīyā on the healthy and the sick.
68. The letter of Ardād on beasts of burden.
69. The letter of Ajā on sandals.
70. The letter on the two shining burdens.
71. The letter of Mānā on crucifixion.
72. The letter on the excellence of religious music.
73. The letter to Fīrūz and Rāsin.
74. The letter of ʿAbdīlāl on the Book of Mysteries.
75. The letter to Simeon and Rāmīn.
76. The letter of ʿAbdīlāl on clothing.

## Notes to this edition

- **Seven books, but six listed.** Al-Nadīm says Mani wrote seven books and
  names six; the *Gospel*, which he discusses elsewhere, is not in this
  list. Compare the list of seven books in the Chinese
  [Compendium](compendium.html#3-the-scriptures-and-the-picture-seven-books-in-all-and-one-picture).
- **The *Šābuhragān*** is the one book Mani wrote in Persian; its chapters
  on the "dissolution" (death and fate) of the hearers, the Elect and the
  sinners agree with the Turfan fragments on the end of the world
  ([Šābuhragān](shabuhragan.html)).
- **The letters.** The list includes letters by Mani's successors as well
  as his own. Two of the titles appear in the Turfan Middle Persian
  extracts: the letter to Kaškar and the letter of Xabarhāt (Müller's
  "Hatā"; see [Mani's Gospel and Epistles](turfan-gospel-epistles.html)).
- **Spellings.** The personal and place names are given as Flügel read
  them, simplified; many are uncertain in the Arabic.

Das Gesetz, welches Mani gab^ und die Gebote, welche

Man! legte seinen Schülern, Gebote auf, (darunter) zehn 
Gebote den Zuhörern***), an die sich drei Siegel**') und 
durchaus Fasten von sieben Tagen in jedem Monat**®) an- 
schlössen. Die Gebote***) aber sind: Der Glaube an die vier 
grossherrlichen Wesenheiten***^), Gott, sein Licht, seine Kraft 
und seine Weisheit. Gott aber, dessen Namen herrlich ist, 
ist der König der Paradiese des Lichts***), seih Licht ist die 
Sonne und der Mond, seine Kraft sind die fünf Engel, der 
leise Lufthauch, der Wind^ das Licht, das Wasser und das 
Feuer***), und seine Weisheit die geheiligte Religion**'). 
Diese umfasst fünf Begriffe***), den der Lehrer, das sind die 
Sohne der Sanftmuth, den der von der Sonne Erleuchteten, 
das sind die Söhne des Wissens, den der Presbyter, das sind 
die Söhne der Vernunft, den der Wahrhaftigen, das sind die 
Sohne des Geheinmisses, den der Zuhörer, das sind die Söhne 
der Einsicht***). 
Die zehn Gebote sind: Unterlassung der Anbetung der 
Götzen, der Lüge, des Geizes**®), der Tödtung, des Ehe- 
bruchs, des Diebstahls, des Lehrens der trügerischen Vor- 
96 
I 
wände ^^^ und der Magie, des Festhaltens doppelter Gedan- 
kenrichtung, was den Zweifel an der Religion verräth^^®), der 
Schlaffheit und Mattigkeit im Handeln ^^^), und das Gebot 
der vier oder sieben *3*>) Gebete. Der Mann stehe bei diesem 
aufrecht, reibe sich mit laufendem Wasser oder mit etwas An- 
derem*'^) und wende sich stehend nach dem grossen Lichte**^), 
dann werfe er sich nieder und spreche beim Niederwerfen: 
Gesegnet sei unser Führer der Paraklet*'^), der Gesandte des 
Lichts, gesegnet seien seine Engel die Hüter, und hochge- 
priesen seine Heerschaaren die leuchtenden***). Das sage er, 
während er niedergeworfen daliegt, stehe dann auf und ver- 
weile nicht länger in seiner niedergeworfenen Stellung und 
halte sich aufrecht. Bei der zweiten Niederwerfong sage 
er: Du Hochgepriesener, o du Leuchtender, M&ni, unser Füh- 
rer***), du Wurzel der Erleuchtung, Zweig der Ehrbarkeit, 
du grosser Baum, der du ganz Heilmittel bist**®). Bei der 
dritten NiederwerAmg sage er: Ich falle nieder und preise 
mit reinem Herzen und aufrichtiger Zunge den grossen Gott, 
den Vater der Lichter und ihr Element, Hochgepriesener, Ge- 
benedeiter, du und deine ganze Grossherrlichkeit und deine 
Welten die gesegneten, welche du berufen hast. Dich preist 
der da preist deine Heerschaaren, deine Gerechten, dein Wort, 
deine Grossherrlichkeit und dein Wohlgefallen, weU du der 
Gott bist, der ganz Wahrheit, Leben und Gerechtigkeit ist**'').

nieder vor den Göttern aUen., den leuchtenden Engeln allen,

dem grossen Gott sind. Bei der fünften Niederwerfung sage 
er: Ich falle nieder und preise die grossen Heerschaaren und 
die leuchtenden Gotter, die mit ihrer Weisheit auf die Fin- 
stermss eindringen, sie austreiben und bewältigen **•). Bei 
der sechsten Niederwerfting sage er: Ich falle nieder und 
preise den Vater der Grossherrlichkeit, den Erhabenen, den 
Erleuchtenden, welcher gekommen ist von den beiden Wissen- 
schaften**®), und so fort bis zur zwölften Niederwerfung. So-

97

Den Sonntag feiern die gemeinen Manichäer, den Montag die

input.command:
python -I - <<'EOF'
p='docs/texts/al-nadim-books.md'; t=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
sec='''### The law that Mani gave, and the commandments he laid down

Mani laid commandments on his disciples, (among them) ten commandments for
the hearers, to which are joined three seals and a fast of seven days in
every month without fail.

The commandments are these: faith in the four great majesties, God, his
Light, his Power and his Wisdom. God, whose name is glorious, is the King
of the Paradises of Light; his Light is the sun and the moon; his Power is
the five angels, the gentle breeze, the wind, the light, the water and the
fire; and his Wisdom is the holy religion. This comprises five ranks: the
teachers, who are the sons of gentleness; those lit by the sun, who are
the sons of knowledge; the presbyters, who are the sons of reason; the
righteous (the Elect), who are the sons of the mystery; and the hearers,
who are the sons of insight.

The ten commandments are: to give up the worship of idols; lying; avarice;
killing; adultery; theft; the teaching of deceitful pretexts and magic;
holding to a double mind, which betrays doubt about the religion; slackness
and sluggishness in action; and the commandment of the four or seven
prayers.

(At prayer) a man shall stand upright, rub himself with running water or
with something else, and turn, standing, towards the great light. Then he
shall prostrate himself and say in prostration: "Blessed be our guide, the
Paraclete, the Envoy of Light; blessed be his angels, the guardians; and
highly praised be his shining hosts." He says this while he lies
prostrate; then he rises, and does not stay longer in prostration, but
holds himself upright.

At the second prostration he says: "You highly praised one, O shining one,
Mani, our guide, you root of enlightenment, branch of honour, you great
tree that are wholly healing."

At the third prostration he says: "I fall down and praise, with a pure
heart and a sincere tongue, the great God, the Father of the Lights and
their element, highly praised, blessed, you and all your greatness and
your blessed worlds, which you have called. Whoever praises you praises
your hosts, your righteous ones, your word, your greatness and your good
pleasure, because you are the God who is wholly truth, life and
righteousness."

At the fourth prostration he says: "I praise and fall down before all the
gods, all the shining angels, all the lights and all the hosts that are
from the great God."

At the fifth prostration he says: "I fall down and praise the great hosts
and the shining gods, who with their wisdom press upon the darkness, drive
it out and overcome it."

At the sixth prostration he says: "I fall down and praise the Father of
Greatness, the exalted, the shining, who has come from the two kinds of
knowledge," and so on up to the twelfth prostration.

As soon as he has finished the ten prayers, he begins another prayer, and
in it they speak praises which there is no need for us to repeat.

The first prayer is said when the sun leaves the noon point; the second
between this time and sunset; then follows the prayer at evening after
sunset; and then the prayer in the first third of the night, three hours
after sunset. At every prayer and prostration the one who prays does just
as at the first prayer; and that is the prayer of the bringer of good news.

As for the fasts: when the sun is in Sagittarius and the moon is full, they
fast for two days without a break; and when the new moon begins to shine,
they also fast for two days without a break. They fast, besides, when the
moon is first seen again after the sun has entered the sign of Capricorn;
then, when the new moon begins to shine, the sun is in Aquarius and eight
days of the month have passed, they fast for thirty days, but break the
fast every day at sunset.

The ordinary Manichaeans keep Sunday holy, and the initiated keep Monday.
So Mani commanded them as an unavoidable duty.

'''
a='## Notes to this edition'; assert a in t
t=t.replace(a,sec+a,1)
t=t.replace("summary: The list of Mani's books, the chapters of his Book of Mysteries, and the titles of seventy-six letters by Mani and the leaders after him, from al-Nadīm's Fihrist (10th century).","summary: The list of Mani's books, the chapters of his Book of Mysteries, the titles of seventy-six letters by Mani and the leaders after him, and the commandments, prayers and fasts Mani laid down, from al-Nadīm's Fihrist (10th century).")
t=t.replace("pp. 102–105 (archive.org","pp. 95–97 and 102–105 (archive.org")
t=t.replace('''chapters of the *Book of Mysteries*, and the titles of the letters "which
Mani and the leaders after him wrote".''','''chapters of the *Book of Mysteries*, and the titles of the letters "which
Mani and the leaders after him wrote", and the section on the law Mani gave
his followers: the commandments, the daily prayers and the fasts.''')
t=t.replace('''- **Spellings.**''','''- **The prayers** (the law section): the "Paraclete" is Mani; the twelve
  prostrations and the four daily prayers are the hearers' rule. Compare the
  Turkish confession of the hearers ([Xwāstwānīft](xwastwanift.html)), which
  also speaks of the four prayers, the three seals and the fasts.
- **Spellings.**''')
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(t)
p='devlog.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read().rstrip('\n')
s+="\n- 2026-10-21 `al-nadim-books`: added al-Nadīm's section on the law Mani gave (the ten commandments, the prayers with their prostrations, the fasts), from Flügel pp. 95–97.\n"
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
EOF

content.content:
Mänl lehrt: Den Anfang**) der Welt bilden zwei We- 
sen **), das eine Licht, das andere Finstemis»; beide sind von 
einander getrennt**). Das Licht aber ist der erste Gb-oss- 
herrliche*'),: durch keine Zahl beschränkt, Gott selbst, der 
Konig der Paradiese des Lichts**). Er hat fiinf Glieder*^), 
die Sanfbmuth, das Wissen, den Verstand, das Qeheimniss, die 
Einsicht, und fiinf andere geistige, die Liebe, den Glauben, 
die Treue, den Edelsinn '^^) und die Weisheit^*). Er be- 
hauptete femer, dass der Lichtgott mit diesen seinen Eigen- 
schaften anfanglos ^^) sei, mit ihm zugleich aber zwei gleich- 
anfanglose Dinge bestehen, das eine der Lnftkreis (Lichtather), 
das andere die Erde^^). M4nl fügt hinzu: Und die Glieder 
des Luftkreises sind fünf, die Sanftmuth, das Wissen, der Ver- 
stand, das Geheinmiss^^), die Einsicht; und die Glieder der 
Erde, der leise Lufthauch, der Wind, das Licht ^*), das Was- 
ser und das Feuer. 
Das andere Wesen ^*) ist die Finstemiss, und deren Glie- 
der sind fünf, der Nebel ^'), der Brand, der Glüh wind, das 
Gift^*) und die Finstemiss. 
Man! lehrt: Jenes Lichtwesen grenzt unmittelbar an das 
finstere Wesen '^*) ohne eine Scheidewand*^) zwischen beiden; 
das Licht berührt mit seiner (untersten*^) Seite die Finster- 
niss, während es nach oben, nach rechts und nach links un- 
begrenzt ist. Ebenso ist die Finstemiss nach unten und nach 
redits und nach links endlos. Man! lehrt femer: Aus dieser 
finstern Erde entstand der Satan **), nicht so, dass er an sich 
vom Anfang her ewig war, doch waren seine Substanzen in 
seinen Elementen anfanglos. Es vereinigten sich nun diese 
Substanzen aus seinen Elementen und gingen als Satan her- 
vor, sein Haupt wie" das Haupt eines Löwen, sein Leib wie 
der Leib eines Drachen, seine Flügel wie die Flügel eines 
Vogels, sein Schwanz wie der Schwanz eines grossen Fisches 
und seine vier Füsse wie die Füsse der kriechenden Thiere*^). 
Als dieser Satan unter dem Namen Iblis der der Zeit nach 
8T 
Ewige (ürteufel®*) aus der Finstemise entstanden war, ver- 
schlang und verzehrte er (Alles ®*), verbreitete Verderben nach 
rechts und nach links, und stieg in die Tiefe, bei all diesen 
Bewegungen Zerstörung und Vernichtung von oben herab 
bringend. Dann strebte er nach der Hohe und gewahrte die 
Strahlungen des Lichts; sie waren ihm aber zuwider. Als 
er später sah, wie diese sich erhöhten, entsetzte er sich, kroch 
in sich zusammen und vereinigte sich mit seinen Elementen. 
Hierauf strebte er von neuem mit solcher Gewalt nach der 
Höhe®*), dass die Lichterde'') das Thun des Satan und wie er 
auf Mord und Verderben sann, gewahrte. Nachdem sie davon 
Kunde erhalten, erfuhr es die Welt der Einsicht, dann die Welt 
des Wissens, dann die Welt des Geheimnisses, dann die Welt des 
Verstandes, dann die Welt der Sanftmuth*®), Als es zuletzt, lehrt 
er weiter, auch der König der Paradiese des Lichts erfahren hatte,

## Introduction

Al-Nadīm's chapter on the Manichaeans (987) gives a long summary of Mani's
teaching, much of it introduced as Mani's own words: "Mani teaches …",
"Mani says further …". It is the fullest account of the Manichaean myth
that survives in Arabic, and it agrees closely with the Turfan fragments
(compare [the Šābuhragān](shabuhragan.html) and [the building of the
world](turfan-cosmogony.html)). This page gives the part on the two
principles, the battle of the First Man, the mixture, the making of the
world and the end. Al-Nadīm's lists of Mani's books and letters, and the
law Mani gave, are on [a separate page](al-nadim-books.html).

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Gustav Flügel's German of
1862. Flügel's notes are not reproduced. Words in parentheses are his or are
added for sense.

## The translation

### The two principles

Mani teaches: The beginning of the world is two beings, the one light, the
other darkness; the two are separate from each other.

The light is the first Great One, not limited by any number, God himself,
the King of the Paradises of Light. He has five limbs: gentleness,
knowledge, understanding, the mystery and insight; and five others,
spiritual: love, faith, faithfulness, nobility and wisdom. He held further
that the God of Light, with these his attributes, is without beginning, but
that with him two things exist that are equally without beginning, the one
the air (the ether of light), the other the earth. Mani adds: The limbs of
the air are five, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight; and the limbs of the earth are the gentle breeze, the wind, the
light, the water and the fire.

The other being is the darkness, and its limbs are five: the mist, the
burning, the scorching wind, the poison and the darkness.

Mani teaches: That being of light borders directly on the dark being, with
no wall between them; the light touches the darkness with its (lowest) side,
while upwards, to the right and to the left it is without limit. In the
same way the darkness is endless downwards, to the right and to the left.

### Satan and the First Man

Mani teaches further: From this dark earth Satan arose; not that he was
eternal in himself from the beginning, but his substances were without
beginning in his elements. These substances from his elements came
together and came forth as Satan: his head like the head of a lion, his

together with the praises, hymns, the pure word and the pious works that
rise up. The moon, Mani adds, hands these parts of light over to the sun,
and the sun hands them over to the light above it in the world of praise,
and they go on in this world up to the highest, pure light. She does not
cease doing this until there remains of the light a part so closely bound
that the sun and the moon cannot purify it any further.

### The great fire and the end

While this is happening, the angel whose task is to carry the earths rises
up, and the other angel ceases to draw the heavens after him, so that the
highest mixes with the lowest; and a fire blazes up and eats its way
through these confused things, and does not stop burning until what is
still left of light in them is released.

This burning, Mani teaches, lasts 1,468 years. And, he goes on, when this
order has been carried through, and the Humāma, that is, the spirit of
darkness, sees the freeing of the light and the rising up of the angels,
the hosts and the keepers, she humbles herself as she sees the battle, so
that the hosts round about her press upon her, and she goes back into a
grave that has been made ready for her. Then he closes this grave with a
stone as big as the world, and shuts her in. The light is then safe from
the darkness and from any harm by it.

## Notes to this edition

- **The five limbs** of the Father (gentleness, knowledge, understanding,
  mystery, insight) are the same five that the Chinese texts call Sense,
  Mind, Thought, Reflection and Intention (see the [Traité](traite.html)).
- **The Friend of the Lights, Joy and the Living Spirit** are the second
  creation: the Friend of the Lights, the Great Builder (here "Joy", or the
  Mother of Life, in Flügel's reading) and the Living Spirit, who calls the
  First Man.
- **Ten heavens and eight earths**: Müller set the Parthian description of
  the heavens' gates, steps and passages beside this passage (see the notes
  to [the building of the world](turfan-cosmogony.html)).
- **1,468 years**: the same figure as the Middle Persian *Šābuhragān*
  (M 470).
- **The Humāma** is the "spirit of darkness", the soul of matter.
