The Māsiya among the Manichaeans hold that something of the light remains
behind in the darkness.

### The beginning of unbroken generation, according to Mani's teaching

Then, Mani says, one of those archons and of the stars, the oppressing
force, greed, lust and sin, mated, and from their mating came forth the
first man, who is Adam; and those who watched over him were two archons, a
male and a female. Then followed a second mating, and from it came forth
the beautiful woman, who is Ḥawwāʾ (Eve).

When, Mani teaches, the five angels saw the light of God, which greed had
secretly stolen and shut up captive in these two creatures, in its
defilement, they begged the bringer of good news, the Mother of Life, the
First Man and the Living Spirit to send someone to this first creature, to
loosen and save it, to reveal knowledge and righteousness to it, and to set
it free from the devils. So, he goes on, they sent ʿĪsā (Jesus), with a god
accompanying him. These seized the two archons, made them prisoners and
freed the two creatures.

And ʿĪsā (Jesus), Mani teaches, set out and spoke to the creature, that is,
Adam; he explained to him the Paradises and the gods, hell and the devils,
the earth and the heaven, and the sun and the moon; he made him afraid of
Ḥawwāʾ by telling him of her violent importunity, and filled him with fear
of going near her. And Adam obeyed.

Then the archon went back to his daughter Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) and lay with her in
the lust that dwells in him, so that she bore a son, ugly to look at and
reddish, named Qāyin (Cain), the red man. This son then lay with his
mother, and she bore a white son named Hābīl (Abel), the white man. Then
Qāyin lay with his mother again, so that she bore two girls, the one named
the Wise of the World (*Ḥakīmat ad-dahr*), the other the Daughter of Greed
(*Ibnat al-ḥirṣ*). Qāyin took the Daughter of Greed as his wife and gave the
Wise of the World to Hābīl, who took her as his wife. The Wise of the
World, Mani says, overflowed with the light and wisdom of God, while in the
Daughter of Greed there was none of it at all.

Then one of the angels came to the Wise of the World and said to her:
"Guard your soul, for to God's joy you shall become the mother of two
perfect girls." And he lay with her, so that she bore him two girls, one of
whom she named Raufaryād ("Come to help") and the other Barfaryād ("Bring
help"). When Hābīl learned of this, he was filled with anger, and sadness
took hold of him wholly, and he said to her: "From whom have you these two
children? I suspect they are Qāyin's; it is he who has lain with you." She,
however, described to him the form of the angel. Still he left her, went to
his mother Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) to complain to her of what Qāyin had done, and said
to her: "Have you heard what he has done with my sister and my wife?"
Qāyin heard this, fell upon Hābīl, smashed his brain with a stone and killed
him. Then he took the Wise of the World as his wife.

Mani teaches further: Those archons, that Ṣindīd (the mighty one), and
Ḥawwāʾ were grieved at what they saw of Qāyin; and the Ṣindīd taught Ḥawwāʾ
the gibberish of sorcery, so that she might bewitch Adam. She went off, did
as she was told, and met him with a garland of tree blossom. When Adam found
her fit for his lust, he lay with her, and she became pregnant by him and
bore a graceful son, fair of face. The Ṣindīd heard of this, fell into
grief and became ill, and said to Ḥawwāʾ: "This creature does not belong to
us; it is a stranger." She wished to kill it; but Adam took it and said to
Ḥawwāʾ: "I will feed it with cow's milk and the fruit of the trees." He
took it and went away. Then the Ṣindīd sent the archons to take away the
trees and the cattle and remove them far from Adam.

When Adam saw this, he took the child and drew three circles round it. On
the first he wrote the name of the King of the Paradises, on the second the
name of the First Man, and on the third the name of the Living Spirit; he
went up to a higher place, humbled himself before God, whose name is
glorious, and begged him: "If I have sinned against you, that is not the
fault of this child." Then one of the three came hurrying, bringing the
garland of beauty, which he carried in his hand to Adam. When the Ṣindīd
and the archons saw this, they went straight away.

Then, Mani says, a tree called *Lūṭis* (lotus) appeared to Adam, from which
milk came out. With this he fed the boy, and gave him the name of the tree.
Later he called him Šātil (Seth). But that Ṣindīd, who kept up his enmity
against Adam and those creatures, said to Ḥawwāʾ: "Go to Adam; perhaps you
will bring him back to us." She hurried off at once and deceived Adam, so
that he lay with her in his lust. When Šātil saw him then, he admonished
him, reproached him and said to him: "Come, let us set out for the East,
to the light and wisdom of God." And he set out with him there, and he
stayed there until he died and entered Paradise. But Šātil, Raufaryād and
Barfaryād, and the Wise of the World, the mother of the last two, followed
with the *ṣiddīqūt* (the community of the righteous) one direction and one
and the same way until the time of their death; while Ḥawwāʾ, Qāyin and the
Daughter of Greed went into hell.

### The earth of light and the ether of light, which are without beginning, together with the God of Light

Mani teaches: The earth of light has five limbs, the gentle breeze, the
wind, the light, the water and the fire; and likewise the ether of light
has five limbs, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight. He teaches further: These ten limbs of the ether and the earth
together make up the Greatness.

This shining earth, he says, has a body; it is bright and serene, with a
gentle radiance and full splendour, against which the clearness of its
purity and the beauty of its bodies stand out: form upon form, beauty upon
beauty, whiteness upon whiteness, clearness upon clearness, grace upon
grace, light upon light, brilliance upon brilliance, lovely sight upon
lovely sight, pleasantness upon pleasantness, elegance upon elegance, rows
of gates upon rows of gates, towers upon towers, dwellings upon dwellings,
inns upon inns, gardens upon gardens, trees upon trees, branches upon
branches with boughs and fruit, lovely to see, a light shining in many
colours, each lovelier and more blooming than the other, clouds upon clouds
and shade upon shade. That God of Light on this earth is an eternal God.

The God on this earth, he goes on, has twelve glories, which are called
the first-born, whose forms are like his form, all of them learned and
understanding; and glories, he says, which are called the house-spirits,
the active and the strong. And the gentle breeze, he adds, is the life of
the world.

### The earth of darkness and its heat

The earth of darkness, Mani teaches, bristles with depths, abysses, clefts,
layers, dams, swamps, scattered stretches of land running out into branches
and filled with dense forest, and springs from which smoke rises from land
to land and from wall to wall, from which fire comes up from land to land
and darkness from land to land. Some of these columns are higher than the
others, others deeper, and the smoke that pours out of them is the poison
of death. It rises from the spring of an abyss whose foundations are of
murky slime, in which are dusty earth, the elements of fire, the thick dark
elements of wind and the elements of heavy water.

The darkness borders on this shining earth, above (the one) and below (the
other). Both, the light upwards and the darkness downwards, are without
limit.

### How a man should enter the religion

Whoever wants to enter the religion, Mani commands, must test himself; and
if he sees that he is able to tame lust and greed, to give up eating all
kinds of meat, drinking wine and married intercourse, and to keep himself
from harming water and fire, from sorcery and from hypocrisy, let him enter
the religion. But if he is not able to do all this, let him not enter. If
he loves the religion but cannot subdue the stirring of the senses and
greed, let him make use of keeping the religion and the righteous (the
Elect), and meet his reprehensible acts by (using) times when he gives
himself wholly to work, righteousness, eager watchfulness, prayer and pious
humility; for that makes him content in this passing world and in the
eternal world to come, and his form on the Last Day will be the second
form, of which, God willing, we shall speak further below.

The Māsiya among the Manichaeans hold that something of the light remains
behind in the darkness.

### The beginning of unbroken generation, according to Mani's teaching

Then, Mani says, one of those archons and of the stars, the oppressing
force, greed, lust and sin, mated, and from their mating came forth the
first man, who is Adam; and those who watched over him were two archons, a
male and a female. Then followed a second mating, and from it came forth
the beautiful woman, who is Ḥawwāʾ (Eve).

When, Mani teaches, the five angels saw the light of God, which greed had
secretly stolen and shut up captive in these two creatures, in its
defilement, they begged the bringer of good news, the Mother of Life, the
First Man and the Living Spirit to send someone to this first creature, to
loosen and save it, to reveal knowledge and righteousness to it, and to set
it free from the devils. So, he goes on, they sent ʿĪsā (Jesus), with a god
accompanying him. These seized the two archons, made them prisoners and
freed the two creatures.

And ʿĪsā (Jesus), Mani teaches, set out and spoke to the creature, that is,
Adam; he explained to him the Paradises and the gods, hell and the devils,
the earth and the heaven, and the sun and the moon; he made him afraid of
Ḥawwāʾ by telling him of her violent importunity, and filled him with fear
of going near her. And Adam obeyed.

Then the archon went back to his daughter Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) and lay with her in
the lust that dwells in him, so that she bore a son, ugly to look at and
reddish, named Qāyin (Cain), the red man. This son then lay with his
mother, and she bore a white son named Hābīl (Abel), the white man. Then
Qāyin lay with his mother again, so that she bore two girls, the one named
the Wise of the World (*Ḥakīmat ad-dahr*), the other the Daughter of Greed
(*Ibnat al-ḥirṣ*). Qāyin took the Daughter of Greed as his wife and gave the
Wise of the World to Hābīl, who took her as his wife. The Wise of the
World, Mani says, overflowed with the light and wisdom of God, while in the
Daughter of Greed there was none of it at all.

Then one of the angels came to the Wise of the World and said to her:
"Guard your soul, for to God's joy you shall become the mother of two
perfect girls." And he lay with her, so that she bore him two girls, one of
whom she named Raufaryād ("Come to help") and the other Barfaryād ("Bring
help"). When Hābīl learned of this, he was filled with anger, and sadness
took hold of him wholly, and he said to her: "From whom have you these two
children? I suspect they are Qāyin's; it is he who has lain with you." She,
however, described to him the form of the angel. Still he left her, went to
his mother Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) to complain to her of what Qāyin had done, and said
to her: "Have you heard what he has done with my sister and my wife?"
Qāyin heard this, fell upon Hābīl, smashed his brain with a stone and killed
him. Then he took the Wise of the World as his wife.

Mani teaches further: Those archons, that Ṣindīd (the mighty one), and
Ḥawwāʾ were grieved at what they saw of Qāyin; and the Ṣindīd taught Ḥawwāʾ
the gibberish of sorcery, so that she might bewitch Adam. She went off, did
as she was told, and met him with a garland of tree blossom. When Adam found
her fit for his lust, he lay with her, and she became pregnant by him and
bore a graceful son, fair of face. The Ṣindīd heard of this, fell into
grief and became ill, and said to Ḥawwāʾ: "This creature does not belong to
us; it is a stranger." She wished to kill it; but Adam took it and said to
Ḥawwāʾ: "I will feed it with cow's milk and the fruit of the trees." He
took it and went away. Then the Ṣindīd sent the archons to take away the
trees and the cattle and remove them far from Adam.

When Adam saw this, he took the child and drew three circles round it. On
the first he wrote the name of the King of the Paradises, on the second the
name of the First Man, and on the third the name of the Living Spirit; he
went up to a higher place, humbled himself before God, whose name is
glorious, and begged him: "If I have sinned against you, that is not the
fault of this child." Then one of the three came hurrying, bringing the
garland of beauty, which he carried in his hand to Adam. When the Ṣindīd
and the archons saw this, they went straight away.

Then, Mani says, a tree called *Lūṭis* (lotus) appeared to Adam, from which
milk came out. With this he fed the boy, and gave him the name of the tree.
Later he called him Šātil (Seth). But that Ṣindīd, who kept up his enmity
against Adam and those creatures, said to Ḥawwāʾ: "Go to Adam; perhaps you
will bring him back to us." She hurried off at once and deceived Adam, so
that he lay with her in his lust. When Šātil saw him then, he admonished
him, reproached him and said to him: "Come, let us set out for the East,
to the light and wisdom of God." And he set out with him there, and he
stayed there until he died and entered Paradise. But Šātil, Raufaryād and
Barfaryād, and the Wise of the World, the mother of the last two, followed
with the *ṣiddīqūt* (the community of the righteous) one direction and one
and the same way until the time of their death; while Ḥawwāʾ, Qāyin and the
Daughter of Greed went into hell.

### The earth of light and the ether of light, which are without beginning, together with the God of Light

Mani teaches: The earth of light has five limbs, the gentle breeze, the
wind, the light, the water and the fire; and likewise the ether of light
has five limbs, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight. He teaches further: These ten limbs of the ether and the earth
together make up the Greatness.

This shining earth, he says, has a body; it is bright and serene, with a
gentle radiance and full splendour, against which the clearness of its
purity and the beauty of its bodies stand out: form upon form, beauty upon
beauty, whiteness upon whiteness, clearness upon clearness, grace upon
grace, light upon light, brilliance upon brilliance, lovely sight upon
lovely sight, pleasantness upon pleasantness, elegance upon elegance, rows
of gates upon rows of gates, towers upon towers, dwellings upon dwellings,
inns upon inns, gardens upon gardens, trees upon trees, branches upon
branches with boughs and fruit, lovely to see, a light shining in many
colours, each lovelier and more blooming than the other, clouds upon clouds
and shade upon shade. That God of Light on this earth is an eternal God.

The God on this earth, he goes on, has twelve glories, which are called
the first-born, whose forms are like his form, all of them learned and
understanding; and glories, he says, which are called the house-spirits,
the active and the strong. And the gentle breeze, he adds, is the life of
the world.

### The earth of darkness and its heat

The earth of darkness, Mani teaches, bristles with depths, abysses, clefts,
layers, dams, swamps, scattered stretches of land running out into branches
and filled with dense forest, and springs from which smoke rises from land
to land and from wall to wall, from which fire comes up from land to land
and darkness from land to land. Some of these columns are higher than the
others, others deeper, and the smoke that pours out of them is the poison
of death. It rises from the spring of an abyss whose foundations are of
murky slime, in which are dusty earth, the elements of fire, the thick dark
elements of wind and the elements of heavy water.

The darkness borders on this shining earth, above (the one) and below (the
other). Both, the light upwards and the darkness downwards, are without
limit.

### How a man should enter the religion

Whoever wants to enter the religion, Mani commands, must test himself; and
if he sees that he is able to tame lust and greed, to give up eating all
kinds of meat, drinking wine and married intercourse, and to keep himself
from harming water and fire, from sorcery and from hypocrisy, let him enter
the religion. But if he is not able to do all this, let him not enter. If
he loves the religion but cannot subdue the stirring of the senses and
greed, let him make use of keeping the religion and the righteous (the
Elect), and meet his reprehensible acts by (using) times when he gives
himself wholly to work, righteousness, eager watchfulness, prayer and pious
humility; for that makes him content in this passing world and in the
eternal world to come, and his form on the Last Day will be the second
form, of which, God willing, we shall speak further below.

EOF

Ḥawwāʾ by telling him of her violent importunity, and filled him with fear
of going near her. And Adam obeyed.

the lust that dwells in him, so that she bore a son, ugly to look at and
reddish, named Qāyin (Cain), the red man. This son then lay with his
mother, and she bore a white son named Hābīl (Abel), the white man. Then
Qāyin lay with his mother again, so that she bore two girls, the one named
the Wise of the World (*Ḥakīmat ad-dahr*), the other the Daughter of Greed
(*Ibnat al-ḥirṣ*). Qāyin took the Daughter of Greed as his wife and gave the
Wise of the World to Hābīl, who took her as his wife. The Wise of the
World, Mani says, overflowed with the light and wisdom of God, while in the
Daughter of Greed there was none of it at all.

Then one of the angels came to the Wise of the World and said to her:
"Guard your soul, for to God's joy you shall become the mother of two
perfect girls." And he lay with her, so that she bore him two girls, one of
whom she named Raufaryād ("Come to help") and the other Barfaryād ("Bring
help"). When Hābīl learned of this, he was filled with anger, and sadness
took hold of him wholly, and he said to her: "From whom have you these two
children? I suspect they are Qāyin's; it is he who has lain with you." She,
however, described to him the form of the angel. Still he left her, went to
his mother Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) to complain to her of what Qāyin had done, and said
to her: "Have you heard what he has done with my sister and my wife?"
Qāyin heard this, fell upon Hābīl, smashed his brain with a stone and killed
him. Then he took the Wise of the World as his wife.

Ḥawwāʾ were grieved at what they saw of Qāyin; and the Ṣindīd taught Ḥawwāʾ
the gibberish of sorcery, so that she might bewitch Adam. She went off, did
as she was told, and met him with a garland of tree blossom. When Adam found
her fit for his lust, he lay with her, and she became pregnant by him and
bore a graceful son, fair of face. The Ṣindīd heard of this, fell into
grief and became ill, and said to Ḥawwāʾ: "This creature does not belong to
us; it is a stranger." She wished to kill it; but Adam took it and said to
Ḥawwāʾ: "I will feed it with cow's milk and the fruit of the trees." He
took it and went away. Then the Ṣindīd sent the archons to take away the
trees and the cattle and remove them far from Adam.

When Adam saw this, he took the child and drew three circles round it. On
the first he wrote the name of the King of the Paradises, on the second the
name of the First Man, and on the third the name of the Living Spirit; he
went up to a higher place, humbled himself before God, whose name is
glorious, and begged him: "If I have sinned against you, that is not the
fault of this child." Then one of the three came hurrying, bringing the
garland of beauty, which he carried in his hand to Adam. When the Ṣindīd
and the archons saw this, they went straight away.

Then, Mani says, a tree called *Lūṭis* (lotus) appeared to Adam, from which
milk came out. With this he fed the boy, and gave him the name of the tree.
Later he called him Šātil (Seth). But that Ṣindīd, who kept up his enmity
against Adam and those creatures, said to Ḥawwāʾ: "Go to Adam; perhaps you
will bring him back to us." She hurried off at once and deceived Adam, so
that he lay with her in his lust. When Šātil saw him then, he admonished
him, reproached him and said to him: "Come, let us set out for the East,
to the light and wisdom of God." And he set out with him there, and he
stayed there until he died and entered Paradise. But Šātil, Raufaryād and
Barfaryād, and the Wise of the World, the mother of the last two, followed
with the *ṣiddīqūt* (the community of the righteous) one direction and one
and the same way until the time of their death; while Ḥawwāʾ, Qāyin and the
Daughter of Greed went into hell.

Mani teaches: The earth of light has five limbs, the gentle breeze, the
wind, the light, the water and the fire; and likewise the ether of light
has five limbs, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight. He teaches further: These ten limbs of the ether and the earth
together make up the Greatness.

This shining earth, he says, has a body; it is bright and serene, with a
gentle radiance and full splendour, against which the clearness of its
purity and the beauty of its bodies stand out: form upon form, beauty upon
beauty, whiteness upon whiteness, clearness upon clearness, grace upon
grace, light upon light, brilliance upon brilliance, lovely sight upon
lovely sight, pleasantness upon pleasantness, elegance upon elegance, rows
of gates upon rows of gates, towers upon towers, dwellings upon dwellings,
inns upon inns, gardens upon gardens, trees upon trees, branches upon
branches with boughs and fruit, lovely to see, a light shining in many
colours, each lovelier and more blooming than the other, clouds upon clouds
and shade upon shade. That God of Light on this earth is an eternal God.

The God on this earth, he goes on, has twelve glories, which are called
the first-born, whose forms are like his form, all of them learned and
understanding; and glories, he says, which are called the house-spirits,
the active and the strong. And the gentle breeze, he adds, is the life of
the world.

### The earth of darkness and its heat

The earth of darkness, Mani teaches, bristles with depths, abysses, clefts,
layers, dams, swamps, scattered stretches of land running out into branches
and filled with dense forest, and springs from which smoke rises from land
to land and from wall to wall, from which fire comes up from land to land
and darkness from land to land. Some of these columns are higher than the
others, others deeper, and the smoke that pours out of them is the poison
of death. It rises from the spring of an abyss whose foundations are of
murky slime, in which are dusty earth, the elements of fire, the thick dark
elements of wind and the elements of heavy water.

The darkness borders on this shining earth, above (the one) and below (the
other). Both, the light upwards and the darkness downwards, are without
limit.

### How a man should enter the religion

Whoever wants to enter the religion, Mani commands, must test himself; and
if he sees that he is able to tame lust and greed, to give up eating all
kinds of meat, drinking wine and married intercourse, and to keep himself
from harming water and fire, from sorcery and from hypocrisy, let him enter
the religion. But if he is not able to do all this, let him not enter. If
he loves the religion but cannot subdue the stirring of the senses and
greed, let him make use of keeping the religion and the righteous (the
Elect), and meet his reprehensible acts by (using) times when he gives
himself wholly to work, righteousness, eager watchfulness, prayer and pious
humility; for that makes him content in this passing world and in the
eternal world to come, and his form on the Last Day will be the second
form, of which, God willing, we shall speak further below.

milk came out. With this he fed the boy, and gave him the name of the tree.
Later he called him Šātil (Seth). But that Ṣindīd, who kept up his enmity
against Adam and those creatures, said to Ḥawwāʾ: "Go to Adam; perhaps you
will bring him back to us." She hurried off at once and deceived Adam, so
that he lay with her in his lust. When Šātil saw him then, he admonished
him, reproached him and said to him: "Come, let us set out for the East,
to the light and wisdom of God." And he set out with him there, and he
stayed there until he died and entered Paradise. But Šātil, Raufaryād and
Barfaryād, and the Wise of the World, the mother of the last two, followed
with the *ṣiddīqūt* (the community of the righteous) one direction and one
and the same way until the time of their death; while Ḥawwāʾ, Qāyin and the
Daughter of Greed went into hell.

### The earth of light and the ether of light, which are without beginning, together with the God of Light

Mani teaches: The earth of light has five limbs, the gentle breeze, the
wind, the light, the water and the fire; and likewise the ether of light
has five limbs, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight. He teaches further: These ten limbs of the ether and the earth
together make up the Greatness.

This shining earth, he says, has a body; it is bright and serene, with a
gentle radiance and full splendour, against which the clearness of its
purity and the beauty of its bodies stand out: form upon form, beauty upon
beauty, whiteness upon whiteness, clearness upon clearness, grace upon
grace, light upon light, brilliance upon brilliance, lovely sight upon
lovely sight, pleasantness upon pleasantness, elegance upon elegance, rows
of gates upon rows of gates, towers upon towers, dwellings upon dwellings,
inns upon inns, gardens upon gardens, trees upon trees, branches upon
branches with boughs and fruit, lovely to see, a light shining in many
colours, each lovelier and more blooming than the other, clouds upon clouds
and shade upon shade. That God of Light on this earth is an eternal God.

The God on this earth, he goes on, has twelve glories, which are called
the first-born, whose forms are like his form, all of them learned and
understanding; and glories, he says, which are called the house-spirits,
the active and the strong. And the gentle breeze, he adds, is the life of
the world.

### The earth of darkness and its heat

The earth of darkness, Mani teaches, bristles with depths, abysses, clefts,
layers, dams, swamps, scattered stretches of land running out into branches
and filled with dense forest, and springs from which smoke rises from land
to land and from wall to wall, from which fire comes up from land to land
and darkness from land to land. Some of these columns are higher than the
others, others deeper, and the smoke that pours out of them is the poison
of death. It rises from the spring of an abyss whose foundations are of
murky slime, in which are dusty earth, the elements of fire, the thick dark
elements of wind and the elements of heavy water.

The darkness borders on this shining earth, above (the one) and below (the
other). Both, the light upwards and the darkness downwards, are without
limit.

### How a man should enter the religion

Whoever wants to enter the religion, Mani commands, must test himself; and
if he sees that he is able to tame lust and greed, to give up eating all
kinds of meat, drinking wine and married intercourse, and to keep himself
from harming water and fire, from sorcery and from hypocrisy, let him enter
the religion. But if he is not able to do all this, let him not enter. If
he loves the religion but cannot subdue the stirring of the senses and
greed, let him make use of keeping the religion and the righteous (the
Elect), and meet his reprehensible acts by (using) times when he gives
himself wholly to work, righteousness, eager watchfulness, prayer and pious
humility; for that makes him content in this passing world and in the
eternal world to come, and his form on the Last Day will be the second
form, of which, God willing, we shall speak further below.

him, reproached him and said to him: "Come, let us set out for the East,
to the light and wisdom of God." And he set out with him there, and he
stayed there until he died and entered Paradise. But Šātil, Raufaryād and
Barfaryād, and the Wise of the World, the mother of the last two, followed
with the *ṣiddīqūt* (the community of the righteous) one direction and one
and the same way until the time of their death; while Ḥawwāʾ, Qāyin and the
Daughter of Greed went into hell.

### The earth of light and the ether of light, which are without beginning, together with the God of Light

Mani teaches: The earth of light has five limbs, the gentle breeze, the
wind, the light, the water and the fire; and likewise the ether of light
has five limbs, gentleness, knowledge, understanding, the mystery and
insight. He teaches further: These ten limbs of the ether and the earth
together make up the Greatness.

This shining earth, he says, has a body; it is bright and serene, with a
gentle radiance and full splendour, against which the clearness of its
purity and the beauty of its bodies stand out: form upon form, beauty upon
beauty, whiteness upon whiteness, clearness upon clearness, grace upon
grace, light upon light, brilliance upon brilliance, lovely sight upon
lovely sight, pleasantness upon pleasantness, elegance upon elegance, rows
of gates upon rows of gates, towers upon towers, dwellings upon dwellings,
inns upon inns, gardens upon gardens, trees upon trees, branches upon
branches with boughs and fruit, lovely to see, a light shining in many
colours, each lovelier and more blooming than the other, clouds upon clouds
and shade upon shade. That God of Light on this earth is an eternal God.

The God on this earth, he goes on, has twelve glories, which are called
the first-born, whose forms are like his form, all of them learned and
understanding; and glories, he says, which are called the house-spirits,
the active and the strong. And the gentle breeze, he adds, is the life of
the world.

### The earth of darkness and its heat

The earth of darkness, Mani teaches, bristles with depths, abysses, clefts,
layers, dams, swamps, scattered stretches of land running out into branches
and filled with dense forest, and springs from which smoke rises from land
to land and from wall to wall, from which fire comes up from land to land
and darkness from land to land. Some of these columns are higher than the
others, others deeper, and the smoke that pours out of them is the poison
of death. It rises from the spring of an abyss whose foundations are of
murky slime, in which are dusty earth, the elements of fire, the thick dark
elements of wind and the elements of heavy water.

The darkness borders on this shining earth, above (the one) and below (the
other). Both, the light upwards and the darkness downwards, are without
limit.

### How a man should enter the religion

Whoever wants to enter the religion, Mani commands, must test himself; and
if he sees that he is able to tame lust and greed, to give up eating all
kinds of meat, drinking wine and married intercourse, and to keep himself
from harming water and fire, from sorcery and from hypocrisy, let him enter
the religion. But if he is not able to do all this, let him not enter. If
he loves the religion but cannot subdue the stirring of the senses and
greed, let him make use of keeping the religion and the righteous (the
Elect), and meet his reprehensible acts by (using) times when he gives
himself wholly to work, righteousness, eager watchfulness, prayer and pious
humility; for that makes him content in this passing world and in the
eternal world to come, and his form on the Last Day will be the second
form, of which, God willing, we shall speak further below.

### The teaching of the Manichaeans on the life to come

When death draws near to one of the righteous (the Elect), Mani teaches,
the First Man sends a god of light in the form of the guiding Wise One,
and with him three gods, and together with them the water-vessel, the
robe, the head-band, the crown and the garland of light. With them comes
the maiden, who is like the soul of this righteous one. The devil of greed
and lust also appears to him, with other devils. As soon as the righteous
one sees them, he calls to his help the goddess who has taken the form of
the Wise One, and the other three gods, and they come near him. As soon as
the devils see them, they turn and flee. But those (gods) take this
righteous one, clothe him with the crown, the garland and the robe, put the
water-vessel in his hand, and rise with him on the Column of Praise to the
sphere of the moon, to the First Man and to the Nahnaha, the Mother of the
Living, until (he reaches) the state in which he was at first in the
Paradises of Light. His body, however, then stays lying, so that the sun,
the moon and the gods of light may draw out of it the powers, that is, the
water, the fire and the gentle breeze; and he rises to the sun and becomes a
god. But the rest of his body, which is wholly darkness, is thrown into
hell.

When death draws near to the man who struggles, who is receptive to the
religion and to righteousness, and who guards them both and the righteous
(that is, the hearer), those gods whom I have mentioned appear, and the
devils are there too. He calls for help, and by the good works he has
done, and by his guarding of the religion and the righteous, he seeks
intercession that may incline to him. They free him from the devils; but he
does not cease to be like a man in the world who sees terrifying forms in
his dream and sinks into filth and dung. In this state he remains until his
light and his spirit are set free and he reaches the meeting-place of the
righteous, and, after a long time of wandering to and fro, puts on their
robes.

But when death comes to the sinful man, over whom greed and lust have gained
the upper hand, the devils come near him, seize and torment him, and make
him see the terrifying forms. Those gods are there too, and with them the
robe that was mentioned, so that the sinful man believes they have come to
save him. But they are there only to fill him with reproaches, to call his
deeds back to his memory, and to make him understand, beyond doubt, that he
must give up hope of help from the righteous. Then he wanders about in the
world without ceasing, beset by torments, until the time when this state
ends and he is thrown into hell with the world.

These are three ways, Mani teaches, according to which the souls of men are
divided. One of them leads into the Paradises: that is the way of the
righteous. The second leads into the world and its terrors: that is the way
of the guardians of the religion and the helpers of the righteous. And the
third leads to hell: that is the way of the sinful man.

*(Al-Nadīm then describes the state of the world to come after the end of
this one: the gods coming from the four quarters to look on the new
Paradise, and the sinners in hell. That passage is the one that Müller set
beside the Middle Persian* Šābuhragān*, and it is translated on [that
page](shabuhragan.html#al-nadms-summary-of-the-same-passage).)*

### The life of Mani

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq (al-Nadīm) says: Mani, the son of Futtaq Bābak ibn Abī
Barzām, was descended from the family of the Ḥaskāniyya. His mother's name
was Mais, or according to others Ūtāxīm, or Mār Maryam, of the family of the
Ašġāniyya. Mani, it is said, had his home in Kūxā (Coche), in the region
that borders on Bādarāyā and Bākusāyā, and he had a lame (turned-in) leg.
His father, it is said, traced his origin to Hamadān. From there he went to
Babylonia and usually stayed in al-Madāʾin, in the quarter called Ctesiphon.
There stands the temple of idols that Futtaq used to visit, as the other
inhabitants did.

One day a voice called to him from the innermost sanctuary of the temple:
"O Futtaq, eat no meat, drink no wine, and keep away from women." Three days
in a row this call came to him again and again. When Futtaq had thought
about it, he joined people who lived in the region of Dastumaisān and are
known as the *Muġtasila*, "those who wash themselves". Remnants of them are
still in that district and in the marshlands down to this day. They
professed the teaching that Futtaq had been called to accept.

When his wife, who was pregnant with Mani, had given birth to him, they
say, she had fine dreams about him, and saw, while awake, as if someone took
him, carried him off into the air, and then brought him back. Sometimes he
stayed away a day or two, then (the other) brought him back.

Later his father went away and brought him to a place where he had
relatives, who were also of his faith. Mani spoke words of wisdom although
he was a child; and when he had completed his twelfth year, he received, as
he put it, inspirations from the King of the Paradises of Light, who in his
own words is God the Exalted. The angel who brought him these inspirations
was called at-Tawm, which in Nabataean means "companion". He said to him:
"Leave this community of faith. You do not belong among its followers; your
task is purity of life and the subduing of the desires. But because of your
youth it is not yet time for you to come forward." When he had completed
his twenty-fourth year, the angel at-Tawm came to him again and said: "Now
the time has come for you to come forward openly and proclaim your own
teaching aloud."

The words that the angel at-Tawm spoke to him were these: "Greetings to
you, Mani, from me and from the Lord who has sent me to you and chosen you
for his mission. He commands you to call (people) to your teaching, and to
proclaim the glad promise of the truth that comes from him, and to give all
your zeal to it."

Mani, the Manichaeans relate, came forward openly on the day when Šābūr
son of Ardašīr came to the throne and set the crown on his head (it was a
Sunday, the first day of Nīsān, while the sun was in Aries), accompanied by
two men who followed him and were adherents of his teaching, the one named
Šamʿūn (Simeon), the other Zakū. His father also went with him, to see how
his new teaching would be received.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reports: Mani came forward in the second year of the
reign of the Roman Gallus, after Marcion had appeared about a hundred years
before him, in the reign of Titus Antoninus, in the first year of his rule,
and Ibn Daiṣān (Bardaisan) about thirty years after Marcion. Ibn Daiṣān got
his name from being born on a river called Daiṣān.

Mani claimed that he was the Paraclete whom Jesus, peace be upon him, had
announced. He drew his teaching from the Magians and the Christians, and in
the same way the script in which the (Manichaean) religious books were
written is borrowed from the Syriac and the Persian.

Before Mani had his meeting with Šābūr, he travelled through the lands for
about forty years, and after his return he invited Fīrūz, the brother of
Šābūr son of Ardašīr, to accept his teaching. Fīrūz also arranged Mani's
introduction to his brother Šābūr. And, the Manichaeans add, he came in to
him while on his shoulders two (things) shone like lamps of light. When
Šābūr saw him, he showed him great respect, and Mani grew in his esteem,
although he had resolved to seize him and kill him. But when he stood
before him, awe of him took hold of him, and he was glad of him and asked
him what he brought him, and even promised to be converted to him. Mani
asked him for a number of things, among them that his disciples should be
respected in Persia and in all the other lands of his kingdom, and that
they should be able to go wherever they wished. Šābūr granted him all that
he asked. Mani had also already called the Indians, the Chinese and the
people of Khorasan to accept his teaching, and had left one of his
disciples in each region.

### The life of Mani

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq (al-Nadīm) says: Mani, the son of Futtaq Bābak ibn Abī
Barzām, was descended from the family of the Ḥaskāniyya. His mother's name
was Mais, or according to others Ūtāxīm, or Mār Maryam, of the family of the
Ašġāniyya. Mani, it is said, had his home in Kūxā (Coche), in the region
that borders on Bādarāyā and Bākusāyā, and he had a lame (turned-in) leg.
His father, it is said, traced his origin to Hamadān. From there he went to
Babylonia and usually stayed in al-Madāʾin, in the quarter called Ctesiphon.
There stands the temple of idols that Futtaq used to visit, as the other
inhabitants did.

One day a voice called to him from the innermost sanctuary of the temple:
"O Futtaq, eat no meat, drink no wine, and keep away from women." Three days
in a row this call came to him again and again. When Futtaq had thought
about it, he joined people who lived in the region of Dastumaisān and are
known as the *Muġtasila*, "those who wash themselves". Remnants of them are
still in that district and in the marshlands down to this day. They
professed the teaching that Futtaq had been called to accept.

When his wife, who was pregnant with Mani, had given birth to him, they
say, she had fine dreams about him, and saw, while awake, as if someone took
him, carried him off into the air, and then brought him back. Sometimes he
stayed away a day or two, then (the other) brought him back.

Later his father went away and brought him to a place where he had
relatives, who were also of his faith. Mani spoke words of wisdom although
he was a child; and when he had completed his twelfth year, he received, as
he put it, inspirations from the King of the Paradises of Light, who in his
own words is God the Exalted. The angel who brought him these inspirations
was called at-Tawm, which in Nabataean means "companion". He said to him:
"Leave this community of faith. You do not belong among its followers; your
task is purity of life and the subduing of the desires. But because of your
youth it is not yet time for you to come forward." When he had completed
his twenty-fourth year, the angel at-Tawm came to him again and said: "Now
the time has come for you to come forward openly and proclaim your own
teaching aloud."

The words that the angel at-Tawm spoke to him were these: "Greetings to
you, Mani, from me and from the Lord who has sent me to you and chosen you
for his mission. He commands you to call (people) to your teaching, and to
proclaim the glad promise of the truth that comes from him, and to give all
your zeal to it."

Mani, the Manichaeans relate, came forward openly on the day when Šābūr
son of Ardašīr came to the throne and set the crown on his head (it was a
Sunday, the first day of Nīsān, while the sun was in Aries), accompanied by
two men who followed him and were adherents of his teaching, the one named
Šamʿūn (Simeon), the other Zakū. His father also went with him, to see how
his new teaching would be received.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reports: Mani came forward in the second year of the
reign of the Roman Gallus, after Marcion had appeared about a hundred years
before him, in the reign of Titus Antoninus, in the first year of his rule,
and Ibn Daiṣān (Bardaisan) about thirty years after Marcion. Ibn Daiṣān got
his name from being born on a river called Daiṣān.

Mani claimed that he was the Paraclete whom Jesus, peace be upon him, had
announced. He drew his teaching from the Magians and the Christians, and in
the same way the script in which the (Manichaean) religious books were
written is borrowed from the Syriac and the Persian.

Before Mani had his meeting with Šābūr, he travelled through the lands for
about forty years, and after his return he invited Fīrūz, the brother of
Šābūr son of Ardašīr, to accept his teaching. Fīrūz also arranged Mani's
introduction to his brother Šābūr. And, the Manichaeans add, he came in to
him while on his shoulders two (things) shone like lamps of light. When
Šābūr saw him, he showed him great respect, and Mani grew in his esteem,
although he had resolved to seize him and kill him. But when he stood
before him, awe of him took hold of him, and he was glad of him and asked
him what he brought him, and even promised to be converted to him. Mani
asked him for a number of things, among them that his disciples should be
respected in Persia and in all the other lands of his kingdom, and that
they should be able to go wherever they wished. Šābūr granted him all that
he asked. Mani had also already called the Indians, the Chinese and the
people of Khorasan to accept his teaching, and had left one of his
disciples in each region.

Later his father went away and brought him to a place where he had
relatives, who were also of his faith. Mani spoke words of wisdom although
he was a child; and when he had completed his twelfth year, he received, as
he put it, inspirations from the King of the Paradises of Light, who in his
own words is God the Exalted. The angel who brought him these inspirations
was called at-Tawm, which in Nabataean means "companion". He said to him:
"Leave this community of faith. You do not belong among its followers; your
task is purity of life and the subduing of the desires. But because of your
youth it is not yet time for you to come forward." When he had completed
his twenty-fourth year, the angel at-Tawm came to him again and said: "Now
the time has come for you to come forward openly and proclaim your own
teaching aloud."

The words that the angel at-Tawm spoke to him were these: "Greetings to
you, Mani, from me and from the Lord who has sent me to you and chosen you
for his mission. He commands you to call (people) to your teaching, and to
proclaim the glad promise of the truth that comes from him, and to give all
your zeal to it."

Mani, the Manichaeans relate, came forward openly on the day when Šābūr
son of Ardašīr came to the throne and set the crown on his head (it was a
Sunday, the first day of Nīsān, while the sun was in Aries), accompanied by
two men who followed him and were adherents of his teaching, the one named
Šamʿūn (Simeon), the other Zakū. His father also went with him, to see how
his new teaching would be received.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reports: Mani came forward in the second year of the
reign of the Roman Gallus, after Marcion had appeared about a hundred years
before him, in the reign of Titus Antoninus, in the first year of his rule,
and Ibn Daiṣān (Bardaisan) about thirty years after Marcion. Ibn Daiṣān got
his name from being born on a river called Daiṣān.

Mani claimed that he was the Paraclete whom Jesus, peace be upon him, had
announced. He drew his teaching from the Magians and the Christians, and in
the same way the script in which the (Manichaean) religious books were
written is borrowed from the Syriac and the Persian.

Before Mani had his meeting with Šābūr, he travelled through the lands for
about forty years, and after his return he invited Fīrūz, the brother of
Šābūr son of Ardašīr, to accept his teaching. Fīrūz also arranged Mani's
introduction to his brother Šābūr. And, the Manichaeans add, he came in to
him while on his shoulders two (things) shone like lamps of light. When
Šābūr saw him, he showed him great respect, and Mani grew in his esteem,
although he had resolved to seize him and kill him. But when he stood
before him, awe of him took hold of him, and he was glad of him and asked
him what he brought him, and even promised to be converted to him. Mani
asked him for a number of things, among them that his disciples should be
respected in Persia and in all the other lands of his kingdom, and that
they should be able to go wherever they wished. Šābūr granted him all that
he asked. Mani had also already called the Indians, the Chinese and the
people of Khorasan to accept his teaching, and had left one of his
disciples in each region.

> of the pestiferous land.

### The Father sends forth a deity

*On the Nature of Good* 42. Here Newman translates the earlier passage on
the realms of light independently:

> But His most resplendent realms were so founded upon the shining and happy
> land, that they could never be either moved or shaken by any one.
>
> …
>
> But the Father of the most blessed light, knowing that great ruin and
> desolation which would arise from the darkness, threaten his holy worlds,
> unless he should send in opposition a deity excellent and renowned, mighty
> in strength, by whom he might at the same time overcome and destroy the
> race of darkness, which having been extinguished, the inhabitants of light
> would enjoy perpetual rest.

### The fate of the souls that loved darkness

*On the Nature of Good* 42:

> … they have suffered themselves to err from their former bright nature …
>
> Those souls shall adhere to the things that they have loved, having been
> left in the same sphere of darkness, bringing this upon themselves by
> their own deserts.

---
title: "Mani quoted by Evodius: the Treasure and the Fundamental Epistle"
text: true
group: scripture
order: 25
summary: Passages of Mani's Treasure of Life (book II) and Fundamental Epistle quoted in Latin by Evodius of Uzalis, on the souls that refuse to be cleansed and are fixed in the "horrible globe", and on the crucifixion of the Prince of Darkness in the Saviour's place.
original_language: Latin (translated from Syriac)
source: 'Evodius of Uzalis, De fide contra Manichaeos (about 400), chapters 5, 7, 11–13 and 28, in the edition of J. Zycha, Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum 25.2 (Vienna 1892), pp. 951–964 (archive.org `CorpusScriptorumEcclesiasticorumLatin252`). New translation from the Latin.'
rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from the Latin of Zycha's edition, read from an OCR scan; not checked against another translation)."
---

## Introduction

Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in North Africa and a friend of Augustine, wrote
*On the Faith, against the Manichaeans* about the year 400. Like Augustine,
he quotes the Latin Manichaean books that circulated in Africa, and some of
his quotations are not found elsewhere: a sentence from the second book of
Mani's *Treasure of Life*, a fuller text of the Fundamental Epistle on the
fate of the souls that loved the world, and the Epistle's teaching that the
one crucified was not the Saviour but the Prince of Darkness.

Evodius also quotes, word for word, the long passage of the seventh book of
the *Treasure* on the "ships of light", which Augustine quotes too; it is on
the [Fundamental Epistle page](fundamental-epistle.html) and is not repeated
here.

**This translation is new and is a draft.** It is made directly from the
Latin of Zycha's edition (1892), read from an OCR scan and corrected by
sense; the Latin is itself a translation from Mani's Syriac. Evodius'
surrounding arguments are summarized in italics. Words in parentheses are
added for sense; [ … ] marks where Evodius breaks off with "and so on".

## The translation

### From the *Treasure of Life*, book II

*Evodius argues that even Mani had to admit that souls sin by their own
will: "for so he says in the second book of the Treasure":*

But those who, through their own negligence, have by no means allowed
themselves to be cleansed from the stain of the aforesaid spirits, and have
obeyed the divine commandments too little and not wholly, and have been
unwilling to keep more fully the law given them by their liberator, nor have
governed themselves as was fitting [ … ]

### From the Fundamental Epistle: the souls that loved the world

*"Again, in the Fundamental Epistle he says this of those souls":*

Those (souls) which, through love of the world, have allowed themselves to
stray from their former shining nature, and have become enemies of the holy
light, and have openly armed themselves for the destruction of the holy
elements, and have followed the fiery spirit, and with their hostile
persecution have also afflicted the holy church and the Elect set in it,
the keepers of the heavenly commandments, are kept away from the blessedness
and glory of the holy land. And because they have allowed themselves to be
overcome by evil, they will remain in that same stock of evil, that
peaceful land and the immortal regions being forbidden to them. This will

+summary: Passages of Mani's Treasure of Life (book II) and Fundamental Epistle quoted in Latin by Evodius of Uzalis, on the souls that refuse to be cleansed and are fixed in the "horrible globe", and on the crucifixion of the Prince of Darkness in the Saviour's place.
+original_language: Latin (translated from Syriac)

+source: 'Evodius of Uzalis, De fide contra Manichaeos (about 400), chapters 5, 7, 11–13 and 28, in the edition of J. Zycha, Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum 25.2 (Vienna 1892), pp. 951–964 (archive.org `CorpusScriptorumEcclesiasticorumLatin252`). New translation from the Latin.'
+rights: "New translation © Manichaean Scripture Compendium, CC BY 4.0. Review state: draft (made from the Latin of Zycha's edition, read from an OCR scan; not checked against another translation)."
+## Introduction
+Evodius, bishop of Uzalis in North Africa and a friend of Augustine, wrote
+*On the Faith, against the Manichaeans* about the year 400. Like Augustine,
+he quotes the Latin Manichaean books that circulated in Africa, and some of
+his quotations are not found elsewhere: a sentence from the second book of
+Mani's *Treasure of Life*, a fuller text of the Fundamental Epistle on the
+fate of the souls that loved the world, and the Epistle's teaching that the
+one crucified was not the Saviour but the Prince of Darkness.
+Evodius also quotes, word for word, the long passage of the seventh book of
+the *Treasure* on the "ships of light", which Augustine quotes too; it is on
+the [Fundamental Epistle page](fundamental-epistle.html) and is not repeated
+here.
+**This translation is new and is a draft.** It is made directly from the
+Latin of Zycha's edition (1892), read from an OCR scan and corrected by
+sense; the Latin is itself a translation from Mani's Syriac. Evodius'
+surrounding arguments are summarized in italics. Words in parentheses are
+added for sense; [ … ] marks where Evodius breaks off with "and so on".
+## The translation
+### From the *Treasure of Life*, book II
+*Evodius argues that even Mani had to admit that souls sin by their own
+will: "for so he says in the second book of the Treasure":*
+But those who, through their own negligence, have by no means allowed
+themselves to be cleansed from the stain of the aforesaid spirits, and have
+obeyed the divine commandments too little and not wholly, and have been
+unwilling to keep more fully the law given them by their liberator, nor have
+governed themselves as was fitting [ … ]
+### From the Fundamental Epistle: the souls that loved the world
+*"Again, in the Fundamental Epistle he says this of those souls":*
+Those (souls) which, through love of the world, have allowed themselves to
+stray from their former shining nature, and have become enemies of the holy
+light, and have openly armed themselves for the destruction of the holy
+elements, and have followed the fiery spirit, and with their hostile
+persecution have also afflicted the holy church and the Elect set in it,
+the keepers of the heavenly commandments, are kept away from the blessedness
+and glory of the holy land. And because they have allowed themselves to be
+overcome by evil, they will remain in that same stock of evil, that
+peaceful land and the immortal regions being forbidden to them. This will
+happen to them because they have so bound themselves with wicked works that
+they have been made strangers to the life and freedom of the holy light.
+They will not, then, be able to be received into those peaceful kingdoms,
+but will be fixed in the horrible globe spoken of before, over which a
+guard must also be set. So those same souls will cling to the things they
+have loved, being left in that same globe of darkness, winning this for
+themselves by their own deserts. For they did not care to learn of these
+things to come, nor did they separate themselves from them when time was
+given.
+*Evodius counts the phrases that show the will: "through their own
+negligence", "have by no means allowed", "have obeyed too little", "have
+been unwilling to keep", "have followed", "have allowed themselves to be
+overcome", "have bound themselves", "winning this for themselves by their
+own deserts", "they did not care to learn … nor did they separate
+themselves". He adds that "in the same epistle" Mani speaks of*
+the cut-off part of the light, that is, the sinful souls.
+### From the Fundamental Epistle: the kingdoms of light
+*Evodius quotes Mani's words that God is*
+abounding in all good things, nothing being lacking or set lowest among the
+splendours of his kingdoms; and his most splendid worlds are so founded
+that they can never be shaken or moved by anyone.
+*and that "a little later" he adds:*
+But the Father of the most blessed light, knowing that a great ruin and
+desolation, which would rise out of the darkness, threatened his holy
+worlds, unless he set against it some outstanding and renowned deity,
+mighty in strength, by which he might at once overcome and destroy the
+stock of darkness, so that, when it was put out, rest might be made ready
+for the dwellers in the light [ … ]
+*Evodius goes on to report two further passages without quoting them in
+full. At the end of the same epistle, he says, Mani writes that the part of
+God that has been mixed (with darkness) cannot all be called back to its
+former freedom. And in the first book of the* Treasure*, he says, it is
+written that the divine substance which Mani speaks of "is today subject to
+the race of darkness, as clay to the potter".*
+### From the Fundamental Epistle: the crucifixion
+*Evodius answers the Manichaean question "What would the Jews have done to
+Christ, if he had not wished to suffer at their hands?" by pointing out that,
+by Mani's own teaching, Christ had no flesh and suffered nothing from the
+Jews. "For so he says in the Fundamental Epistle":*
+For the enemy, who hoped that he had crucified the same Saviour, the father
+of the righteous, was himself crucified; at that time one thing was done and
+another shown. So the Prince of Darkness was fastened to the cross, and he
+it was who wore the crown of thorns, with his companions, and had the
+scarlet robe; he also drank the vinegar and gall which some have thought
+the Lord drank. And all that he (the Saviour) seemed to endure here was laid
+upon the leaders of the darkness, who were also wounded by the nails and
+the lance.
+## Notes to this edition
+- **"The horrible globe"** (Latin *globus*, Greek *bōlos*) is the mass in
+  which, at the end, the darkness and the souls that loved it are shut up
+  for ever. Compare the "grave … closed with a stone as big as the world" in
+  [al-Nadīm](al-nadim-teaching.html).
+- **"The cut-off part of the light"** (*lucis succisiva pars*): Evodius gives
+  only these words, with Mani's gloss "that is, the sinful souls".
+- **The crucifixion passage** is the Manichaean "docetic" teaching that the
+  Saviour did not suffer in a body of flesh; compare the Middle Persian
+  retelling of the Passion in [the Turfan fragments](turfan-passion.html),
+  which follows the Gospels closely.
+- **Evodius' text** also quotes the Acts of the apostles "written by
+  Leucius, which (the Manichaeans) accept", on "beautiful figments, feigned
+  show and the compulsion of visible things"; that is not by Mani and is not
+  given here.

### The different opinions of the Manichaeans about the leadership after Mani's death

The Manichaeans relate: When Mani was raised up into the Paradises of Light,
he appointed Sīs as leader (imam) after him, before he was raised up. Sīs
kept up the religion of God and its purity until he died, and the leaders
took over the religion one from another, without any difference of opinion
arising among them, until there came out of them a breakaway sect, known by
the name of the Dēnāwarīya, who found fault with their leader and refused
him obedience. The seat of the leader was held to be fully lawful only in
Babylon, and no leader was allowed to have his seat in another city. That
sect, however, contradicted this rule, and its followers kept up their
opposition, which it would be useless to describe further here, against it
and against other claims, until the whole leadership came to Mihr, which
happened under the reign of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, when Khālid ibn
ʿAbdallāh al-Qasrī was governor of Iraq.

Then a man named Zād-Hurmuz joined them; he stayed with them for a time,
but then left them. He was a man richly blessed with worldly goods. He
renounced them and turned to the class of the righteous (the Elect). But
there too he claimed to see things that he had to reject, and meant to go
over to the Dēnāwarīya, who had their seat beyond the river of Balkh. So he
came to al-Madāʾin, where there was a secretary of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf who
had great wealth. The two were on friendly terms, and Zād-Hurmuz told the
secretary of his plan, and of the reason that had driven him out of the
main community, and that he wanted to go to Khorasan to join the
Dēnāwarīya. The secretary said to him: "I am your Khorasan; I will build
you the temples and provide you with what you need." So he kept him with
him and built him the temples.

Zād-Hurmuz then wrote to the Dēnāwarīya to ask them for a leader whom he
could appoint. They wrote back that it was not lawful for the seat of the
head to be anywhere but in the middle of the kingdom, in Babylon. He then
asked around for someone fit for it, but no one was found except himself.
So he held the office himself; and when he saw his dissolution coming, that
is, when death drew near, they begged him to appoint them a leader. "That
is Miqlāṣ," he replied; "you know his worthy conduct; I am content with him
and trust his management for your good." When Zād-Hurmuz had died, they
unanimously handed the leadership to Miqlāṣ.

### The split of the Manichaeans into two sects, the Mihrīya and the Miqlāṣīya

Miqlāṣ departed from the main community even in matters of religion, for
example in the social ordinances, until Abū Hilāl ad-Dayḥūrī came from
Africa and the leadership of the Manichaeans passed to him, which happened
in the days of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr. He called on the followers of Miqlāṣ
to give up what Miqlāṣ had prescribed to them about the social ordinances,
and they obeyed him in this. Then, during this time, a man named Buzurgmihr
appeared among the Miqlāṣites; he made a number of them his followers and
brought in strange things as innovations. This state of things did not end
among them until the leadership came to Abū Saʿīd Raḥā. He brought them
back to the view of the Mihrīya about the social ordinances, and so their
faith and their state remained unchanged, until, under the caliphate of
al-Maʾmūn, a man appeared among them whose name, I think, was Yazdānbaxt
("God's fortune"). He was of another opinion in everything, and tried to win
them by cunning; and a small group among them inclined to him.

Among the things with which the Miqlāṣīya reproach the Mihrīya is that they
claim that Khālid al-Qasrī set Mihr on a mule, gave him a silver seal-ring
and dressed him in coloured clothes. The head of the Miqlāṣīya under the
reigns of al-Maʾmūn and al-Muʿtaṣim was Abū ʿAlī Saʿīd, who was followed
later by his secretary Naṣr ibn Hurmuzd of Samarqand. They allowed the
members of the sect, and those entering it, things forbidden in the
religion, kept company with the sultans and ate together with them. One of
their leaders was also Abū l-Ḥasan ad-Dimašqī (of Damascus).

### Mani's death, and his opinion of the prophets

Mani was killed under the reign of Bahrām son of Šābūr; and when this had
been done, he had him crucified and hung up in two halves, each half at a
different gate of the city of Jundaišābūr; the two places are called the
upper Mar (passage) and the lower Mar. Others relate that Šābūr shut him in
a prison, and that when Šābūr died, Bahrām (?) freed him from it. Others
again: on the contrary, he died in prison. But that he was crucified is
beyond doubt. According to some he had turned-in legs; according to others
only the right leg was turned in.

Mani treated all the prophets disrespectfully in his books, belittled them,
accused them of lying and claimed that devils had taken hold of them and
spoke out of their mouths; indeed in some places in his books he says
outright that they were devils. ʿĪsā (Jesus), who is held in high honour
among us and the Christians, he claims was a devil.

"""One-off: insert al-Nadim on the leadership, Mani's death and the prophets before the life-to-come section."""
p = 'docs/texts/al-nadim-teaching.md'
t = open(p, encoding='utf-8').read()
sec = open('scratch/nadim4.md', encoding='utf-8').read()
a = '### The teaching of the Manichaeans on the life to come'
assert a in t
t = t.replace(a, sec + a, 1)
R = [
    ('pp. 83–95 and 100–101 (archive.org', 'pp. 83–95 and 97–101 (archive.org'),
    ('- **The Humāma**',
     "- **The leadership after Mani** (pp. 97–99): this part is al-Nadīm's\n  history of the Manichaean church under the Umayyads and Abbasids. Mani's\n  successor *Sīs* is Mār Sīsin (see the [Hymnscroll](hymnscroll.html),\n  hymn 3); the *Dēnāwarīya* are the eastern Manichaeans of Transoxania.\n- **\"Jesus … a devil\"**: al-Nadīm's report is hostile. The Manichaean texts\n  distinguish the divine Jesus, whom they praise, from the Jesus of the\n  Jews; compare the Fundamental Epistle on the crucifixion, quoted by\n  [Evodius](evodius-quotations.html).\n- **The Humāma**"),
]
for x, y in R:
    assert x in t, x[:50]
    t = t.replace(x, y, 1)
open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(t)

p = 'devlog.md'
s = open(p, encoding='utf-8').read().rstrip('\n')
s += "\n- 2026-10-21 `al-nadim-teaching`: added al-Nadīm on the leadership after Mani (Sīs, the Dēnāwarīya, Mihr, Miqlāṣ), Mani's death and his opinion of the prophets (Flügel pp. 97–100). print('ok')

happened under the reign of al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, when Khālid ibn

but then left them. He was a man richly blessed with worldly goods. He
renounced them and turned to the class of the righteous (the Elect). But
there too he claimed to see things that he had to reject, and meant to go
over to the Dēnāwarīya, who had their seat beyond the river of Balkh. So he

secretary of his plan, and of the reason that had driven him out of the
main community, and that he wanted to go to Khorasan to join the

unanimously handed the leadership to Miqlāṣ.

Miqlāṣ departed from the main community even in matters of religion, for
example in the social ordinances, until Abū Hilāl ad-Dayḥūrī came from
Africa and the leadership of the Manichaeans passed to him, which happened
in the days of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr. He called on the followers of Miqlāṣ

faith and their state remained unchanged, until, under the caliphate of

### From the history of the Manichaeans: their emigrations and their leaders

The first who, apart from the Samanians (the Buddhists), went into the
cities beyond the Oxus belonged to the Manichaean sects. The reason was
this. After the Chosroes had had Mani killed and crucified, and had
forbidden the people of his kingdom to engage in religious disputes, he
began to put to death the followers of Mani wherever he found them. So they
kept fleeing from him until they had crossed the river of Balkh and come
into the territory of the Khan, in whose lands they settled. "Khan" in the
language of that country is a title by which the people call the princes of
the Turks.

After the Manichaeans had settled in Transoxania, (they stayed there) until
the time when the power of the Persians was scattered to the winds and the
Arabs gained the upper hand. Then they came back into the cities of Iraq,
chiefly at the time of the break-up of the Persians and under the rule of
the Umayyads. For Khālid ibn ʿAbdallāh al-Qasrī took them under his
protection; only the seat of the head in these regions was bound solely to
Babylon. Later the leader moved to the cities where he was safest.

A second time they emigrated under the reign of al-Muqtadir. They went to
Khorasan, fearing for their lives, and those of them who stayed behind hid
their beliefs and wandered about in these cities. In Samarqand about five
hundred men had come together. Their worship became known, and the ruler of
Khorasan wanted to kill them. Then the ruler of China (I think it was the
prince of the Toquz Oγuz) sent to him the message: "In my lands there are
three times more Muslims than there are followers of my religion in your
lands," and swore to him that if he killed one of them, he would kill the
whole community (of Muslims) for him, destroy the mosques, and set people in
all the lands to lie in wait for the Muslims and kill them. So the ruler of
Khorasan left them alone, and had them pay the poll-tax.

In the lands of Islam there are only a few of them. In the City of Peace
(Baghdad) I came to know about three hundred of them under the reign of
Muʿizz ad-Dawla; but at the present time hardly more than five of them are
to be found in the capital. These Manichaeans are called Ājārī, and they
live in the villages of Samarqand and Sogdia, and above all in Nūnkaṯ.

*(Al-Nadīm then lists the "heads" of the Manichaeans under the Abbasids and
before, beginning with al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, the tutor of the caliph Marwān;
the list is of Muslims accused of Manichaean heresy and is not given here.)*

### From the history of the Manichaeans: their emigrations and their leaders

The first who, apart from the Samanians (the Buddhists), went into the
cities beyond the Oxus belonged to the Manichaean sects. The reason was
this. After the Chosroes had had Mani killed and crucified, and had
forbidden the people of his kingdom to engage in religious disputes, he
began to put to death the followers of Mani wherever he found them. So they
kept fleeing from him until they had crossed the river of Balkh and come
into the territory of the Khan, in whose lands they settled. "Khan" in the
language of that country is a title by which the people call the princes of
the Turks.

After the Manichaeans had settled in Transoxania, (they stayed there) until
the time when the power of the Persians was scattered to the winds and the
Arabs gained the upper hand. Then they came back into the cities of Iraq,
chiefly at the time of the break-up of the Persians and under the rule of
the Umayyads. For Khālid ibn ʿAbdallāh al-Qasrī took them under his
protection; only the seat of the head in these regions was bound solely to
Babylon. Later the leader moved to the cities where he was safest.

A second time they emigrated under the reign of al-Muqtadir. They went to
Khorasan, fearing for their lives, and those of them who stayed behind hid
their beliefs and wandered about in these cities. In Samarqand about five
hundred men had come together. Their worship became known, and the ruler of
Khorasan wanted to kill them. Then the ruler of China (I think it was the
prince of the Toquz Oγuz) sent to him the message: "In my lands there are
three times more Muslims than there are followers of my religion in your
lands," and swore to him that if he killed one of them, he would kill the
whole community (of Muslims) for him, destroy the mosques, and set people in
all the lands to lie in wait for the Muslims and kill them. So the ruler of
Khorasan left them alone, and had them pay the poll-tax.

In the lands of Islam there are only a few of them. In the City of Peace
(Baghdad) I came to know about three hundred of them under the reign of
Muʿizz ad-Dawla; but at the present time hardly more than five of them are
to be found in the capital. These Manichaeans are called Ājārī, and they
live in the villages of Samarqand and Sogdia, and above all in Nūnkaṯ.

*(Al-Nadīm then lists the "heads" of the Manichaeans under the Abbasids and
before, beginning with al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, the tutor of the caliph Marwān;
the list is of Muslims accused of Manichaean heresy and is not given here.)*

---

## Introduction

Severus, patriarch of Antioch (512–518), devoted his 123rd Cathedral
Homily to refuting the Manichaeans, and to do so he quoted at length "one
of the books (of Mani) of which one should not speak", which another
version calls "one of his secret books". The Greek is lost, but the homily
survives in two Syriac translations, by Paul of Callinicum and by Jacob of
Edessa. Kugener and Cumont edited the Syriac and translated it into French
in 1912. The quotations are Mani's own words in their oldest form outside
the Coptic and Iranian texts: the two eternal principles pictured as the
Tree of Life and the Tree of Death, the Tree of Death divided against
itself, and the rising of the powers of darkness to the border of the land
of light, which made the "mixture" necessary.

**This translation is a draft.** It is made from Kugener and Cumont's
French, which follows Jacob of Edessa's version; their notes on Paul's
variant readings are not reproduced. Only the quotations of Mani are given;
Severus' commentary between them is summarized in italics.

## The translation

*Severus: "He says, in one of his books which one should not speak of, or
rather which are worthy of darkness and error, the following":*

### The Tree of Life

As for the things that exist perpetually and at all times from the
beginning, he (Mani) speaks of Matter and of God, each of them existing by
its nature. So exists the Tree of Life, which is adorned there with all its
beauties and splendours, which is filled and clothed with all its goods,
and (which is) firm and stable in its nature.

Its land holds three regions: that of the North, which is outside and
below, and the East and the West, (which are likewise) outside and below.
And below, there is nothing that is plunged or clothed by it in any of the
regions; but the infinite is outside and below. There is no foreign body
around or below the infinite, nor in any place of these three regions; but
it (the Tree of Life) is of itself below and outside, to the North, the
East and the West. And nothing surrounds it or encloses it in these three
regions, but it is in itself, of itself, enclosing in itself its fruits;
and the kingdom is in it.

*Severus says that Mani then adds, "after many endless follies", about the
good (Tree):*

It is not seen in the southern region, and that because it is hidden in
what is in its bosom. For God has surrounded this place with a wall.

*And he adds other things:*

Its light and its goodness (of the Tree of Life, or the good Tree) are not
visible, so that it may not give an occasion of desire to the Evil Tree
which is in the South, and may not be for it an occasion of being excited,
tormented and put in danger. But it is enclosed in the glory, and gives no
occasion, because of its goodness. It has protected itself in its justice,
and it is in this glory, while being continually in the nature of its
greatness in the three regions.

### The Tree of Death

And the Tree of Death has no life by its nature, and has no fruits of
goodness on any of its branches. And it is continually in the southern
region. And it has also a place of its own, (namely) that which is above
it.

*Severus: "First they say this about the same Matter":*

The Tree of Death is divided into a great number (of trees); war and
cruelty are in them; they are strangers to peace, filled with complete
wickedness, and never have good fruits. It (the Tree of Death) is divided
against its fruits, and the fruits (are divided) against the Tree; they are
not united to the one who begot them, but all produce the moth for the
corruption of their place; they are not subject to the one who begot them,
but the whole Tree is evil; it never does anything good, but it is divided
against itself, and each of its parts corrupts what is near it.

*Severus notes that these are a series of extracts set side by side rather
than one continuous passage.*

### The rising of the members of darkness

*Severus: "They have also written these violent things":*

These things concern Matter, its fruits and its members. But the occasion
of rising up to the worlds of Light was given them by their rebellion. For
these members of the Tree of Death did not know one another and had no
notion of one another. For each of them knew nothing more than its own
voice, and they saw (only) what was before their eyes. When one (of them)
cried out, they heard (it). They perceived that, and they rushed with
violence towards the voice. They knew nothing else. So they were stirred
and driven on by one another to go as far as the borders of the glorious
land of Light. When they saw the sight (of the Light), wonderful and
splendid, which is far above their own, then they gathered together, that
is, the dark Matter, and they plotted against the Light, so as to mix with
it. They did not know, in their folly, that a powerful and strong God
dwelt there. So they sought to climb and to rise, because they had never
heard of the divinity, or had (never) understood who it was.

[ … ] (they were seized) with desire for the sight of those blessed worlds,
and they thought that it would become theirs. All the [ … ] corrupting
(Matter) rose up, then, and climbed with countless powers, whose number
cannot be told. All were clothed with the matter of fire. And these
members were different. For some had hard bodies and were of infinite
size; the others, bodiless and intangible, had a subtle tangibility, like
the demons and the spectres of phantoms. After rising, the whole of Matter
climbed, with its winds, its storms, its waters, its demons, its phantoms,
its princes and its powers, all searching carefully how they might get into
the Light.

### Why the mixture was needed

Because of the agitation that was stirred up from the depths against the
Land of Light and against the holy fruits, it was necessary that a portion
of the Light should come and mix with these Evil Ones, so that the enemies
might be caught by means of the mixture, that there might be peace for the
Good, that the nature of the Good might be preserved, [ … ] that, on the
other hand, the Shining Ones might be rid of Matter by the power that had
been mixed (with it), so that Matter might be destroyed and the Tree of Life
might become God in all and over all. For in the world of Light there is no
burning fire that could be hurled against Evil, there is no cutting iron,
there are no choking waters, nor any other such evil thing. For all there
is light and noble region, and it cannot harm it; but there is this way
out, that is, this means, so that the enemies, scattered by the portion
broken off from the Light, may stop their onrush and be caught by means of
the mixture.

*Severus' homily goes on to refute these passages at length, quoting some of
them again; those repetitions are not given here.*

## Notes to this edition

- **Which book?** Severus does not name it. Scholars have suggested Mani's
  *Pragmateia* or the *Book of Mysteries*, but this is a guess; the list of
  Mani's books is on [a separate page](al-nadim-books.html).
- **Three regions**: the Tree of Life fills the North, East and West, and is
  limited only on the South, where the Tree of Death is. Severus mocks the
  idea that the infinite God should be bounded and need a wall.
- **"The moth"** (Greek *sēs*): the fruits of the Tree of Death breed the
  moth that destroys them, as moths destroy wool.
- **Compare** the same myth in [al-Nadīm](al-nadim-teaching.html) (the two
  principles and the rising of Satan to the border of the light) and in the
  [Fundamental Epistle](fundamental-epistle.html) (the Father sends forth a
  deity against the darkness).
